BOBBY SHAFT°. The following short poem, recently published by Daniel Henry, Inn,, in a volume entitled 'tinder a Boors Cap." is suggested by a wall-known Northumbrian rhyme : Bobby Staifto's gone to sco— ff-Byer buckles on his knee— He'll come back and marry me, Pretty Booby Shaft° With his treasures won at sea, Spanish gold and Portngee, , Aid his heart, still fast to me, Pretty Bobby Shafto ! In a captain's pomp and pride, With a gold sword by his side, Zell come back to claim his bride, Pretty Bobby Shafto! So she sang, the winter long, Till the sun came, golden-strong, And the blue-birds oanght her song! AR of Bobby Shaf to. Days went by, and autumn came, Eyes grew dim, and feet went lame, But the song, it was the same, All of Bobby Shaft°. Never came across the sea, Silver boAles on his knee, Bobby to his bride-to-be, Fickle Bobby Shaf to! For where midnight never dies, In the Scorn King'a caves of ice, Stiff and stark, poor Bobby lies— Htrgbo ! P.obbv Shafto !

EASTER WINGS. A shower of roses on a happy head From hands beloved: the wintry day Grew sweet as summers fled. "And shall be aye," . We said. Row bright Their bloom, how brief; Long had it passed from sight, When higher 11;e woke 'oeath one withered leaf, Spread golden wings, and floated into light. So Love is born. Joy is its rosy bower, In whose delight we say, "Ah, this Is Love's own perfect flower, Its fullest bliss And power ! lint deep Lie precious things. Joy's soul is still asleep. Earth fades, then open heavenly wings: And this is Love, if Love be ours to keep. —Harper's Monthly. •

"Oh, I see," said the Bishop, "composition and decotnposition!" briernstrtnwo BA:ITLONIAN INSCRIPTION. —GRANT By KING NESUCHADIMLZAR.—Among the inscriptions brought home by Mr. liasean: from his explorations at Aboo flubba is one of peculiar interest, which has formed the subject of a translation by Messrs. Pinches and Badge, of the British Museum. The inscription is engraved on a conical block of white marble, and is in almost perfect preservation. The • front face of the stone is covered with a quaint and valuable series of demonological and astrological emblems, such as figures of the serpent, crab, scorpion bull, two-h^aded dog, and a remarkable compound figure of a scorpion sagittarins. The monument dates from the 12th century before Christ, and is a grant of certain civic and viceregal rights to a man named Riti-Merodach over the city of Bit-Karziyabku by King Nebuchadnezzar 1., who seems to have been a usurper, as hie father's name does not appear in the inscription. Early in his reign a remarkable cornet appeared, whicia, according to a tablet in the British Museum, iii said to hate had a tail like a scorpion. Upon this omen the King march4li to obtain satisfaction for certain border forays on the Kints I of Elam and South Kurdistan. It is thought that the curl- oqs above referred to—the scorpion sagittarius,which is placed as if marching before the King—is intended for a representation of this comet. The expedition suffered greatly from want of water, and met apparently with a seri- ous reverse in a battle fought on the banks of the Mai, the modern Disful. The army was saved from total defeat by the assistance of Riti-Merodach, who burned his city and destroyed the bridges so as to hinder the advance of the ererey. In return for this timely succour the Babylonian King made his friend ruler of the district, free from all , taxes of tribute. This inscription is the largest' historical ; document of aticient Babylonia which has been recovered,' • and its importance even in ancient times is curiously proved by the fact that there was obtained from Nineveh a small fragment of a duplicate copy of the inscription made by -order of King Aesurbanipal 500 years after the original locument was written. On a certain occasion one of his friends having lamed that an agent of the Post-office Department and a " drummer" were in the village—the former to collect what was due to the Government from Lincoln, as Postmaster, the latter to receive from him, as trader, what he was owing the firm re- presented by himself—and knowing Lincoln was never over- burdened with spare funds, went to the store and offered to lend him a sum sufficient to meet the claims he was so soon to be called upon to settle. "You ere very kind," said Lin- -coin, "butt do not think I shall require your assistance." Within a few minutes the age nt entered their presence, and Lincoln took an old stocking from a drawer, out of which he DOured a lot of copper and silver coin—the latter mostly In pieces of small denv„illation. "There is the very money have taken on acce unt of the Post-office," he remarked to the agent," and think you will find it the exact amount due to you." I', was, to a cent. This business had hardly been conclude d, when in came the "drummer." Lincoln had recourse. to another old stocking, with a similar result. So soon a", the two were again by themselves the friend said, I 50p pose, were a third creditor to present himself a third Vocking would enable you to settle with him," smil- ing- "Yea," returned the fatnr,. President. "Look here." •arlo be held up three stockings. "In each of these is the sum ;le severally owe to three parties, the only persons in the World to whom I am pecuniarily indebted. I see you are amused at my method of transacting business. I never al- low myself to use money that is not mine, however sorely pressed I may be, and I intend to be prepared to pay my bills when they become due without delay or inconvenience to those whom I owe. The simple system which I have adopted—using a stocking to represent each creditor and placing in it the money, to be passed to the creditor himself at some future day—renders the former unnecessary and the latter possible."—lndianapolis Sentinel. 11E-nonernn er 7:117, INDUSTRIAL CLASSES—Henry Sally writes on this subject to the British Quarterly:—His views are embodied in general terms in the following paragraph: —We venture to th,r.ir the. cause of cv wding and all its !exalts is not so very difficult to find, nor even (the far harder _task) AO very difficult for an Ezglish community to ' without number F- •" s been

Thi root of the mischief undoubtedly is to be found in the twofold necessity—first, that the labouring classes should have work to do if they would live; and secondly, that they should live near their work. The first need brings them in shoals to Loudon and gi•eat citiea Lecanee there Is no work for them on the land, until rural villages seem half depopulated; while the second crowds them together ia filthy dens in any neighbourhood where work, or charity, or instruction in the art of thieving is to be had. "You say the officer arrested you while you were quietly minding your own business ?" said a New York Judge to the 1 prisoner before him. "Yes, your honour; he caught me i suddenly by the coat collar, and threatened to strike me with his club unless I accompanied him to the station- house." "You were quietly attending to your own busi- ness,l nese making no noise or disturbance of any kind 2" "None ' whatever, sir." "It seems very strange. What is your business?" "I'm a burglar." I doctor, attending the other day a worthy baronet, received by mistake as his fee a couple of mint lozenges rolled up in paper. In the evening, the baronet found the sovereign and shilling in his pocket, in lieu of the mint lozenges, and on meeting the doctor, asked him how he liked his fee. "Oh, it was very sweet," was the reply. The real fee was soon after presented, enclosed with the follow- ing : The fee was sweet—l thank you for the hint. Theis are as sweet; they've both been through the Mint. A bashful young man went three times to ask a beautiful y ming lady if he might be the partner of her joys and sor- ; lows sal other household furniture; but each time his heart f tiled him, and he took the question away unpopped. She saw the anguish of his soul, and had compassion on him. 5, next time he came, she asked him if he had thought to bring as trewdriver with him. He blushed and wanted to know for what. And she, in the fulness of her heart, said she did not know but that he would want to screw up his courage before he left. He took the hint and the girl. A NEW SHRIMP.—In aa account of the zoological r tsults of the work of the United States Fish Commisßion, commu- nicated to Nature, by 13.-dph S. Tarr, is the following appe- tising passage :—" Crustacea were represented by many new ' and interesting forms, especially of shrimps, including many curious types. In 2,300 fathoms we dredged a shrimp nearlg a foot in length." Can we transplant and aeclima. tise these? Temperature presents no difficulty, as the water at that depth is quite as cold as upon our coasts. It must be only a question of pressure, and these delicious cra3ncekshould rather expand than contract when that is diminished, That Gravesend luxury, "Tea made with shrimps," will become a very substantial meal when these are substituted for our familiar pigmies.—Gentleman's Magazine.

Goorexon-Noxisinets.—On hailing a cab in a London street, it is surprising how generally the door is officiously opened by one-who expects to get something for his trouble. The surprise lessens after counting the many loungers about tavern doors, or after observing the quickness with which a street performance, or procession, draws from neighbouring slams and stable-yards a group of idlers. Seeing how numerous they are in every small area, it becomes manifest that tens of thousands of each swarm through London. They have no work," you say. Say rather that they either refuse work or quickly turn themselves out of it. They tre pimply good-for-nothings, who, in one way or other, live on the good-for-somethings—vagrants and sots, criminals and those on the way to crime, youths who are burdens on hard-worked parents, men who appropriate the wages of their wives, fellows who share the gains of pros- titutes ; and then, less visible:and less numerous, there is a corresponding class of women. Is it natural that happiness should be the lot of such? Or is it natural that they should bring unhappiness on themselves and those connected with them? Is it not manifest that there must exist in our midst an immense amount of misery which is a normal result of misconduct, and ought not to be dissociated from it? There is a notion, always more or less prevalent, and just now vociferously expressed, that all social suffering is removable, and that it is the duty of somebody or other to remove it. Both these beliefs are false. To separate pain from ill-doing is to fight against the constitution of things, and will be followed by far more pain. Saving men from the natural penalties of reckless living eventually neces- sitates the infliction of artificial penalties in solitary cells, on tread-wheels, and by the lash. I suppose a dictum on 'which the chrrent creed and the creed of science are at one may be considered to have as high an authority as can be found. Well; the command "if any would not work neither should he eat," is simply a Christian enunciation of that universal law of Nature under which life has reached its present height—the law that a creature not energetic enough to maintain itself must die; the sole difference being that the law which in the one case is to be artificially enforced, is in the ether case a natural necessity. And yet this parti- cular tenet of their religion which silence so manifestly justifies is the one which Christians seem least inclined to accept. The current assumption is that there should be no suffering, and that society is to blame for that which exists. —Herbert Spencer, in "Contemporary Review" for April. LITERARY MEN AND MARRIAGE—Soon after I took my degree I married. It was delicately said by a friend that, but for my intention so to do, I should have read for honours and distinguished myself; for what was the use of ' gaining a fellowship (and taking it away from some poor 1 fellow who really wanted it) to lose it the next year or so by matrimony? Success, however (when I think of that raegas business), seems hardly to have been a certainty, and ; it may be even thought by some people that I did not I sacrifice much academical distinction on the altar. I am I only setting down some reminiscences more or less in con- nection with literature, so I say nothing about my mar- riage. If I were. writing an autobiography, I should have to say a great deal about it, or else leave out the source and cause of the happinesi of my life. I may remark, however, to those who propose to themselves a literary life, and eau find a wife one-tenth as good as has fallen to my lot, that they had better make sure of her early; for of a truth they will need a comforter. There is,'no calling; it is true, so bright and pleasant, so full of genial friendship, as well as of far-off but todching sympathies, so radiant with the glories of success; but there is also no pursuit so doubtful, so fall of risks, so subject to despondency and disappoint- ments, so open to despair itself. It will not be denied that I have confessed to ignorance enough, but I know a few things well, and this is one of them. Oh! my young Mead with a "turn for literature," think twice and thrice before committing yourself to it; or you may bitterly regret to ind yourself where that "turn" may take you. Let every man be fully satisfied in his own mind, and have a reason for the faith that is in him. The calling (though by no means a phenomenal one, as it is the custom to assert) is an exceptional one, and even at the best you will have trials and, troubles of which you dream not, and to which no other ailing is exposed. I say again, verily you will need a com- forter, and the best af comforters is she who sits by the hearth at home. Nevertheless, I need scarcely add, however confident you may be of winning .your way to fame and fortune, be not so selfish as to link yoar fate with hers upon the prospects of an untried pen. For, if you do so, eve' though you have genius, it will be the genius that is allied to madness. One indirect but important advantage to a man of letters in early marriage is that, if a happy one, it rescues him from Bohemianistn. It is a charming "ism," and he who has not a strain of it in his character is to be pitied; but it is but an " ism"—a branch of dissent, and not the Catholic and Universal Church of Humanity.— Corn/nil. A PAIR OF SIMPLETONS.—Not the least amusing feature of some simpleton stories is the credit for superior sagacity which the "heroes" take to themselves- after performing an exploit of superior folly. This Arabian anecdote may serve for an example :—A silly fellow, observing one morning that his house was ready to tumble about his ears from decay, and being without the means of repairing it, went with a long face to his wife, and informed her of his trouble. Now, the wife was just about as big a noodle as himself, so she says—" Why, my dear, need you distress yourself about so small a matter? You have a cow worth thirty dirhems; take her to the market and sell her for that sum. I have some thread, which I will dispose of today, and I warrant you between us both we shall manage very well." The man at once drove the cow to the market, and gave her over for sale to the public appraiser of cattle. The salesman showed her to the bystanders, directed their attention to all her good points, expatiated on her numerous good qualities, and, in short, passed her off as a cow of inestimable value. To all this the simpleton listened with delight and astonishment; he heard his cow praised for qualities that no other cow could ever possess, and determined in his own mind not to lose to rare a bargain but purchase her himself and baulk the chapman. He therefore called oat to the appraiser and asked him what she was going at; he replied, at fifteen , &silents and upwards. "By the head of the Prophet," said the wiseacre, "had I known before that my cow was such a pnodigy of excellence, you should not have caught me with , her in the market for sale." Now, It happened that he had just fifteen dirhems and no more, and these he thrust upon the broker, exclaiming." The cow is mine ; I have the best claim to her. He then seized the cow and drove her home, , exulting all the way as if he had found a treasure. On reaching home he inquired eagerly after his wife, to inform her of his adventure, but was told she was not returned from market. He waited impatiently for her return, when he sprang up to meet her, exclaiming, "Wife, I have done something to-day that I believe will astonish you I have performed a most marvellous exploit." "Patience," says the wife, "perhaps I have done something myself to match it. But hear my story, and then talk of cleverness if you please." The husband desired her to proceed. "When I went to market I found a man in want of thread. I showed him mine, which he approved of, and having bargained for it, he agreed to pay me according to the weight. I told him it weighed so much, which he seemed to discredit, and weighed it himself. Observing it to fall short of the weight I had mentioned, and fearing I should lose the price I at first expected, I requested him to weigh it over again, and make certein. In the meantime, taking an opportunity unobserved, I stripped off my bracelets, and put them slyly into the scale with my thread. The scale' of course, preponderated, and I received the full price I had demanded." Having finished her story, she cried oat, "Now, what think you of your Wits?" NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, Bre. •Mr. James Howard, M.P., Clapham Park, Bedfordshire, I has had the misfortune to lose, through inflammation in 'ithe feet, the beautiful two-year-old Shire filly for which he ,Ipaid 145 guineas as a yearling at the Waltham sale. A great loss has been sustained by Mr. F. Barchard, of Horsted, Sussex. Three precious bulls—one a polled Aber- deen Angus, of the Erica tribe, recently purchased at a long figure from Sir G. Macpherson Grant, M.P., and the other shorthorns, members of the Wild Eyes and Oxford strains respectively—have been suffocated in a fire which broke out on the Home Farm.
COMPULSORY SrAtrouTEß.—A great step in favour of ' slaughter WAS gained when the Central Chamber of Agri- culture, at its last meeting, agreed to the following resolu- .. „ . .

tion This Council wo—uleview with favour proposals for compulsory isolation and disinfection, and proposals for compulsory slaughter, with adequate compensation." Thii precisely expresses the proper view of the case, and the heads of the Agricultural Department, who have expressed themselves in favour of slaughter under such circumstarses as Mr. Howard limits it to, would do well to ponder over the advantage to be gained by such a measure as would in- duce stockowners to consent to what is by far the cheapest, as it is the only effectual, means of getting rid of an out- break at the very ontset.--/Ifark-lane Express. Tint TREATMENT or MANGELS.—Daring this very mild and forward season farmers should carefully look to their mangel heaps, by throwing off all the dirt and straw cover- ing, then cause to be cleaned off the small rootlets, for nearly every root will be found to have some small ones growing on them, similar to potatoes when placed in a dark and warm cellar, and which very much weaken the plant

then stacking them afresh. The gain will be found far beyond the expense, as mangels during the slimmer months, after they have been thoroughly dried by the sun and wind, are very serviceable to cattle of all sorts wished to be pushed on; they also will save much horse corn, being better and heartier than tares or clover, and very much safer feed A friend, a large farmer, has made it an invariable rule for many years to have his mangels one year under the other. By following tbie simple plan, and by occasionally turning them, they will keep well. USEFUL AND ORNAMENTAL—When at Underley the other day, a calf-house, in which Mr. Punchard had contrived to embody the useful and ornamental, excited a good deal of attention. The farm buildings, large as they are, had be- come full, and it was found necessary to extend into the park. An prdinary calf-house would have formed an eyesore, so, in place thereof, there has arisen an ornamental Chinese pagoda, with tiled roofs of various colours. The building is sept- angular, accommodating seven yearling heifers. Each calf- space is heater, or triangular shaped. rhe roof of the pagoda comprises the hayloft, and in the centre of the building is a septangular pillar, on each base of which is the hayrack, and beneath this the trough for the calves. The hay is plashed down the pillar from the hayloft. From its general appearance, it seems to comprise the essentials of utility and ornament, and probably will have been erected as cheaply, if not at less cost than on ordinary building. Possibly the above description may be of use on other estates where an eyesore to the landscape is sought to be avoided. ENSILAGE.—Sir J. B. Lawes, wit° is disposed to question the advantage of ensilage—from mere theory and hearsay evidence apparently—may be recommended to read the re- port of the third Ensilage Congress, in the current number of the 'American Agricultural Review. Mr, Mayer, super- intendent of Mr. Havermeyer's Farm, at Mahwah, New Jersey, endorsed his employer's statement to tin; effect that with the silos now on the farm he could "keep 15 times as many cows on the same acres as be eould before he had them" (the silos). This is rathena "tall" statement, and unless Mr. Havermeyer was drawing upon his imagination, one cantata think that he made a little mistake. Several speakers testi- fied to the excellence of both milk and butter from cows fed on ensilage. One gentleman had 3,200 tons of ensilage, and he declared that if anyone had failed in using it, the reason must have been that it was used improperly. On the other hand, it was stated that at a condensed milk factory (after two years' use of ensilage milk), there were com- plaints of the milk not keeping so well as formerly, and milk from farmers who fed their cows on ensilage was de- clined. So convinced were some of the farmers who sup- plied the factory of the value of enailage, however, that seven out of 15 preferred to give up their connection with the factory rather than their silos. Another piece of ad. verse evidence was as to the death of horses from eating en- silage. This Dr. Baxter attributed to suffocation from stomach worms, driven to the throat by the acidity of the ensilage. The writer of the report insists on the necessity of rapidly filling silos, to avoid heating. The super-silos used by Mr. Henry Woods are essential to the complete filling of silos in one operation. Again, if rapid filling be important, silos should not be very large, except where the farm staff is a powerful one. Mr. Robert Fonlis, of Caimie Lodge, Fifeshire, who has written a pamphlet de- scribing his experience in making and using ensilage, de- clares not only that there is a great increase in the milk of cows fed on ensilage, bat that the better is "like the best summer butter." One point is pretty well certain: ensilagy Of I may coin a word, like others, in this connection) milk and butter cannot be worse than ternipy milk and butter. lOn cold, heavy land, as pointed out by "An Essex farmer" in a pamphlet he has just published, ensilage promises to be / particularly useful; for on such laud turnips do not thrive, ! mangels are expensive on such land, and sheep-folding can be practised only in summer, so that there is much difficulty in keeping sufficient stock to supply the requisite amount of
manure.

CHINESE Lawn.—The living are rather regarded by the Chinese as the economists of posterity. They used at one time to confiscate neglected lands. In reality, the only pro- perty in the soil is in China the right to the fruits of it, and it is only that right that can be transmitted or alien- ated. It is what the Chinese call the " tiennmienn;" the property of the land itself " tienn-ti " remains in the hands of the nation, as represented by the Government, and the latter affirms its right in fixing a rent, which it alone re- ceives. Thus., when a landowner sells or lets an estate, the price paid or the rent received never represents more than the value which he and his ancestors have, by their labour, Incorporated and added. It is necessary, on the other hand, to say that the State never thinks that it has a right to In- crease the rent in proportion as the value of the land is in- creased by the labour of the tenants. The rent of the land, has been established, not from its value, but from its area, and this, once fixed, ha e never been changed This rent is nearly the only tax in China. Such is the respect for labour and for its fruits that the State will not for any considera- tion augment the rent nor create new taxes which may tend to diminish indnetry. It is true that the rent (be the same little or be it much) is paid out of the produce of labour. and it is with this that the State has been able to carry out and maintain its great works, comprising canals, sewers, do., which have since permitted and facilitated the development of private labour. The other resources of the Empire com- prehend the revenues from the Cestilms, mines, and the salt monopoly. The Emperor's revenues, which make up his civil list. come partly from the salt duties, by his Mongolian flocks and by the tribute from the vassals of China. I have just said that the rent was fixed on the amount of area (not on the value of the land), but it is necessary also to say that accinnt has been taken of the possibility of great land im- provements becoming realised For instance, the lands of the plains and the non-irrigable mountain lands pay a smaller rent than those easily watered, and lands recovered from the water are for a while exempt from taxation until they enter one of the four principal great classes, but there is no other base of classification. It can be said, to sum up, that the Chinese State, after having managed the territory for the greatest public benefit, acts as a landlord, who, after having divided hie house into floors, fixes his rents accord- ing to the respective advantages of these floors, without troubling himself about the means or the occupations of those to whom he lets them. The rent of land varies in a classification extending front 7d. to 2s. the acre, including repairs of highways, land tax, and other payments. This represents an average of not more than 2s. 6d. per head of the whole population. So, for that small sum, when it is once paid, every Chinese is absolutely free to undertake any form of industry or trade which pleases him, and to go where he likes.' He has no taxes on doors or windows, no license excise or Customs duties to pay; he has no formali- ties to fulfil, no license to take out, no impediments to fear; he is free as the air of which he breathes so freely. I may say in truth that this single impost is the instrument of securing his liberty. All other taxes are considered by Chinese as unlawful inroads on the rights of labour, and no- thing astonishes them more than to hear that they exist in other countries. BEET Struau ENTERPRISE.—Oa Wednesday a gathering took place at Bury St. Edmunds in connection with an en- terprise for the revival of the beet sugar making industry in England. The requisite capital for carrying out the work has been raised by a private company, and the authorised slim consists of £200,000 in shares and £75 in debentures. The factory at which the beet root is to be dealt with is situated at Lavenham, about ten miles from Bury \ St. Edmunds. Some years ago Mr. Jas. Duncan made a similar experiment there. In his time the raw sugar, after ex- tracted from the beet root, was sent to London to be refined. In the present instance it is intended to deliver actual sugar Irons the factory. Eighty farmers in the neighbourhood have engaged to supply beet to the factory, the requisite seed being in process of sowing in the current month. 1,000 acres of land are devoted to the purpose. The roots, on be- ing brought in from the field, will be cut into slices by a machine, and then soaked with water to extract the juice. This liquor will afterwards be treated with strontia, which acts as a precipitant, carrying down the particles of sugar with it. The precipitate thus formed, consisting of com- bined sugar and strontia, will be decomposed by means of carbonic acid gas, which throws down the strontia and leaves a pure and strong syrup. This will be boiled in vacuum pans in the ordinary way until sufficiently concentrated to crystallise. It is stated that the Queen has caused three acres of the Shaw Farm of the late Prince Consort to be sown with sugar beet, and the Prince of Wales has adopted a similar plan with one acre at Sandringham Sir Lyon Playfair, at the meeting referred to, urged the farmers to persevere with the cultivation of the beet, so that the manufacture could be carried On with that regularity which was necessary to make it successful. Mr. Engelhardt, who was one of the speakers, predicted that Lavenham would soon become a busy place and stated that the conductors of the undertak- ing wish- ci to put up 20 or 30 factories in different Darts of the kingdom. He was confident that England was capable of growing half the sugar it now consumed. • CO-OPERATIVE DAIRY FARMING. The Manchester Guardian has the following :—A Dairy Factory established at Brunswick on a co-operative basis has been extremely successful. I recently asked the manager to furnish me with the results of his past year's working. He has not only responded to this request, but has forwarded elaborate plans showing exactly how the factory is built, ' and how the various apartments are connected and worked, i together with a balance-sheet for the past two years. It ' appears that this factory cost, including the machinery and land upon which it stands, £lO,OOO, the expense being sea-eater as it is within the city. Batter retails at 3s. per kil- ogramme (about 2±1b5.), coffee cream is is. per litre (about n pint), and thick cream Is. 6d. In London, it may be i mentioned, there are two qualities of cream sold, but at a I much higher price. Milk reaches Bd. a gallon, skim milk I 34d. a gallon, and buttermilk about sd. the gallon. The soft cheeses known as Limburg, Harz, and Backstein cost per cwt. 255. between July and November, and 20s. the other I months of the year—that is about 24d. a pound. Each cheese weighs about Ilb., and is sold retail at 3d. These soft cheeses contain a considerable larger quantity of water than the harder and drier cheeses of England, and are twice as profitable as English skim milk cheeses. The success of the factory has been sagreat that a large number of farmers who wish to join cannot be received, inasmuch asethe plant will not deal with more milk than is taken at the present time. In commencing it received 2,000 litres of milk a day, and last summer the supply reached 8,000. The first factory in North Germany was built in 1877 at Kiel; another followed at Magdeburg; then this at Brunswick, since which numbers have been built, the success having been generally great. The engine usfd is of 12-horse power, and this works the sepa- rators, churn, batterworkers, pumps, lift, and, in fact,every- thing that can be done by steam. The cheeses referred to are made at the rate of 16Ibs. per 100 litres of milk, so that assuming this to be worked at 3d. a gallon in Eegland, or 55. 6d. the 100 litres, the cheese would cost over 4d. a pound when ripe; bat it should sell at the very least at 6d. a pound wholesale, being far superior to anything to be obtained in this country at such a price. The manager kindly sent me a case containing various samples of these cheeses, and of the factory butter just as it is sent out in small round white earthenware pots with lids, on which the name of the factory is stamped. This is an infinitely better system than our own, for the factories here have commenced by sending out the batter in grease-proof paper upon which their designation is printed. I confess that not only were the cheeses remarkably good, being ripe, but the batter superior to anything I have tasted in English dairies where it is made for keeping in this manner. Sour curd or hand- kdse is also sold, realising lid. a pound, 100 litres making 20Ibs. In the year 1881-2 the batter yielded was 276 per cent, of the milk, and the cream 15 per cent. In the next year the cream was 13, and the butter 2.61 per cent. In this year over 2,000,000 litres of milk were delivered to the factory, of which over 600,000 were sold fresh ; the rest, deducting two per cent, for loss in measure, was passed through the Fesca cream separator, a machine re- sembling the Danish, but which the manager considers is not so good as the Laval, as it is rather troublesome to manage. The cream obtained by the centrifugal ma- chine was 200,000 litres ; of this, three thousand were sold retail and the re 4 churne4 in the huge Holstein churns of the factor?. The skim milk measured 1,300,000 litres; 650,000 of this quantity being sold and the rest converted into cheese. Of the 170,000 litres of buttermilk left after chnrning 17,000 were sold, 120,000 being used for horses and pigs, and the rest used with the skim milk for cheese- making. The 700,000 of skim and buttermilk made 130,000 Limburg and other cheeses. One remarkable feature is that the horses employed in the factory are largely fed on butter- milk, getting from five to ten litres per head p. isy ac- cording to what can be spared, and this is four,d t ) answer remarkably well and to be a great saying in the purchase of corn. Here, moss litter is also largely used and highly ap- proved of, especially as it is very cheap. The swine, which are kept for consuming the waste and unused butter and skim milk, are purchased at the age of about three months, when they cost 20s. each, and are fed for three months, being sold at about 2001 b. weight, when they reach 70s. They have a little meal daily during the last month. The figures supplied to me show the actual quantity of milk de- livered in each month, May and Jane standing highest with nearly 250,000 litres, and September the lowest with 142,000 litres. The sale of skim milk was much the highest in June, and buttermilk in June and July, while the;sale of
Limburg cheeses In March was simply _en- Ormons. America

has within ten years developed a milk factory system which can scarcely be comprehended. The Germans have within three years begun work on this kind of system, and there is every reason to suppose that they will also develop it very largely. In England we have but just commenced, and, although there is every reason to expect great success, our people do not seem to take it in hand as they ought to do. In the usage and care of the implements of the farm, the ' old adage that "a stitch in time saves nine," is peculiarly applicable, and a word in season on the subject may not 4 now be out of place. Taking the farms of the United Bing- dem as a whole, we should say that lack of care in the , machinery department entails an annual loss of something like 25 per cent, on the capital therein invested. This does not, of course, arise from wilfulness or heedlessness, but simply from the fact, in the majority of cases, that the matter is never thought of. It does not seem to enter into the calculation of many farmers that implements need any attention, and they are thus left to the tender mercies of their greatest enemy, rust, the latter being at once the manufacturer's friend and enemy,—his friend by reason that many more implements are needed than would be required were greater care observed; his enemy by bringing him into bad repute on the score of defective workmanship, whereas only the owner of the implement is to blame. It does not seem to strike many farmers that implements and machines require dry stabling and cleanliness just as do their horses and cattle. Yet these necessaries that pay in the one case will pay equally well in the other. If possible, and it is always possible on every farm, there should be a water-tight implement shed, with a dry fl 'or. The practice of leaving implements lumping about in any corner, so long as they are out of the way, is not only slovenly, and bodes ill for the other man- agement of the farm, but it is costly. As the seasons go round, and as each machine or implement is done with for he time being, they should be cleaned of all dirt, wiped dry, and oiled, especially frictional parts. There are always wet days and spare hours ien every farm when this could be done, and it will be found the best paying work. Once let it be understood to come Into the ordinary routine of work on the farm, and the men would do it the same as they now groom their horses or fodder and water their cattle. Any workman using a spade knows how much easier the imple- ment works when it is clean than when it is rusty, and that in its use the clean spade saves him the exercise of a per- centage of muscular power, consequently he keeps his im- plement clean. Ought not the same consideration to be shown for the horses that have to work the larger implements of the farm? Thus far we might go on the humanitarian principle; but, if the matter were well thought out, there is another principle underlying—that of the pocket, which would have greater effect. The machinists' and smiths' bills on most farms are quite 25 per cent, heavier than they need to be were greater care exercised. Further, what farmer has not experienced the loss and inconvenience resulting from a machine or an implement not being in workable condition when it is required? Thus, whilst all machinery should be put away in proper state, it ought to be a rule of procedure on all well-managed farms, as each season of the year draws nigh, to have such out and properly examined, cleaned, and seen that they are in the best working order some little time before they are actually needed in the fields. If there , are any weak or doubtful places there will be time for them to be remedied, and thus put in the stitch in time, and pro- . bably prevent a breakdown at a busy time, entailing loss • and delay. Were implements treated with reasonable care, ; many of them would go on working smoothly and well for doable the length of years that they do under mismanage- , ment. When times are bad it behoves us to look around • corners to see where retrenchment and saving can be I effected, and the above is one of those corners where sub- stantial saving will accrue from judicious management. The present time—between seed time and harvest—is most , opportune to see to the state of the implements and ma- chinery. TULL, Juts.

A small boy in Belfast, Maine, whose deportment at school" had always ranked 100 per cent., came home one day re- cently with his standing reduced to 9Es "What have you been doing, my son ?" asked the mother. "Been doing.?" , replied the young hopeful; "been doing just as I have all j along; only the teacher caught me this time." PUTTING A POINT ON IT.—A lady with a fatal squint came once to a fashionable artist for her portrait. He looked at her, and she looked at him, and both were embarrassed: He spoke first. "Would your ladyship permit me," he said, "to take the profile? There is a certain shyness about your ladyship's eyes which is as difficult in art as it is fas- cinating in nature." Tuts Waiter. Honsz.—There is a wheel horse in every family—some one who takes the load on all magmas. It may be the old daughter, possibly the father ; but gener- ally it is the mother. Extra company, sickness, give her a heavy increase of the burden she is always carrying. Even I summer vacations give less rest and recreation to her than I to others of the family. I once heard a husband say I "My wife takes her sewing machine into .the country, and has a good time doing up the fall sewing." At the time I did not appreciate the enormity of the thing ; but it has rankled in my memory, and appears now to be an outrage. Woman's work is never done. But, because it is nevor done she needs resting times. Every night tho heavy trick is pat up, the wheel horse .is put into the stable, and labour and care are dismissed till the morrow. The thille of the household van cannot be turned up at night; and the tired hornie•mother cannot go into a quiet stable for moose. She goes to sleep at night feeling the pressure of to-morrow. She must ksep an eye 'ready to open at any moment to answer the need of children, and open both eyes bright and early to see the machinery well staeted for a new day. I There is never any time that seems convenient for the I mother of little children to leave home even for a day; but 1 with a little kindly help from her hashand, and a little I resolution in herself, she may go, and be so much better for' it that the benefit will overflow from her Into the whole household. She will .bring home some new idea, and Au work with all the enthusiasm which comes from a fresh heart.

THE MANAGEMENT 01.,' POULTRY. SOME EXPERIMENTS IN CROSSING. We have at various times recommended certain crosses for the production of laying and table fowls, and from the reports given by seine of our readers who have tried these crosses they have been very successful. By experience of this kind we are enabled to get definite information as to the value of certain qualities when put together, for it i$ a fact that whilst we may 6ave a very good idea as to what sort of progeny two varieties bred together will produce, it is only when we have tried the cross that we can speak with any degree of certainty. There are so many things which turn up that we have never anticipated, and thus in this case, as in all others, "an ounce of practice is worth a ton of theory," and, as in experiments of this kind there should be some sort of continuty, it is very valuable to get hold of some facts which show a persistent attempt to discover the qualities of various crosses. A report has recently appeared in an American poultry journal from a gentleman in New York State, in which he gives the result of some experi- ments he has made in crossing with the Langshan. His object was to obtain a breed, the cockerels of which would mature quickly and fatten easily, and the pullets of which , would begin to lay early, and not only so, but be good I winter layers—truly the very characteristics that would stamp any breed as almost perfection. As he has found the Langshan to excel as winter layers, he, in his experiments, made that the basis of all his crosses, and, as will be seen, there was Langshan blood in every one of them. The first cross was a Langshan cockerel mated with Brown Leghorn hens. As our readers are aware Leghorns are noted for their laying qualities. The produce were shert-legged compact birds, not so large as the Langehan but larger than the Leghorn. As egg producers they have been unsurpassed, beating in this respect the pure bred Leghorns of both colours. They commenced to lay four to six weeks before the pure bred Leghorns, and are said to have laid more steadily. Only one showed the slightest desire to sit. The cockerels of this cross matured quite as early as pure Leghorns, and were considerably larger. They carried a great deal of meat on the breast, and were good on the table. The second cross was a white cockerel with Langshan hens, and in this case the progeny was either entirely white or entirely black. This is often the case when crossing white and black fowls together, and though cuckoo coloured or speckled plumage is often obtained, yet more often the birds partake entirely of one or other of their parents' plumage. The white birds partook more of the Leghorn qualities and the black of the Langshans. So far as the laying results were concerned these White Leg- horn-Langshans were not so early in egg production as the Brown Leghorn cross, but earlier than either of the pure Leghorns. The breeder thinks that they aremot quite so constant as layers, and their egg production is more affected by the cold weather, bat the difference is not great. The third experiment was a Silver Spangled Hamburgh cock crossed with Langshan pullets, and the former are known as about the best layers of the Ilamburgh varieties. The breeder says that he did not give this pen a fair trial. The birds were hatched later, so that they cannot be spoken of with the same certainty. They have, however, laid well, and promise to sustain the rephtation of both parents, but the cross is so small that nothing is to be gained for table bids by it, and as a farmer's bird their size is against them, which is always an im- portant consideration in the production of all round fowls. Nearly all the birds were black, with single combs, and were about the size of pure black leghorns, that is, between the brown Leghorn and the Langshan. The fourth cross was with a Langshan cockerel and hens half Plymouth Rock and half common. Unfortunately the breeder failed to raise a single pullet from this cross, and so the laying quali- ties could not be tested, which is regretable. The hens were most of them very large, and the chicks matured very early, feathering rapidly, and being fall breasted were found to be about the best of all as broilers. When older they developed to almost the size of Langshans, and with all the compact- ness and solidity of Plymouth Roche. They were found to be equally good as roasters, and the breeder is very much taken with this cross. The fifth cross was a Creveccenr Cockerel with Langshan hens and pullets. As might be expected this cross made an excellent table bird. The shape is magnificient for a market fowl, especially at six months or over, the bodies being very long and deep, producing that shape which is so •much admired and so valuable in the Dorking. The chicks matured early, and they were all black in colour, with small create and beards, clean or featherless blacklegs, and small combs. As broilers they were not found to be so good as the Langshan, Plymouth Rock and common cross, but as roasters they were un- equalled. The birds grew to a large size, especially the females, which appeared to be better proportioned than the males. Bat as egg producers this croes was not found to be a success, and they were very slow in commencing to lay. , This we are not surprised at, for Creves are not at all good layers, and the table qualities would be developed at the expense of the laying powers. From this most interesting experiment we get the follow- ing results. For market qualities, Sine and value as roasters, Crevecceur-Langshans were the beat, with the Langshan. Plymouth Rocks close up to them, yet still second; the White Leghorn-Lanshans were third, the Langshan Brown Leghorns fourth, and the Hamburgh-Langshan worst of all. For market qualities, early maturity as broilers, the Lang- shan-Plymouth Rocks stood first, Tie Creve-L mgehans second, the Langshan Brown Leghorn, and White Leghorn- Langshans equal thirds, and the Hamburgh-Langshans last of all. For early layers, the best were the the Lang- shan Brown Leghorns; second, the White Leghorn-Lang- shans ; third, the Hamhurgh-Langshans ; and fourth, the Crevecteur-Langshans. There being no pullets from the Lanaahan-Plyinouth Rocks, they could not be tested. For the best winter layers, the various crosses stood in the same relationship as the early layers. The breeder says that if a bird is desired to combine both egg-producing and table qualities, which is the one the farmer is searching for, he should advise one Of the Langshan-Leghorn crosses, his own preference being for the Langshan Brown Leghorn. Of coarse, it is to be pointed out that this experiment only lasted during one season, and that it would not be fair to accept the testimony as final after eo short an experiment, for the succeeding years might bring variations into the results. Still, so far as it has gone, the information given is very important, and we should be glad if those in this country who have the opportunity would experiment with the same care as has been shown in this case. We are still bothered with east winds, but as soon as they disappear we may expect warm weather. Sitting hens will begin to be greatly troubled with Bees, unless some pro- vision is made for keeping them down. These pests breed daring the spring and sumnier in immense numbers, and- often so irritate hens that they desert their nests, besides being a great cause of gapes in the chicks. This may in a large measure be prevented by providing a good dust bath, in which plenty of carbolic powder is mixed. Hens can be allowed off their nests about 15 cr 2'o minutes, if the weather is as at present, but a little longer when milder, and this gives them plenty of time to dust themselves. If in an exposed place a piece of fiannel,may be put over the eggs when the hen is off, so as not to hurry her back again. TO prevent insects a plan has been recommended which seems effective. This is to saturate some of the nest straw with petroleum or paraffin, taking care to have some clean straw on the top, and no harm is done to hen or eggs. In America sulphur nest eggs are sold, and some persons use pieces of lump sulphur or black sulphur. But we think the dust bath is the most effective, if the nests are remade for each batch of eggs.

ARMY STATISTICS —A preliminary return of the British Army for 1883 (prepared in anticipation of the general an- nual return), shows that the average strength of the regular army during the year was 281,971, as against 189,229 in 1882, the total for last year having been the lowest for over 20 years, except in 1870, when it was 180,444. The num- ber of accepted recruits was, however, 32.924/ against 23,555 I in IPB2, and this was the highest total for over 20 years. It is not often a youth. lakes his seat as suddenly as the one of whom we are abtait to speak, or keepa it as. persis- tently. He was the keenest blade in the class, and when an unpopular professor said, "Gentlemen, your next subject for composition will be manners," he at once rose and asked, "Can we write on bad manners, sir 7" The professor looked over his spectacles at the all-conquering youth, and quietly answered, "Certainly; you can write about whatever you are best acquainted with." ; TRH GOYERNORSIII, or MALTA.— The liesily. He will be the virtual head of the Civil Administration of Malta. At present the salaryl of the Governor-in-Chief, amounting:to £s,oolibper annum, is paid out of the island revenues, but in future, it is ,stated, that only E 3.050 will be derived from that source, the remaining £2060 being contributed from, the Imperial Exchequer. Scstoou BOAIIDS.—A parliamentary return issued on Saturday shows that in 126 of the-227 municipal boroughs of England, and in 16 out of the 23 municipal boroughs of Wales, school beards have been formed, there being school attendance committees in‘the remainder. There are 1,738 school boards in English parishes and 276 in Welsh parishes. The total population under school boards in hngland is 15101,634, in Wales 979,924 and under school attendance committees 9,512,292 in the former and 38Ce529 in the latter.

COTTAGE GARDENING • CARBOTS.—The main crop of these 3hould be sown now on a piece of ground that has been well worked and made rich for the growth of a previous crop, though there is no objection to a few inches of manure if placed at a depth of not less than 1f t. fin. Too much crude manure near the surface has a tendency to cause carrots to fork or branch at the root, instead of forming one straight, downward root. When the carrot is not suited with soil it is one of the most unprofitable vegetables in the garden. Where failure is the rule we would only grow a few of the variety called James's Scarlet. When we have. sown them in drills we have sown the Early Horn variety alternately, as it becomes ready for use much earlier, and when drawn more space is allowed for the others. A still day should be selected for sowing, the seed being so light that the least wind will give considerable trouble to the sower. The seeds also adhere toN each other, and, to separate them for the convenience of sowing, they ought to be mixed with sand or fine ashes. if rubbed between the hands a few times they will disunite and give no further trouble.

WINTER VEGETABLES that are likely to find their way into the cottager's garden are the Broccoli, of sorts, Bore- cote or Kale, and Savoy's, with now and then a few Brussels' Sprouts, whicir are the sweetest of all the early greens. Amongst Broccoli the following may be selected to give a succession :—Adam's Early, Knight's Protecting, Champion. and Cattell's Eclipse. The latter has been cut in May and June, when vegetables are scarce. The Kates should include the Cottager'S.Kale, the Curled or Scotch Kale, and the As- paragus or Buda Kale. This is the most prolific, hardiest, latest, and sweetest of all Kates, and we hope every ccttager who has a garden will give it a trial during the coming sea- sod; they will be found to be the most deliciotis green ever tasted in April, and even in May. Of Savoys, the Dwarf Green Curled and the Drumhead deserve a place. Some cottagers go in largely for these, and, by Christmas time their gardens are empty, because they filled them with la. voys, which are seldom of little use after that period. All the above, as well as a few Cauliflowers and a few Cabbages for summer and autumn use should now be sown. We do not expect every cottsger to purchase every variety named, though that would not be very ruinous, for a 4d. or 6d. packet would contain sufficient seed to supply plants for half a dozen cottagers, and if they had a previous under- standing as to what each is going to sow they could barter, so that all of them might be supplied with the whole se- , iection.

THE FRONT CiArtnnts.—Annuals : In selecting these the purchaser will be in a. measure guided. by his special re- quirements. If he only desires those half hardy and hardy Annuals which are suitable for cat flowers, he will select the following from the first :—Asters, Stocks Zinnias, Phlox Drummond% Sweet Scabious, and the Everlastings. Amongst Asters, the Chrysanthemum flowering and the Victoria are the most taking varieties. To our eye there is want of gracefulness in the quilled section, and they do not look so well in the bouquet or the vase. All the above are best sown in a frame or under some kind of protection. A few Asters and Stocks may be raised in pots in the window, If a-frame is not at hand, and afterwards pricked out in well prepared beds to be nursed prior to planting out in their permanent quarters. The most eligible for cutting amongst the hardier Annuals are the Candytafts, Larkspurs Sweet Peas, Lovalies-Bleeding, and Lupins, which may be sown in patches where they are to remain. The space for them to occupy may be defined by making two circular marks with a stick—one a few inches intide the other. The seeds may then be sown in the inner circle, or in the grooved line which defines it. All the small seeds are benefited by hav- ing very fine sifted soil for a covering, which can be pre- pared in some corner and carried in a vessel to be spread on with the hand. Sweet Peas and seed of similar size will require half an inch of covering, and, as the Peas will grow three feet or four feet high, they should be in patches against a wall or fence. Few things are more delightful than Sweet Peas trained up each side of the doorway or intermingledwith Roses, Clematis, or Jesamine, covering a rustic arch over the entrance. Pita Wirsnow.—Most • window plants are benefited by being, placed out of doors for a few hours occasionally during genial or showery. weather. The rain *ill wash away all davit that may have settled on the foliage, and the plant altogether will look refreshed and invigorated. , If the plants are placed on the window ledge, as is frequently the case, they should be made secure, as a slight current of air would cause them to fall down and be totally ruined. The most secure protection is a board four inches wide, nailed across in front of the poti. If the board received one or two coats of stone colour paint it would not look conspicuous, and not be out of character with either brick or stone. .If the pots are also plunged in boxes containing ashes they may stand in the open garden with perfect immunity from danger from ordinary wind. Hyacinths and Tulips that have served the purpose of decorating the window should not be heedlessly put on one side as if of no further use. If they are placed in a sheltered position for a week or two,, kept well watered, and then planted in good light soil, so- that the bulb is covered-over two or three inches, they will, give a supply of flowers-for years. FeW fail to flower the following year, and they are the most delicate,of the hya- oinths; but if the practice of planting.some out annually ie purseed the stock will be kept up.

FOOTPRINTS OF ArieSSIST MAN,---DT. Flint, who has. been conducting investigations of ancient shell heaps and burial places for the laet five years in Nicaragua, ham found a burial jar containing bones and old- Venetian beads, with two gold ornaments like those found at Chiriqui, showing that gold ornaments of this type after the Spanish conquest had farniehed them with a pattern for glass beads. They are exceptional among Nicaraguan antiquities. The most interesting of Dr. Flint's discoveries are what he believes to be human footprints in layers of clay under lava rock on the borders of Lake Managua, Dri Flint writes that he has cut out several, and, with some foesil leaves, has despatched them to the Harvard' Museutn. COAL MINING IN JAPAL—WRINKLES FOR ENGLISH ENGINERRS.—Those who jump to the very general conelu- pion that Oriental progress is hopeless should study the recent history of Japan. As an example of what has been done there since the Japanese have awakened from their torpor of self-sufficiency, I quote from "Nature "the fol.. lowiiig particulars concerning a. coal mine near-Nagaski. The workings "not only extend beneath the island of Takashima itself, but also beneath the sea, and have a total length of about seventy miles. About 2,500 people an em- ployed there, and the output of coal is about 1,200.t0ns per day." This in spite of one of the most serious difficulties of coal-mining,," the temperature is so high that spon- taneous combustion. is constantly occurring," whith, to- gether with thaeseape of fire-dadtp, makes the- mine very dangerous. It has been said that the recent progress of Japan is merely a superficial imitation of Wectern customs. This is glaringly contradicted hy what has been, already done, and is projected in conneteton with this coal mine. The Japanese are here teaching us how to e.se a coal mine as a scientific-observatory for the solution of some obscene and difficult scientific problems. They have commenced, and are continuing systematically, a. series of experimenta. on electrical earth currents.; they are applying the tele- phone and microphone, to the examination of sounds pre, duced by the movements cf the solid rock; they are ob.. serving and measuring earth-tremors by means of an instru- ment devised for the purpose) a tromomeer ; by using two delicate lovela they are determining whether the seasonal movements they have already discovered, to occur on the surface of the soil eatend underground • they are attempt- ing to maasure the influence of the tide (which rises and falls overhead about eight feet) in producing a bend or crushinfe, in the reef of the mine. "Observations on at- mospheric electricity, may subsequently be added." ' All these observations are c.areied on in connection with others above ground, on variations of the tidos, of temperattre and atmospheric presents. The escape of are-damp and the en- trance of water into the mine are also measured and re- corded, and thno the influence of tides, atmospheric pres- sure, and temperature upon the liability to explosions will be removed from the range of speculation to that of estab- lished and measured fact. The Japanese who caw to this country to learn the rudiments of mining are already be- ginning to teach our mining engineers some of the-scientific elements of their business. One of our most recent steps in ' the- application of, modern science to mining is that of issuing warnings when there is a considerable fall of the barometer. This. le based on a general observation that the barometer lee usually been low when great explosions have occurred. The more systematic observations of the Japanese have re.N.own that the Increased escape of gas pre- cedes the fall ci the barometer by about eight hours, and . therefore that, the warnings come too late.—Gentlanan's Magazine,

I SUPP3SBD. DISCOVERY 617 A VITAL CENTRE IN TZE ' Efesar.—At a recent meeting of the Berlin Physiological Society rrof. Kronecker reported on the diecovery of a co- ordination contra in the movements of the ventricles of the heart, made by Herr Schraoy, a student in his department of the Physiological Inatitute, and which he (Professor Kroneeker) had repeatedly verified. In an examination of the changes in the dimensions of the henrt in the process of contraction needles were thrust in the most various direc- tions into the heart of a dog after it had been laid bare, an operation which, as was known by experience, had no in- on the movements of the heart. When in this opera- tion the needle came upon a certain small spot on the lower border of the upper third of the septum cordis the ventricles of the heart at once ceased to beat, and, diastolically di- lated, fell into fibrillar convulsions, which were soon fol- , lowed by the death of the ventricles of the heart. It vms not possible by any appliances to restore the ventricles to their normal action. The vestibules continued to beat nor- mally, but the ventricles no longer discharged their blood, and soon, in consequence of the palsy of the heart, general death set in. This instantaneous death of the heart through a prick in a particular part of the septum—the stoppage thereby produced of each co-ordinate contraction of the , muscles ol the heart—was up to the present wholly without analogy. What approached nearest to this fact was the well known phenomenon that a compression of the coronary artery produced in a short time a cessation cf pulsation and fibrillar convulsions. On withdrawing the compression, however, the pulsations of the ventricles were resumed. In the case of a prick, on the other hand, the effect followed altogether much more quickly, quite instantaneously, in fact, and the yen ricks, not able again to discharge their functions normally, were for ever motionless. This phe- nomenon Professor Kronecker explained in the following manner. By the prick of the needle a co-ordinating centre in the movements of the ventricles of the heart having its seat at the spot in question in the septum was touched and destroyed. The finding of this centre afforded the physio- logical key to the riddle not unknown in surgery, that many very slight heart wounds—pricks of needles, for example,

which did not even penetrate—produced sudden death. It was now the task of anatomical investigation to eemonstrate the existence of this centre now experimentally proved to exist. Professor Kronecker and Eferr Schmey have demon- strated this important experiment to the satisfaction of the society.

GENERAL NEWS. The damage done by a fire at Belmont Code exceeds £12,000, many valuable paintings being destroyed. A young man has died near Canterbury with symptoms of hydrophobia, having been bitten by a panther in China. A woman named C: egg has been arrested at Manchester. While drunk she threw her child on the fire, causing its

death. , Belmont Castle, Forfarshire, an old and historically in- teresting structure, was destroyed by fire on Monday evening. Life states that the late Mr. Charles Reade has net left More than about £20,000, the bulk of which goes to his god- son. Mr. Charles Lister. A man named Cronin wee arrested, on Tuesday, at Cdonlea, County Waterford, for the murder of his uncle, near Dungarven, four years ago. The Roman Catholic Bishop of 'Ferns, Dr. Warren, died on Tuesday morning. The deceased prelate, who wan 'con- secrated in 1876, took no part in politics. The financial condition of Cyprus does not improve- This Year, as last, it will be found secesear v to make up out of Imperial revenues a deficit of abeut£3o,ooo. Three of the Australian cricket team—Alexanles, Boyle, and Midwinter—arrived in Lenden on Monday, everleol. The remainder of the team are come:lg on to. Plymouth in one of the Orient steamers. 'FATAL ACCIDENT.—In the Southampton Docks, on Satur- - day, two men were hoisting a rnaintopmast and trosstree on a shin under repair, when the crosstree fell some 80 feet on to the deck, carrying with it a rigger, who was picked up dead, and killing a man on whom it fell. A third rigger had his aim broken and his shoulder dislocated. THE MERCHANT SHIPPING BILL—Mr. Chamberlain had - a further private interview on Tuesday at the Board of Trade Office, with the shipowners and underwriters who conferred' with him on the Merchant Shipping Bill about a fortnight ago. It is stated that another meeting will be held, pro- bably next neck, to complete the revision of the bill- CABINET COUNCIL.—A Cabinet Cauncil, which met on Tuesday at three p.m., lasted for a little over an hour. Several of the Ministers afterwards met in Mr. Gladstoae's private room at the House of Commons and held a short consultation. Lord Carlingford leaves London on Therm- day for Darmstadt, as Minister in attendance on Her Majesty. Tun SHOEMAKERS' SYRIKE.—A strike ef London shoe- makers, which included about 4,000 men and directly af- fected 20,000 other persons, has just been brought to a close after lasting five weeks. The men sought for the establish- ment of a minimum price list, which was firmly resisted by the masters. The result of the struggle is that a Board of Conciliation for tfie adjustment of wages is to be formed. Tamer OF LETTERS.—Complaints have lately been made by the public around Wolverhampmc and Willenhall aa to the non-delivery of letters. The robberies hive b6en traced ten postman of Willenhall named Henry John Becher, who was on Monday brought before the Willenhall magis- trates. It was shown that lettere containing Pest-effice orders and stamps had been found ,oecretta in one of the rooms of his house. He was committed for trial. STReeNGE RECOVERY or' PLATE.—On Saturday, two boys Playing near the tiarelaw Dam, a reservoir near Pore Glas- gow, found in the water a small parcel containing some sil- ver plate. Another and larger parcel was afterwards taken from the dam by police officers, who found in it about four- teen dozens of silver forks, spoons, table knives, and other valuable property, which was evidently the proceeds of a robbery. The plate was stamped with the Maeonic "com- pass and square." CENTENARIANS.—The death is announced of Miss Sarah Clark, at Hammersmith, at the great age of 105. A nephew of the deceased, Mr. Charles Clark, is now living in Man- chester, and has attained his 89th year. A woman named Annie Leeson, aged 103, years, bee just died at Selihull, near Birmingham. The old lady lived with her son, who ic 79 years of age. She was in full possession of her facul- ties, and freqvntly took walks and attended tea meetings and other gatherings. MURDEROUS ATTACK ON A ,N7,llSE.—Richard Garland, who has undergone ten and seven years, penal servitude, and is now under police supervision, was charged at Croy- don, on Saturday, with the attempted murder of a nuree named Wyatt, at the Croydon Union Infirmary, on Good . Friday. The prisoner crept up behind her and felled her tc the ground with a poker. She is still unable to appear, and the prisoner, who was wrapped in blankets, and who ap- peared vary ill, was remanded. THREATENING A CHIEF CONSTABLE. An Irishrnar named O'Shea was sent to prison for 18 months at Glas- gow on Wednesday for having written a threatening letter to Chief Constable Wean. It was proved that the pri- soner, who had some coneection with the ten men convicted of destroying a Glasgow gasholder, wrote to M‘Call threa- tening that he would be "done away with" if he did not cease mannfacturing " evidence against innocent men— presumably the ten then awaiting trial. BIRTH OF "A PRINCESS "—A supplement to the Loaders • Gazette, published on Monday eeereine, contains the fol- lowing :—Eastwell Park, April 20th, I.sB4.—This morning, at 10 minutes past 11, her Royal and Imperial Highness the Duchess of Edinbargh was safely delivered of a princess. The Earl of Derby, Secretary of State for the Colonies, was Present, in the absence of the Secretary of State for the Home Department. Her Royal and Imperial Highness and infant Princess are doing well. The happy event was made known by the firing of the perk and tower guns." AN INSURANCE COMPANY'S " CONSCIENCE MONEY."— The actuary of a large London insurance company has just completed ad exhaustive investigation of the accounts for . the past ten wears, and has brought to light that 'during that period the conscience fund" ewerZs,ooo. of. this company has amounted to The fund is made up of sums sent anonymously to this company by people who have in previous years 'received money on account of fires, and whose conscience subsequently prompted them to make . restitution. CLERICAL ABSENTEEISM IN Losnoen—At the recent vestry meeting at Et. Ethelburga, Bishopsgate, one of the speakers complained that altheurth the rector of the parish , is in receipt of an income of £1,065 a year, hie duties are entirely delegated to a curate, who teceivee an annual sti- pend of £l4O only. It was stated that since the legal con- test between the perish and the rector, on the subject of ritualistic practices, which ended in a victory for the .church- - wardens, seven yearranince, the rector had net been seen in the pariah. St. Btheiburga is stated to have a population of 199 persons. EDINBURGH UNTYRESITY TERCENTEITARY.--On Saturday .• Sir Stafford Northeote left Edinburgh for Londcn. He was accompanied to the railway station by 'Mrala G. Currey, the Dean at Faculty, and Mr. James Campbell; M.P , all of whom wore primroses. While the right bon, gettleman was • Waiting, a considerable, number of gentlemen -were intro- - duced to Ern. Sir Stafford Nortlmote carried a bouquet of ;•Primroses in his -hand. M. de Lessens, Dr. Stodkvitz, M. -Pasteur, and Sir John Lu'ebock travelled Joy the, name train, and for all these visitors loud cheers were given when it aatarted. rFEMA.LE SUITTRAGII A./4D THE FRENCIIISE Bran. —ln i•Viser of the intended division on Mr Woodall's amendment to the Franchise B 11, an analysis has been .madenf opinion 10 the present -House of Commons on the Woman's Buff raze 'question. This shows important results. ,Of -485 members Who have either voted or ,paired in favour of Weman's 'Suffrage, or who have declared by speech or In writing that would support it, it iscialmed that 219 are friends of 'the cause and 232. opposed. Oti those favonrine such a anea- '42lerrei 170 are Liberals, 57 Concervative,s, and-22 Irish einem- 7', • Its opponents commies,. 101 Liberate, 127,Conseeva- w"7:2; and eight Irish mentbera.
