in A National League "convention," held at Thurles, Couuty Tipperary, on Thursday, resolved not to permit hunting under any circumstances. 'rhe honorary degree of D.C.L. was cenferred upon the Archbishop of Canterbury at the Convocation bell on Thurs- day in the Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford. A boat with two fishermen, named Hutton, father and son, while fishing off Runswick, near Whitby, on Thurs- day, was run down by a passing steamer, and both were drowned. telegramfrom Marseilles states that Madame Taglioni, the farnous'dancer, died there on Thursday, aged, 80. The deceased was of Italian descent, and was born at Stockholm, in March, 1804. Two single Men, named Dempster and Tweedie, were working on Wednesday in a quarry at Lcraharbriggs, near Dumfries, when a large block of stone fell upon them, kill- ing them instantly. On Thursday morning a violent collirion occurred on the Midler& Railway near Leicester, which resulted in consider- able damage to rolling stock, and blocked the mffin lines for nearly three hours. Sir 'Henry James, Q.C.,M.P., was on Wednesday night seected as the Liberal candidate far Bury, in place of Mr. R. N. Philips, who Is about to retire. It is expected that the Attorney-General will address the constituency at an early date. The late Duke ,cf Buccleuch was interred on Wednesday in St. Mary's Chapel, within Dalkeith Park. Lord Thurlow wan present, and laid a wreath on the coffin by command of the Queen. Ties Prince of Wales was likewise rep:resented, and also sent a wreath. The Lord Mayor of London, on Wednesday afternoon, opened the London International end Universal Echibition at the Crystal Palace, in the presence of a large assembly. The exhibition is divided into 33 sections, of which that devoted to fine arts is one of the most attractive. Tana BEIZTON MUEDEIL—The stockbroker Delton, who murdetted his mother at Brixton, was on Wednesday placed at the bar at the Central Criminal Court, and evidence having been given that he was insane and incapable of pleading be was ordered to be detained in an asylum during Her Majesty's pleasure. The Central News learns on reliable authority that the French Government has not yet made any demand to the Pekin Government in connection with the threatened war indemnity. Prince Chun, whose influence is nofil paramount at Pekin, is the father of the Empress, and has long been regarded as chief of the war party. Coos FIGHTING.—Two men were charged at Ulverston, on Thursday, with promoting a cock fight near that town. A large crowd witnessed the main, as also did several police officers, who bad been informed of the gatherinsr, and searched the fight from hiding places. One of the prisoners was ened £5 and the other discharged. The Duke of Westminster, on ThursdaT afternoon, laid the foundation stone of a new wing of the London Temper- ance Hospital, Hampstead-road. Mr. Cash, the chairman of the board of management, read an address, which stated that the cost of the new wing would beaLl4,ooo, of which £7.,000 had been subscribed or promised. Mr. Lawes, the defendant in the famous libel suit, has filed his statement of accounts in the Bankruptcy Court. He owes about £25,000, more than half of which is due to Mr. Belt for the amount of the verdict and costs; while Sir J. B. Lawes is scheduled as a creditor for £ll,OOO. Against these formidable sums the assets amount to about £5OO. The Bishop of Exeter, speaking to hie clergy at his trien- nial visitation, referred to the resolution recently brought forward to remove the Bishops from the House of Lords. %Bishop Temple said it was by no means clear that it would not be better for the nation to admit the heads of Noncon- formists bodies to the House of Lords than to remove the . Bishops from it. :YORK CONTOCATION.—The Convocation of York re- assembled on Thursday and discussed a variety of ques- tions, including that of lay help in the church, upon which a resolution was mcevedby the Bishop of Carlisle. A resolution was adopted deprecating any altera- tion of the marriage laws. Convocation was at the close of the day's sitting prorogurd until the'22nd proximo. The annual meetings of the Derbyshire Congregational Union were held on Tuesday and on Wednesday at Chester- field, under the presidency of Mr. G. H. Wheatcroft. Re- ports were submitted showing what changes had occurred in the pastorate, and setting forth the satisfactory financial condition of the Union. The Rev. F. Knowles, of Reiner, was appointed chairman, and the Rev. F. Bellamy secretary for the next year. THE QUEEN I,..BEADLAUGH.—On Wednesday Mr. Brad- laugh applied to the Lord Chief Justice of England, who was sitting at nisi-prius, to appoint a day for the hearing of this Case, in which the Atterney-General, On behalf of the Government, proceeds against Mr. Bradlaligh for having sat and voted in the House of Commons without having taken the oath as prescribed by law.—His lordship said that un- til the judges returned from circuit it would be impossible to fix a day. CHILD MURDEU.—At the Manchester City Police Court, on I hursday, Emily Clegg, 32 years of age, and residing at 1, Cumberland-street, Harpurbey, was brought up, on re- mand, charged with the wilful murder cf. her female infant child, Frances Clegg, four months old, on the 21st instant. The prisoner, it will be remembered, threw her child upon the kitchen fire, and shortly afterwards put it under the water tap to extinguish the flames. Sho was committed fe.r

trial at the assizen.- FIRING A DWELLING-HOUSE.—A. man named John Ross, a hairdresser, was tried at the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, on the charge of setting fire to a dwelling-house with intent to defraud 'an insurance company. It appeared in the course of the evidence that at the time the fire broke out several persons were sleeping in the house—one of them a woman who was said to be upwards of 100 years of age. The jury convicted the prisoner, and sentence of ten years' penal servitude was passed. AN EXPERT BURGLAR—The Recorder of Birmingham on Wednesday had before him a 'young man named Harding, who was indicted for housebreaking and robbery. The pri- toner was regarded as a mast expert burglar, and during his terms of freedom there was invariably reported an in- crease in that class of offences in the town. In addition to numerous housebreaking implements, Harding was also equipped when arrested with a revolver. He was sent into penal servitude for seven years. ..T.A3RD SPENCER IN LONDON.—The *OCR of Earl Spencer, who arrived in London on Thursday was somewhat unex- pected. His Lordship, who arrived early, walked to Downing- ' street about noon, and was for some time in consultation with Mr.filadstone. It is stated that Earl Spencer's visit to ' England has reference to to the bill which the Government proposes to introduce to amend the purchase clauses of the Irish Land Act, and that the opportunity has , also been taken to consult him, as a former lord president, on the sub- ject of the Lords' amendments to the Cattle Diseases Bill. A SHIPWRECKED CREW RESCUED FROM AN ISLAND.— The ship East Lothian, of Glasgow, arrived in the Tay on Wednesday, from Calcutta, after a passage of ;140 days. Captain Carse reports that having been detained by light baffling winds he called at Flores, one of the Western Islands, for fresh provisions, and there found the crew, consisting of twelve men and the captain, of the barque Skiddaw, of Glasgow, which had been wrecked on the island same time previously while on a voyage from Doboy to Liverpool with pitch pine. The shipwrecked crew were taken on board the East Lothian, and were landed at Dundee on Wednesday afternoon. MR. FAWCETT AN THE EWA: OF LORDS.—Mr. Fawcett addressed& meeting of his constituents in the Shoreditch Town Hall on Wednesday evening. His remarks bore chiefly on the Franchise Bill. Answering the question— What would the Lords do with that measure, he said that judging from experience he should assert with some dents that that if the people were unwevering in their determin- ation to repeat not once but twice, and thrice if necessary, the majority 0f.130, then the Houae of Lords would think once and twice and thrice ktefore they pat themselves ,in opposition 10.80 clear an expression. of popular desire cud popular determination. A SHIP MASTER SENT TO QAOI..—At the Liverpool Sessions, om Wednesday, Daniel Cameron, master of a offencefirste la sosf tnwietidcehin ehaen a was nt, f convicted "wilful brigantine, was committed to prison ttr three months, .as a neglect f duty,"he d aen_ wctieldolu Tuesday. -rendant's ship whilst at sea sprung a leak, but without tak- ing any measure to plug the hole or clear the hold of water, Cameron set fire to the vessel and left her with his crew. 'Fire Recorder admitted that the evidence pointed to a "much stronger imputation" than Simple neglect of duty, but he did not tleinkothe defendant had any fraudulent in- autism in actingae he did. THE MHRDER OF Mies. Sam-RE.--The Barbavilla can- spiracy case was reaumed at Dublin, on Wednesday. The ,Connsel for the Crewn having addressed the Court, the Lord Chief Baron summoned,up, and the jury found the prisoners guilty of murder-conspiracy, viz., Swords, Elliott, Bernard, Byrne, and Bryan Fitspatrimk. They were each sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. The Lord Cklef Baron said lieentirely cencurred LI the verdict, and added that the pri- soners were guilty in the eyes of the law as well as morality of the murder of Mrs. Smythe. Swords asserted hie inno- cence, and Elliot made a similar declaration. There had been two previous trials, and each time the , jury failed to agree. On the application of Counsel, the trial of the other prisoners was postponed to the nezt commission. A hCOTCH SUNDAY DRIKKINg CUM.—Some very singu- lar evidence was given before tire Dundee magistrates on Saturday in a case where a member of the "Artisaz' Club" was summoned for illegally selling whisky. It transpired that ot. psyment of one shilling anyone ,could become is member of the club, with the attendant privileges ofeaitting up all arght to drink and spending Sunday in the same fashion. On Sunday week 510 rni3n sal seven women ertered the club. Fully one-third of them when they deft were more or less intosricated, and the police bad a very busy time re- moving the" incanables" into safe keeping. The consu,tep- ripe of liquor on that day was given by the barman a5"295 "295 glasses a ; 1,200 pints of bottled, and 18 gal- lons of draught beer." A fine of only £5 was imposed, with the alternative of 30 days' imprisonment. Spencnns n Irma MEMBERS.—Mr. Justin 111'Cirtby,, M.P., in addressing a meeting of Irishmen at Manetteste, on Sunday, disclaimed any connection between the frish patty and any Political party in England. He spoke favour- ably of the Franchise Bill, saving its effect would be, by giving the Irish party the auesion of 30 or 40 associate. to enalals them to hold the fate of English ministeries and political parties in the ho/low a their bands—Mr. William 0 Brien, addressing his constituents at %fallow, on Sunday, said that so long as a vestige of foreign demi/nation remained to cramp the energies and blight the happiness of the Trish people, so long would they have work to do. Th basinese ef the Mail parliamentary party was to knock al they could out of England for Ireland. He eau' ioncd ; farmers arnt labourers to be united, as dissension between them worthl datrov the hopes of Ireland.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at a quarter-nest four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Tile Earl of Abingdou took the oath and his seat an succession to the title. The Army (Annual) Bill was brought up from the Corn- mone and read a second time. The Earl of BELMORE asked Her Mat,' esty's Goverrevient whether, in view of the difficulty of properly ventilating underground railways with openings'rnto the outer ale, they would consider the propriety of reeking the assent of Par- liament to the proposed new railway under the public parks contingent on the company undertaking to work the line by electric power ?—Lerd SUDELEY said that the Bill referred to had been permitted to proceed on the distinct neederstand- Mg that no ventilating shafts would be allowed, and they had the assurance of Sir J. Hawkshaw that the line could be worked without any difficelty as regarded ventilation, and that no shafts would be necessary. GENERAL GCEDON.—The Earl of Casere Evoke Before the House adjourns I wish to give notice of a question to the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. I beg to give notice that to-morrow night I will inquire whether he will give this House information as to the present critical posi- tion of General Gordon, and whether Her Majesty's Govern- ment contemplate taking any steps for hie relief. (Opposi- tion cheers.) Their lordehips adjourned at 10 minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at Eve minutes to four o'clock. Quustrwers : GENERAL GORDON, &c.—On the motion of Mr. LABOUCHERE, an officer of the House was ordered to at- tend the Court with certain papers stated to be neceseary in the suit against Mr. Bradleugh.—The LORD MAYOR gave notice on the second reading of the Government of London Bill to move its rejection.—Many questions were put from the Opposition benches with respect to the position of General Gordon. These were answered by Mr. Gfetostsroreu, who has returned to his Parliamentary duties evidently benefited by the comparative leisure of the recess. The right hon. gentleman generally confirmed the accuracy of I the telegram reported to have been received by Sir Samuel Baker from General Gordon. Shandy was surrounded by hostile tribes, and there was serious apprehension on account of Berber. There were hordes of hostile tribes in the neigh- bourhood of Khartoum. But the supplies are abundant, sod there is no apprehension on the part of General Gordon of danger. In a telegram dated the let April, he had stated that for two months to come he would be as safe at Khar- toum as he would have been at Cairo. The Premier re- minded Mr. Bourke that on a former occasion he had-stated that the Government had come to an important decision with regard to Egyptian finance, and it was imposeible to move a step in that matter without the necessity of com- municating with other Powers. When there was any sub- stantial information on the subject to be given to the House he would take care to communicate it.—Lord E. Fizz. manning confirmed the statement in the newspapers that a portion of the garrison and some of the civilian population of Shendy had been surrounded and massacred whilst at- tempting to escape.—With respect to the business of the House, the PREMIER stated that a morning sittimgvould be held next day, at which the Cattle Plague Bat would be taken. On Thursday the Chancellor of the Exchequer would intro- duce his Budget. The Franchise Bill would be taken next Monday, and he hoped to be able to make arrangements for the second reading of the Merchant Shipping Bill as soon as possible.—Mr. Harris, newly elected for Poole in the place of Mr. Schrieber, took his seat amid cheers fronttthe Con- servatives. MISCELLANEOUS MOTIONS.—At the unusually early hour of a quarter past five the Orders of the Day were reached, and the motion was made to go into Committee ef Supply on the Civil Service Estimates. Fourteen notices of amend- menet', raising all kinds of questions, barred the way; but not all were moved. Dr. Cameron called attention to the system of public prosecutions in Scotland, 35 members, chiefly Scotch representatives, supporting his protest in the division lobby, the House being so nearly empty that the Ministerial Whips could muster only 52 votes. Sir Herbert Maxwell descanted on the impropriety" of appointing solicitors in practice to postrnasterships, and Hr. Jesse Collings called attention to the action of the Charity Com- missioners with respect to the Allotments Extension Act, 18S2. He accused the Commissioners of conspicuously failing to assist in bringing the Act into operation, and cited many instances in support of his contention. Mr. MIINDELLA pointed out that a Select Committee had been appointed to inquire into the matter, and it was before this body that Mr. Collings's charges should be brought. It was ' impossible for the Rouse of Commons to form an opinion upon the n.—At nine o'clock these matters had apparently been disposed of, and the House was about to go into Com- mittee of Supply, when Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, reverting to 1 the subject to which attention had been called by Sir Herbert Maxwell, complained that the Postmaster-General had made no reply. Mr. Duff answering for the Government. With the assistance of Mr. Cavendish Bentinck, General Alexander, and finally Mr. Biggar, 35 minutes were occupied by this novel diversion. • Mr. Stanley Leighton next ap- peared, going back to the question raised by Mr. Jesse Collings, taking the opportunity at the same time to offer some remarks on Sir H. Maxwell's subject. SUPPLY.—At ten o'clock the House went into Committee. and made some progress with the Civil Service Estimates, The Premier returned to the House about this hour. and remained for some hours listening with lively interest to the discussion OR the votes for the Royal Palaces and the Duke of Wellington statue. Mr. Rueorfes moved to omit the vote of £2,000 on account of the improvements at Hyde-park-corner, which raised the question of dealing with the Wellington statue.—At twenty minutes to one in the morning the Committee divided, and the vote was agreed to by 54 votes against 51, a result received with cheers and counter-cheers.—Sir ROBERT PEEL gave notice to raise the question egein on Report, Mr. Gladstone agreeing that full opportunity should then be provided for discussing the matter.—Mr. Rylands and Mr. Cavendish Bentiack were terers for the Opposition, the minority being chi fly com- posed of Conservatives, though on this matter of artistic taste Mr. Biggar declared againstthe Government.—Progress being reported, the House resumed. BILLS.—The Public Health (Confirmation of Bye Laws) Bill was read a second time.—The Real Assets Administra- tion Bill was read a third time.—Mr. Trevelyan brought in a Bill to improve the administration of the Irish Con- stabulary. The House adjourned at a quarter-past two. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TunstetY. The House met at a quarter-past four o'clock. The Army (Annual) Bill was read a second time, and the Committee stage was negatived. THE Sonemet.—The Earl of CARNARVON severely criti- cised the course pursued by the Government in reference to the Soudan garrison, and remarked that though they had denied that they had abandoned General Gordon their con- duct looked very like desertion of that brave man.—Earl GRANVILLE said General Gordon, agreeing with the policy both of evacuation and not employing military force, ad- vised the Government to send him out; and, though he was promised co-operation, invould have been contrary to the character of his mission to have backed it by a military expedition from this country. He repeated what had been stated twice in the other House, that the Government left themselves under obligation with regard to the personal safety of Gederal Gordon, but they entirely declined to say , more on the subject at that moment.—The Marquis of SALISBURY said the noble Earl did not appear to value the deep anxiety felt by the whole of the country with regard to the fate of General Gordon,; and he believed it would insist upon some more actir demonstration of sympathy.— The Earl of NORTHBROOK repeated that General Gordon accepted the mission on the distinct understanding that it was to be pacific.—After observations from Lord Bury, Lord Waveney, and the Earl of Malmesbury, Earl GRANVILLE stated that the object of General Gordon's mission was two- fold—to assist the garrisons in coming away from the Soudan and to arrange, if possible, for settled government there. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--eTZFESDAY.

The Speaker toek the chair at ten minutes p ist two. FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—ID reply to Mr. Hicks, Mr. ,Donsom said that it was true that 15 cases of foot-and- mouth disease were found among bullocks sent from Liver- pool to Wimpole. The local inspector reported that the ,cattle came from America. Mr. Dodson undertook to have full inquiry made. ,LINNERAL GORDON.—ID reply to a number of auestions from Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett ard others, as to whether the

Government would lay before the House the despatch from General Gordon on which the Prime Minister founded his statement that General Gordon at Khartoum is in a posi- tion of security, Mr. GLADSTONE said the papers would be laid before Parliament with all the despatches, and this par- ticular despatch from General Gordon would be included; but the judgment of the Housemust be founded on the series —not on any particular one. In answer to Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, Mr. G,LADSTONE said that he had heard nothing of any yeinnteer expedition for the relief of Khartoum. The Government would certainly not take part in anything of the kind, for if it was desirable that such an expedition should be sent it would be their duty to undertake it them- selves.

CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) BlM—After some re marks from Mr. EIOGAR, who complained of the vexatious character of the restrictions imposed on the movement of cattle in Ireland, the House went lab() Committee en the Contagious Diseases (Animals) clause 1 Mr.• Donstm moved an amendment restoring the clause to the condition in which it stood before it was amended in the House of Lords. He objected to the alteration made by the Unter Rouse as going beyond the necessities of the case, and urged that his amendment would afford ample security against the introduction of foot-aect mouth disease from foreign countri4es.— Mr. HENEAGE and Mr. CHAPLIN op- posed the amendment on the ground that the bill, as altered lov the Lords, gave a security against the introduction of a disepe that would not be obtainable under the amendment prepostd by the Government..—The debate was continued by ' Mr. B. Arnold, Baron de Worms, Colonel Nolan, Mr. Duck- him, Mr. W. E. Forster, Mr, Rogers, Mr. Barclay, mr. Howard, Mr. Hastings, and after a reply from Mr. Dobson, the committee divided, when the numbers were— _ _ _

FIICKS- BECJI e,oriAt innci this course, asserting that if it meant . that the Bill wio tcr,be abandoned the country would accept

it as a proof of the insincerity ef the Government in deal- ing with the question.—Mr. W. E. FORSTER argued that the Government were only taking what was the usual coarse under such circumstances.—Mr. GLansrong reprobated the odioue charge made by Sir Michael hicks Beach against the Government, whose action in asking for time to consider their position he justified by stating that it was the usual course in the event of a vote, which, in the opinion of the Government, might have the effect of destroying the utility of the Bill to which it related.—After some further discus- sion the motion was agreed to, and the sitting was shortly afterwards suspended till nine o'clock. Irma NATIONAL SCHOOLS.—At the evening sitting Mr. BIGGAR moved a resolution, declaring it just and expedient that the teachers of convent national schools in Ireland should be remunerated on equal terms with the other teachers of primary national schools in that country.—Mr. HEALY seconded the motion—After some remarks from Mr. Meldon, Mr. Newdegate, Mr. C. Russell, Mr. Badmond, Mr. McCoan, Sir P. O'Brien, Mr. Harrington, Mr. Findlater, and Mr. P. Martin, Mr. TREYELYAN said the Government could I net assent to the resolutisn, as the rules of the commis- sioners were absolute, but, while it was necessary to main- tain a distinction between the teachers in the convent schools and the certificated day teachers who underwent examination, and who had to live by their school labours,. the Governmeit were anxiously considering the question in the hope of being able to find some means of apportioning the grants given to the convent schools to the results achieved.—After a few observations from Col. Coulthurst and Mr. Archdale, the House, divided, when the motion was negatived by 71 against 44.—Mr. MELDON moved a re- solution deprecating the delay of the Government in re- dressing the grievances of the Irish National School teachers as to resalts fees, pensions, residences, etc., but at one o'clock in the morning the House was counted out before the hon. gentleman had finished his speech.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. A House was not made until ten minutes to one. SITES FOR CHURCHES &C., BILL. Colonel NoLAN, when moving he second reading of the Sites for Churches, Teachers' Residences, &c., (Ireland) Bill, stated that it was designed to a large extent to allow of the voluntary sale, by owners of land, for sites for churches, schools, parochial residences for clergymen, and teachers' residences. The measure would in certain cases have a compulsory action, but that was guarded so that it should not cause inconvenience to owners, and if it were thought desirable to insert further safeguards, Pie should be glad to purchase support by making large concessions in that direc- tion. The causes which prevented sites being given for tb. purposes named were the way in which land was tied up in Ireland, the prevalence there of feudal ideas, and reli- gious intolerance. Mr. O'Simmvax seconded the motion, believing that, small and unpretending as the measure was, there were few that would do more service for Ireland. Mr. ARNOLD, while admitting that a grievance had been shown, felt that if English members voted for the bill they would be pledged to extend the principle of the compulsory acquirement of land for religious purposes to England, and that difficulties would arise from the great number of sects whose rival claims would have to be satisfied.

e` Colonel Kinn ItleaturaN said the bill was opposed to com- monsense, and would be used as an instrument of intimida- tion and torture for both landlords and tenants. lie moved that the bill should be read a second time that day six months. _ _ .

Mr. WARTON condemned the measure as absurd. Mr. GRAY ridiculed the idea that the hill woulel be used for intimidation, observing that the Local Government Board would protect landlords from any attempt to employ its machinery for the purpose of vexation. Mr. MARTIN supported the bill, and considered that it provided ample protection for landowners. Mr. TREVELYAN observed that both the process proposed by the bill, and the object to which it was to be applied, were new, sand though there was something in the principle which the Government approved of, they were not prepared to assent to the second reading, because by so doing they would, in their opinion, establish one of the most serious precedents ever laid down in the House of Commons. The bill would enable schools carried on for profit and religious schools not under public inspection to ha established on sites compulsorily purchased. As regards board schools, the Government were prepared to apply to Ireland the prin- ciple that had been adopted for England; but their objec- tion to the second reading of this bill was based upon the provision relating to the compulsory purchase of land for clergymen and schoolmasters, who had no greater claim to facilities for the acquirement of small farms than had tax collectors, doctors, and lawyers. He .had great hopes that the Government would be able to introduce this session a bill which had been already prepared, and which it was pro- posed to proceed with as soon as possible after the Irish Sunday Closing Bill, and which they believed would go far to satisfy all the legitimate aspirations of the promoters of this measure. Under those circumstances he trusted that the second reading would not be pressed to a division. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr. L. Stanley, and Mr. O'Donnell supported the bill.—Mr. Slums, speaking in its favour, re- marked that Mr. Trevelyan would be remembered as the Chief Secretary who admitted the existence of every Irish grievance, but never made an effort to remedy one of them. —Mr. DILLWYN would vote for the second reading.—Mr. FINDLATER also stated his intention of supporting the prin- ciple of the bill.—Mr. PLITNYET, although be sympathised with the object of providing suitable sites for places of wor- ship where they were wanted, could not admit the ex- pediency of applying the compulsory powers of the bill to that purpose.—Mr. ARCIIDALN declared that the landlords of Fermanagh had made liberal provision for the residences of the masters of schools. The House then divided, and the bill was defeated by 122 votes to 77 ; majority, 45. Mrscur.Labruous.—Mr. Brand brought in a bill to acquire Shensall Common, near York, for military purposes.—Mr. Cowen brought in a bill to provide for the better assessment and collection of municipal rates. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—THITRSDAT. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. INTERNATIONAL AFRICAN ANOCIATION.—The Earl of

FIFE asked whether Her Majesty's Government had any in- tention of recognising the International African Association. —Earl GRANVILLE said that as he understood it the Asso- ciation was a society which had been principally promoted by the King of tbe Belgians, not as a. sovereign, but as an individual on philanthropic grounds. He had that day re- ceived a telegram from the Government of the United States intimating that they recognised the flag of the Association as of the same character as that of a friendly Government ; but Her Majesty's Government would have to go much more fully into the subject before they could give a definite answer to the question now put.—ln reply to the Earl of DONOCKIIIMORE, who wished to know whether the Govern- ment had decided to send an expedition to Berber or to the relief of General Gordon, Lord GRANVILLE said that notice of the question ought to have been given. Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter to five o'clock.

local regulation, the duty on a four-wheel carriage would be the same as the duty on a two-wb el carriage. He ,+1:-k) proposed that where owners first ran a carriage after tee 31st of September only half toe tax shush' be paid. To loss through those changes would leave the original surplu- £l4l,ooo, which, he was bound to say, was not too large. He proposed to undertake also operations in connec- tion with the gold coinage and the interest on the National Debt. It was estimated that there were in the United Kingdom ninety million whole sovereigns and twenty million half-sovereigns. Of these 55 per cent, were light. The total deficiency amounted to £710,000. The sovereign was an international coin, but the half-sovereign was a purely domestic coin, and a very expensive coin to maintain. His plan for meeting the deficiency and restor- ing the coinage was to issue instead of half-sovereigns, ten- elahling pieces of gold containing only nine-tenths of the present amount of gold. He should restrict the legal tender of the new ten-shilling pieces to £5. This would enable the Government to withdraw the whole of the light coinage and substitute coins of the full weight without imposing any charge on the public, and he propounded a plan by wkich the Government would be able to maintain the integril of the coinage in the future without any charge upon the taxpayer. In connection with the interest on the National Debt, ne proposed to constitute a two and three-quarter per cent, stock with a qu,rterly dividend not liable for redemption until 1904, and to offer it to the holders of any denomination of three per cent. stook at a rate not exceeding £lO2 for each £lOO of three per cent., or, at the option of the fund holders, such an amount of the present two-and-a-half percent. stock at £lOB for each £lOO three per cent. stock. The right hon. gentle- man concluded by moving formally the resolution or the renewal of the Income Tax. (Cheers.) Mr. Wm.'s hoped the Chancellor of the Exchequer would at the first convenient opportunity take into con- sideration the incidence of the tobacco (Intim—Mr. MAC. IVER, Who was three times called to order by the Chairman for irrelevancy, suggested an impost on manufactured goods imported from the Colonies.—Mr. Alderman LAWRENCE ex- pressed approval of the proposals in regard to hackney cat- riages.—The debate on the budget was continued by Mr. Hubbard, Mr. Buxton, Mr. Gorst, Mr. Anderson, Mr. Pell, Mr. Monk, Mr. W. H. Smith, Mr. Arnold, and others.

div.head: NEW WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL
div.p: NEW WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL
AT WARRINGION.

On Monday afternoon two foundation stones of the new Wesleyan Sunday school, which is now in course of erec- tion, on a site adjoining the Bold-street Chapel, were laid by Dr. Mackie (in the absence of Mr. McMinnies, M.P.) and and Mr. C. Mitchell, of Liverpool, the latter gentleman offi- ciating on behalf of his wife, who was unable to be present. These schools, it may be explained, are being built to meet a want of accommodation and convenience which has long been felt in connection with the present school in Buttermarket-street ; and in this respect it is probable that all requirements will ba amply met for many years to come. The new erection which is, as we have stated, on a site closely adjoining the chapel, is intended to accommodate 800 persons, and it has been specially designed to answer all the purp,ses to which Sunday schools are usually put. The central portion of the building will be taken up by a large room, of the dimensions of 50 ft. by 53 ft. 9 in., provided with a gallery on the east, west, and south sides, the north side being appropriated for a rostrum or platform. On the east and wen sides of this room the gallery will be sup- ported on cast iron columns, in the manner usually seen in chapels, but on the south side the gallery will stretch back over the four class rooms and vestibule, which will occupy the lower story of the front of the building. At the east and west sides of the main erection there will be lower buildings, which will be apportioned Into class rooms, secretary's and librarians's offices, lavatory, etc. In all there are to be 13 classrooms, the largest of which, the infants' and the males' and females' select rooms, measure 21ft. by 1711 and 21ft. by 151 t. Pin. respectively. The large room, it may be men:ioned, Is to be provided with movable seats so that it can be used for other purposes besides that of merely seating an audience. Ample means of ingress and egress are to be provided, there being besides the main front entrance, two side entrances. From one of these stone stairs lead down to a cellar or heating room, in which will be placed the heating apparatus necessary to warm the building by means of hot water pipes. Good ventilation is secured by vertical inlets sup- plied with "hit and miss" gratings for the purpose of regula- ting the supply of cold air, while the vitiated atmosphere is let out by means of outlets in the ceiling. With regard to the exterior of the building it was originally intended that an ornamental tympanium should be placed on the top directly above the main entrance, and also a smaller one over this entrance, but on its being found that the cost was likely to be larger than had at first been anticipated, these embellishments, which would certainly have given the school a more pleasing and attractive appearance, were sacrificed to the main purpose of providing interior accom- modation. Bricks manufactured by Mr. Edwards, of Ruaben, are used in the erection of the building, the dress- ings being of Cefn stone. The roof will be covered by Welsh slates and red ridge tiles. The architect is Mr. Owen, of Cairo-street, Warrington, and the contractors are Messrs. Collin and Son, Academy-street, Warrington. With respect to the cost a statement will be found in the report given underneath of the meeting on Monday eveniog. The ceremony of laying the found Aiwa stones took place under most favourable circumstances, although the absence through illness of Mr. McMinnies, M.P., who was to have laid, one of the stones, somewhat detracted from the eclat of the proceedings. The weather was suitable for an open-air ceremony, and consequently there was a large gathering of spectators. At half-past two the Sunday school teachers and scholars assembled at the Buttermarket-street schools, and there forming into procession walked to the site in Bold-street, preceded by the Sunday school banner. At the new schools a temporary platform had been formed to ac- commodate the children and the others who were present, ' and this was soon more than filled. Amongst those pre- sent were—The Rev. T. McCullagh, president of the Wes- leyan Conference; Mr. Charles Mitchell, Dr. Mackie, the Revs. J. Eglinton, J. McTark, J. A. Beet (of Wrexham), R. W. Starr (of Liverpool); Messrs. T. B. Carter, R. G. Hen- shall, J. B. Isaacs, J. Taylor, E. Guest, J. Hartley, R. Gar- nett, T. Prince, M. Bowden, W. Barlow, E. Bolton, &c. The Rev. Thomas Rippon was unable to be present through ill- ness, which, on sianday, prevented his preaching.

Mr. T. B. CARTER said he would read the contents of the bottle which was to be deposited in the stone, and then read from a sheet of paper, which was to ba put in the bottle, the following names :—The President of the Wesleyan Con- ference (the Rev. T. McCullagh); the ministers of the War- rington Circuit, the Revs. J. Eglinton, superintendent, J. McTurk, and T. Rippon ; officers of the Buttermarket-street Sunday School, Mr. J. Taylor and Mr. J. B. Isaac, superin- tendents; Mr. T. B. Carter, treasurer; Mr. R. G-. Henshall, general secretary; names of the committee, Messrs. E. Ford, W. Y. Lawton, W. E. Nicholson, W. Weave, W. Parkinson, James Evans, John Toft, J. J. Sanderson, T. Prince, E. J. Guest, Joseph Dobson, and John Hartley; trustees of the Bold-street Chapel and School, Messrs. Joseph Smith, M.D., R. Cook, E. B. Bowser, A. Lamplugh, T. B. Carter, John Guest. T. J. Down, •E. J. Guest, R. G. Henshall, John Taylor, J. B. Isaac, E. Ford, W. Gleave, Simnel Moss, J. J. Sanderson, J. Hartley, T. S. Smith, M. 8., and Wm. Barlow. Also the name of the architect of the schools, Was. Owen, Esq., and of the builders, Messrs. John Collin and Son • and also the estimated cost of the school, including furnishing, £3,300. There were also some current coin of the realm, viz., Is., 6d., 3d., Id., 11., and id. (Laughter.) There would likewise be deposited in the bottle a copy of the "Methodist Recorder," a programme of that day's proceedings, a circuit plan, a Warrington Examiner, and a Guardian." . -

The Rev. J. Eousrox then said they all knew from the announcement that the first stone was to be laid by their esteemed and excellent representative—the representative of Warrington—whom God long preserve, J. G. McMinbies, Esq. He was sorry to say that Mr. McHinnies, who for some time past had been on the Continent, as he (Mr. Eglinton) understood, in search of health, had returned home in a state of great prostration. He regretted very much to say that he had received from Mr. McMinnies that morning the „ .

following letter :—" Dear Sir,—At almost the last moment I have to relinquish my intention of laying the foundation of your schools. lam laid up with a ”ry pl!nful illness; and am quite. helpless. I enclose a cheque kir VCI in aid of your enterpfise, which I hoped to have personally advocated. —I am, yours faithfully, J. G. McMissrms." (Ap- plause.) He need not tell them with bow much regret he received that letter, a regret which was shared by all the officials of that school, and, he hoped, by the people generally. And he could not help thinking that it would also be received with sorrow by the inhabitants of Warrington—(hear, hear,)—amomrst whom Mr. McMinnies was deservedly well " respected. They should take some opportunity—either at that meeting or the even- ing meeting—of e ',pressing their sympathy with Mr. McMinnies, and also their great regret. However, they knew, whatever be the fate of any of them, work must go en, so in their extremity they had turned to a gentleman who occupied a prominent position in the town, and who no less than Mr. mc.Miunies was in keen sympathy with the great work of Sunday school teaching, and several of the officials connected with the school waited upon Dr. Mackie, who received them most kindly, and under .the circumstances very willingly responded to their request to come and lay that stone. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Eglinton then presented Dr. Mackie with a trowel and mallet with which to lay the foundation stone, an expressed the hope that they would be kept in his possession for the remainder of his days, and
afterw. ards bequeathed to his heirs and successori. (Ap-

plause.) Dr. MAMIE then formally laid the foundation stone, and, addressing the assembly, said he appeared before them that afternoon at something like three or four hours' notice. But it would have made no difference if the friends who had called upon him had found him fast asleep, and it had been a quarter to three o'clock. lie considered be was so indebted to Warrington for all he had and all he was, that, irrespec- tive of a Sumlty school, he must ever be at the bidding of any of his fellow-townsmen. (Hear, hear.) Ile lamented on their behalf that Mr. McM;anies was not there that after- noon, but there were three reasons that made him feel—al- though it was presumptions on his part, as it would no doubt appear in the eyes of many, to accept that position—why he might be forgiven or his offence palliated. Mr. McMinnies and he had been acquainted for the last 30 years, and he was sure that Mr. McMinnies would be glad to know the evert in that out-of-the-way, that round-about manner, he ( Dr. Mackie) had endeavoured to fulfil the lune- tiott—,he glorious and honourable duty—which was iaid upon him. Mr. McMinnies they knew MOst certainly would not have gone back from the discharge of that duty if health had permitted. (Hear,

div.head: HOUSE OF CONIMONS.-THIIIISDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF CONIMONS.-THIIIISDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. EGYPT LIM THE SOLID/N.—Several questions were put to Ministers on Egyptian affairs, and in reply to one by Mr. Bartlett, it was stated by Lord E. FITZMITYRICH that no information had been received at the Foreign Office to the effect that Nub sr Pasha had declared that he would resign unless relief were sent to Berber. It was also stated that Lord Granville had sent to our Consul at Suakim certain suggestions on the subject of the slave trade for his obser- vations upon them. He hoped to lay papers on Egyptian subjects on the table by Tuesday next.—ln reply to a ques- tion whether a relief expedition would be sent to Berber and Khartoum, the PREMIER said Berber was in danger, and communications respecting its conditim had been received from Egypt; but, considering the interests involved, it would not be proper to make any statement. As to Khartoum, the Government saw no reason to modify the opinion they had already given that there was no military or other danger now threatening the place. The Government shared in the feeling of interest and strong sense of obligation felt in the country with regard to the safety of General Gordon, and they had put themselves in a position to fulfil those obliga- tions, If the occasion should arise, in the sense in which they believed the country along with themselves recognised them. He had no reason to believe that there was any danger of the garrison of Barber baing overtaken by the fate of the garrison at Sinkat. The rumour that the Council of Ministers 'at Cairo had decided to vnd an expedition consisting of half English and half Egyptian troops to Berber was widely apart from the fact, but to give any further information would be prejudicial to the public in- terest.
_ TEE CATTLE BILL.—Mr. DODSON intimated that the in- tentions of the Uovernment with regard to the Cattle Diseases Bill will be made known to the House after the questions on Friday. _ _ THE BUDGET.

In Committee of VTa—yrs—a-ti'd—ileans the EH/NCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER made his annual financial statemem. The right hon. gentleman stated that as to the esti- mate of revenue for the coining year it was not very easy in the present position of the country to forecast what it would be. In many branches trade was still depressed,l and the income from land, whether by owners or far mere, was still unsatisfactory. He thought there was a general tendency towards improvement, pauperism was steadily de- creasing, and although there was some complaint amongst persons in east, circumstances there was a steady increase in the accumulations of the cmintry. (Applause.) ....--........_ Mr. MITCHELL expressed his deep regret, and that of his I wife at her not being able to be present. If it had been possible she would have been there. Her interest, not only as regarded the Battermarket school, but Warrington Methodism generally, was not a whit less than it was in 1871, when he took her from Warrington. He heartily re- joiced that the desire that had so long been cherished had now been accomplished. There was no stronger proof of the decay of any church or society than the proof that they had when a sunday school was neglected, or the interest that was taken in it was declining. There was no branch ' of Christian work that had accomplished such blessed re- sults in every grade of society as Sunday School work. How much the country owed to that work they should never know until the great day revealed it. The love of Chris- tian truth that was thus spread in the minds of the chil- dren would yield a blessed harvest, and was doing so now. The records, not only of ministers, but of missionaries, who were going amongst the densest parts of the crowded popu- lations, showed that they found those who had sunk to the deepest depths of depravity, and who, coming in contact with the missionaries, were reminded of brighter days, and were led to the truth which once they despised and rejected. , He then presented a cheque for £5O towards the cost of the schools. (Applause.) Th. Rev. THOMAS MCCULLAGH, President of the Confer- ence, said that he was glad to have an opportunity of say- ing something in connection with the interesting proceed- ings of the day. He had not seen the Buttermarket school, !but it had been spoken of in one of the addresses given as a place of inconvenience and discomfort. If so it was un- worthy of them, and be was glad now that they were about ,I to erect premises more worthy of their character, resources, II wealth, liberality, Christian enterprise, and of the actual , requirements of the case. (Hear, hear.) He need say nothing in praise of Sunday Schools in Lancashire, where they flourished to a greater extent perhaps, than in any other part of her Majesty's dominions. But, holding the office which he now had the honour to sustain, he might be permitted to sey a word or two about the connection of idethouism and Christian education. (Hear, hear.) He would remind them that Methodism originated in a University—in tbe ancient and renowned University of Oxford—and that the first founders of their societies were not ignorant and blatant apostles of rhapsody ; but that they were educated men, were scholars, and that they were gentlemen as well as Christians. The two Wesleys themselves—the sons of a learned father —were first educated in two famous public schools—John in the Charter House and Charles in Westminster School— and then both of them proceeded to Christ Church, Oxford, and John obtained a fellowship in Lincoln College in that Unieersity. They originated what was called the united societies. Their first society was one of students at Oxford, and their first studies were in the Greek Testament, a fact which their learned friend and brother and their former be- loved minister, Mr. Beet, would very highly appreciate. The first studies of the first Methodists, significantly enough, were in the original Greek and the New Testament. They were not, therefore, likely to say what an ignorant religious man was reported to have said, when he heard of the edunition of ministers," What have we to do with Greek ? Did Paul know Greek ?" asked that ignorant man. They mast not forget that it was they who founded amongst the people in London the United Societies, in 1739, from which the Methodists of to-day had their origin, and that they ob- tained as the first Wesleyan chapel in the metropolis an old foundry, and put it into shape for religious worship. Very soon was established in connection with it an elementary day school. (Rear, hear.) They must not forget that in connection with the first Methodist chapel there was a Methodist day school, at the old foundry, and that its first master was a prison philanthrophist, and anticipated in the form of Christian philanthrophy the labours of Howard himself. Then Wesley established the Kingswood School, a name which had become famous in connection with the educational institutions of the day. At first the school was for the children of the laity as well as for others, but for want of funds it ultimately became neCeeearily a, seminary for the education of preachers' sens. The SCIIOOI, in new premises near Bath, etia eXisted. ile plid an official visit to it a few weeks ago end Vag tt in its enlarged condition. He there eaw whet he questioned was to be found in any other school in the country—what was called a 8.A.. class. (Applause.) In that class, he believed, were thirteen people, all of whom tied passed the intermediate examination for his Bachelor of Arts degree. (Hear, hear.) Then whilst they had that school for the education of the sons of the clergy they had not forgotton the laity. They had very efficient colleges, both at Sheffield and. at Taunton, which were affilieted to the London University, ad recently £10,090 was granted from the thanksgiving fund for the purpose of encouraging the establishment—by grants and by subsidies—of middle class schools for both sexes. Several of these schools had been established already and more were in course of com- pletion, and, again, in connection with the elementary edu- cation of the masses of the couetry they had now, in Great Britain 854 day schools with 131,500 scholars, land they ° took a very high position amongst the day schools of the country, comparing favourably with Board Schools, belid he was eve lChurch of England, British, and other schools. If &tikes were the founder, as he was said to have been, he (the Sneaker) forgot not the fact in connection with it, that a Methodist lady of Gloucester—afterwards the wife of one of the early Methodist preachers, and one of hispredecessors in the chair of the conference—suggested first to Ralkes the idea of the Sunday school movement. One Sunday Raikes pointed out to this lady a number of children playing in the streets, and asked "What ehould we do itacenneatia4 with these children ?" to which she answered, "Let us teach them to read and take them to church." YOLNG MEN'S SOCIETY (CONGREGATIONAL Cnuncu).— The fifth soiree of the above society took place on Wednes- day evening, in the Marshall Memorial Schools. The enter- tainment consisted of songs, recitations, dialogues, harmo- nium solos, d;c., by members of the class assisted by a few friends. The audience frequently testified their apprecia- tion of the eff rts put forth for their amusement and benefit. During the evening refreshments were handed round to the company, consisting of fruits, coffee, tea, Jrc.

1 - POLICE NEWS.—A man called Walton was charged with being drunk near the Navigation Inn, on Sunday night. P.C. Roscoe heard him using bad language to a boy, and advised him to go home, upon which Walton struck him, and he had to have the assistance of P.C. Hunt to arrest him. A private in the Cheshire Militia, called Fiaherty, came out of the Navigation Inn, and attempted to rescue him. He drew off his belt, and struck the police-constable with it. —Mr. Arthur Arrowsmith saw the assault, and ap- peared as a witness against both prisoners.—Halton was also accused of assaulting P.C. Hunt.—The Mayer said the charge against both men was very serious, and they were both remanded to the Eddisbnry Petty Sessions for the assault. Halton was fined 5s and coats for beicg drank.— The prisoner had the doubtful honour of being the first to I be incarcerated in the new police cells in High-etreet.

The Fifteen went in first ; Marriott opened the game and showed his stamina by curving out his bat, with 25 runs to his credit. W. Gorst served his side well with 29, and G. Bernard 16, the iFifteen's total amounting to 149. The First Eleven had six wickets put down for 16 runs when time was called. HUTTON-WITH-ROBY LOCIL special meeting of the newly.elected board was held in the Public Offices, Blacklow-brow, on Tuesday, for the purpose of electing chairman and members of committee. There were pre- - sent—Messrs. T. Dobell, T. Didzell, G. Banner, 2. .T. Grimshaw, J. B. Harrison, J. E. Parker, R. Brown, C. Cooper, E C. Leventon, and J. Siddeley. Mr. Harrison proposed and Mr.. Brown seconded a proposition that Mr.. Dobell be re-elected chairman of the board. Mr. Parked' moved as an amerdment that Mr. Leventon be chairman, seconded by Mr. Cooper. On being put to the vote, four voted for the amendment and four for the resolution, whereupon Mr. Dobell gave his vote in favour of himself, and so was re-elected. tine fealowing were elected to serve on the several committees :—Highway and Sanitary: Messrs. Leventon, Brown, Siddeley, Dalzell, Banner, Grim- shaw, and Parker. Finance: Banner, Cooper, Barnyeate, Siddeley, Harrison, and Parker. Sewage Farm j Pinning. ton. Dalzell, Harrison, Burnytate, Leventon, and Brown. PRIBENTATION TO THE Ray. W. T. SOUTHWARD.-0/1 Thursday week a deputation consisting of Messrs. W. 'Busby, junr., W. H. Crook, and Thomas Evans, waited upon the Rev. W. T. Southward, M.A., for the purpose of pre- senting him with an illuminated address and 36 volumes of books, subscribed for hy a number of friends in Huyton, on his leaving for St. Catherine's College, Cambridge. The address, beautifully illuminated by Mr. 11arples. of Liver- pool, is as follows:—" W. T. Southward, M.A. In the name of a numerous body of your friends associated with us, and on oar own behalf, we ask you to accept this address and the volumes of books accompanying it as a token of the affection and esteem you have secured by year ministration of nearly five years as curate in the parish of Huyton. It is a source of deep regret that you will n.o longer be resi- dent amongst us, but we feel bound to offer you our con- gratulations on your preferment to the chaplaincy of St. Catherine's College, Cambridge, and what your friends in Huyton will lose in yeur departure will' be the gain of new friends drawn to yen by the kindness of your nature, your moral and intellectual worth, and your zeal for Christianity. We wily appreOhlte And thank you heartily for what you have done in the past; siZnl ;lave won our esteem as a pastor and a friend, and by the alltined excellence of your addresses from the pulpit you have cOmmanrild our adMiCgo tion as a scholar and a Christian gi-ntleman. Earnestly hoping that a bright, happy, and useful future is before you, we wish you God speed in your new duties, and remain," signed on behalf of the aubscribers, Wni. Busby, junr., W. H. Crook, churchwardens; Thomas Evans and Isaac Foun- tain, sidesinen.—Mr. Sputlaward thanked them in appro- priate and feeling terms for their handsome gift. The books consisted mainly of standard works of reference in theological, musical, classical, and scientific subjects.

div.head: EXAMINER. BATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. BATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1884.

IT is with a feeling of r2gret, which we are quite sure will be very widely felt, that we lay before our readers the announcement that Mr. McMiNNIEs intends to retire from the representation of the borough at the close of the present Parliament. We publish in another column the letter on the subject which the honourable gentleman has ad- dressed to Mr. S. RIGBY, as chairman of the Warrington Liberal Association. The cause of his retirement is revealed in the single phrase we quote from the letter—" advancing age and declining strength." It was hoped. that rest and residence abroad would be the means of restoring •the health of Mr. McMlms4lEs, but, although he is now so far improved as to warrant his return to the House of Commons, he feels that he cannot count upon being equal to the arduous labours of another Parliament. It is natural that the members of the Liberal party should " hope against hope" that this decision will not be final, but we fear it must be regarded as irrevocable, and, as "health "as EMERSON says, "is the nrst wealth," no one can blame Mr. MCMINNIES, under the circumstances, in the course he feels compelled to take. He is member for Warrington as the result of the triumphant majority oi the last election, and member he would remain, after another elec- tion, if he could be prevailed upon to allow himself to be again nominated. He has shown himself Liberal in every sense of the word, while he has displayed such ability, tact, and geniality in serving his constituents of every class and creed, that he commands the respect of his opponents and excites the enthusiasm of his supporters. Warrington was proved to be a Liberal borough when it returned Mr. MCMINNIES to the House of Commons by a majority over Sir Gilbert Greenall of 529, and we need hardly say that Liberalism has grown under his fostering care. If he shculd really have to lay aside the honour he has worn so well, we are quite sure he will leave the Liberal party in such a condition that there need be no fear as to the return of the Liberal candidate, whoever he may be, who may be nominated to succeed him. But it is not for us at the present moment to say what should be done; that will be the duty more especially of the general Liberal Council, which will be called together within a few days to consider the letter addressed to them through the Chairman of the Associa- tion. If there is the faintest hope of suCcess, the desire will be unanimous that Mr. McMINNIEs should be asked to withdraw his proposal to retire, for, from the highest to the lowest, the members of the party are proud of him, alike as a local linder and as their representative in the House of Com- mons.

Timm Opposition seem to have recovered ill ' some degree from the knock-down bloW which the PRIME MINISTER delivered when Sir STATFORD NORTHCOTE raised a forroal debate, under cover of a motion for the ad- journment of the House, on the question of the policy of the Government in relation to the affairs of Egypt and the Soudan. They show great recuperative capacity—especiall when there is a chance of doing mischief. And what could be more mischievous than incessant questions and discussions as to what is being done and about to be done in the Soudan? Lord CARNARVON complained on Tuesday that an unciphered telegram had In one case been despatched to Berber, implt ing that officers of the Government should be careful to send instructions in cypher, so that information as to the carrying out of various plans should not by any chance get into the hands of the rebels. Lord GRANVILLE at once admitted that if such a telegram had been sent it was a mistake, but pertinentll added: "It is exactly the mistake which the Government have been exposed to by the constant pressure on the part of this Houser and still more of the other House, calling upon us to say what we will do and what vi,e, won't do. It is exactly the same mischief:, There was a time when from motives 0' patriotism the party in Opposition, whether Liberal or Conservative, refrained from prey sing for information as to particular opera" lions in foreign affairs, on receiving all, intimation from those in office that it was ne` in the public interest to state what was beiog done. But all that is at an end now; rot' withstanding that HER MAJESTY'S MiHiSterS, have in both Houses again and again definea the lines of their policy in the Soudan as be; ing evacuation along with the removal 01 the Egyptian garrisons, the Opposition, solely, as it would seem, with a view to erfrt barrass the Government, put questions nigh" after mght of such a nature that it would 13e impossible to give direct answers to theril without playing into the hands of the enenl. Y" Indeed, if certain members of the Opposition were the paid agents of the Soudanese, theft could not more effectually serve the cause the rebellious tribesmen. There is, to hc_ sure, a profession of great anxiety as to the position of General GORDON; even Lot° SALISBURY talks of his being exposed t° certain death at the hands of the Arabs., while Lord BURY improves the occasion o_3" speaking of" holding those in power respou_ sible for his bloody fate." It is said by C°°,.l seriatives in both Houses that Ge.ner4__ GORDON is being abandoned, and Lord bAL.tris. BURY prophesies, if silence is persisted. 1 a catastrophe which will cover Englarl; with disgrace." It is much more latelh °re would think, that an open mouthed disclostu. would lead to a catastrophe by cnabling:_f, rebels to check-mate the plans in prOgr "

Yesterday Mr. A. T. Squirey, eolicitor to the Dock Board, sketched the history of the Liverpool Dock estate. It originated in 1709, andsince that time had been managed under the direction of Parliament as a public trust. The whole of the revenues were expended on the dooks, and any excess was under the obligations of the Act of Parlia- ment applied to a reduction of the rates. 'The only per- sonal interest of the members of the trust was in keeping down .the rates, they themselves being merchants, -ship- ownersoke. DITTON VESTRY MEETING.: A 'DEAD LOOK.—The ad- journed meeting of the parishioners of Ditton Church was held on Saturday evening, but not in the "Brown Cow," as had been announced by several newspapers, but in the vestry adjoining the church. As 'neither the vicar '(the Rev. J. Cassels Brown) nor his warden (Mr. A. E. Smith) had put in vi appearance, Mr. R. Lewis, the people's warden, presided. There were present—Messrs. if. Hallowee, W. W. Smith, A. G. Kyle, Balehaw, James Brown, Joseph Gorton, R. Bailey, S. Cartwright, and R. Glover.—Mr. Smith said he had got the credit of making certain insinua- tions andimputations against the Vicar at the last meeting. 'He had no intention of imputing anything against their parish priest—the Chairman was very glad to hear that declaration. Certain indiscreet expressions were used at ',the last meeting, but he denied that there was any resolu- tion of adjournment to the 18rown Cove."—Mr. liallowes proposed Mr. Kyle as vicar's warden, but that gentlemen refused to take any office at all in connection with that church.—Mr Roberta did not see how they could expect anyone to take office if the wardens were to be several pounds out of their pockets each year.—Mr.Ha,lowes said that was the fault of the wardens. An appeal to the congregation would be sufficient to raise the money-Mr. Smith remarked that the vicar had premised to indemnify any warden for any deficiency that might arise during the ensuing year.— The Chairman asked for volunteers for the office of vicar's warden, but none were forthcoming; and an attempt was then made to appoint a people's warden, but without succese. No parishioner would accept the office, and Mr. Hallowes remarked that the pablie spirit of Bitten was very low. After waiting several minutes, the Chairman declared the meeting adjourned indefinitely. He supposed the old wardens would have to consider themselves in harness until the authorities acquitted them. He should officially inform the vicar and the bishop, through the archdeacon, that at a vestry duly summoned it was found impossible to appoint any churchwardens. He wished the Press to convey to the public that up to the present time the conduct of affairs at that church had been perfectly harmonious. There had , been no bickering, no squabbling, and no interruptios of the i services, and each person had, he thought, tried to do his duty in the venous offices they bed occupied in connection , with the church. He should not like Bitten Church to get a bid name with the public, because neither the church or the people connected with it deserved it.—The pro- ceedings, which had lasted about thirty minutes, then terminated.

CONSECRATION OF VIM BISHOP OF CI:MPHIL—Dr. Stubbs was consecrated Bishop of enterer in York Minster yester- day morning. the ceremony being most imposing. At eleven o'clock the Dean and Chapter, clergy and officials proceeded to the west &or nave to receive the Archbishop, the assisting Bishops, and the Uishop-elect. The proces- sion returned to the choir where the Epistle was read by the Bishop of Manchester, and the Gospel by the Bishop of Durham. Dr. Kay, chaplain to the Bishop of St- Albans, preached the sermon. The comecration ceremony was per- formed by the Archbishop of York. FOOMBALL.— Wigan v. Warringtcn : On Saturday after- noen the abova match was played at Wigan. The Wigan Club has held the Wigan Union Challange Cup since its institution, and are also left in the final tie with Amu% to be decided on Saturday week, this match being arranged for their practice and clearing Oa debt against the club. The Choice of goals was won by the visitors' captain. The kick etf was followed by a run by Barnes and put into touch in the home team's quarter. Boardman threw out, and a drop by Clarke forced Wigan further on their line. Morris was then prominent, making to ust round, and being pressed threw to Slavin, who ran splendidly almost right through -eel on the line, Jolley and Barnes pushed him back into touch, a touch down resulted. The state cf the game until a moment or so of half-time was level scoring. A scrum- mage near the Warrington line enabled Morris to get pos- session of the leather and to cross the line. The place was a failure. Turner restarted frOrn the centre after a short rest. Per a length of time the visitors played with great dash, but they could not prevent Wigan from mewing, as klevin,Bray- abaw, and Mason, each got a try, though the last named actually had the ball given him. Owing to Clarke kicking eat instead °reeving, the try was disputed that Slevin got, "ing to going into touch. Anderton kicked the goals. Belshaw, by means of a grand run and pass to Whittle, was the cause of the latter getting a try, Turner failing at goal. Barnes also dropped a goal, but owing to neither of the on- hares (who were standing near touch line) seeing, it was not allowed. A second time Whittle crossed the home team's line, and was successful in a maul with the opposing back, bat foing di.poted the visitors gave way. At the conclu- sion Of the game the :core V:l3 Wigan two vale, one goal _disPuted, one t:'. and to minor points; Warrington one uyt and four minor points. • •

VISIT OF BARGER TO RUNCORN.—FrOM our announce- ment columns it will be seen that OR MOllday evening next Mr. TOM Barger, the ventriloquist and mimiz, will give his inimitable entertainment in Runcorn Public Hall. Tit Err OF Cxcrrnma..—At the Kirkdale Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, Andrew Walsh (42), a labourer, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for stealing a muffler and coat from Thomas Daley, at Widnes. on the sth inst. WIDNES CHURCH OF 'ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.— Vie weekly meeting of this society was held on Thursday evening, under the preeidency of Mr. John Format, and there was a good attendance. A programme of songs, read- ings, and recitations was contributed to by Messrs. J. Iles• keth, G. Hesketh, F. Hartland, John White, A. Carter, and F. Cave. Miss Wilkinson accompanied the songs on the Piano. The Rev. J. Wright Williams delivered an address Eleven new members were enrolled. It MR. GLADSTONE AND THIS SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE "LIBERALS.—Mr. Gladstone, replying to the resolutions re- cently passed by the council of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Associa-tion, expresses his gratification at the manner in which the Franchise Bill has been received in the coun- try, and at the large majority by which the second reading has been carried. On the subject of "obstruction," he ex- presses his fears that it will not be pessible for the Govern- ment at the present time to again approach the question Gf

..... _ P.,rliamentrary procedure. DEATH AT WIDNES.—The police have reported to the Coroner the death of George Titnperley, 70 years of age, who lived in Widnes-road. For five years deceased had been unable to follow his employment, and had been in receipt of club money. He had been confined to his house for the past three years, gradually becoming more feeble, but no doctor had been in attendance upon him for several months. On Sunday he because very ill, but his relatives did not think it necessary to send for a doctor until Thurs- diy afternoon, and at half-past four when Dr. MeCambridge arrived at the house Tinuperley was dead. Dr. McCain. bridge attributes death to natural decay. MARRIAGE OF /A WIDNES MANUFACTURER.—The marriage rites between Mr. F. C. Liddell, a ,netnher of the firm of Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co., alkali manufacturers, Widnes, and Miss Kathleen Lane Fox, of redcastor, near Leeds, were solemnised in London on Tuesday. The Widnes works were rendered gay with flags and bunting in honour of the occasion. As a token of the respect and esteem in which he is held by them, the workmen have presented Mr. Liddell with the complete works of Scott and Dickens, making in all 55 beautifully bound vblumes. The presenta- tion was madeby the oldest.workmen, and Mr.T.Glover made a few appropriate remarks. Mr. Liddell suitably acknow- ledged the gift, referring to the amicable relations which had always existed between the masters and their work- people. BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.-011 SURCIay a bey, 9 years of age, named John James Kinsey, son of Samuel Kinsey, labourer, 14, Muspratt-street, died from burns re- ceived on Thursday, the 10th instant.—About eight o'clock on the evening of that day, the deceased got out of bed and went downstairs with his mother, and other members of the family remaining in bed. He was attempting to reach something from the mantelpiece when his shirt caught fire, and he was enveloped in flames. The mother hearing bis screams ran downstairs, and extinguished the flames my throwing a sack around him, but not before the whole of his body had keen seriously injured. His wounds were dressed by Dr. McCambridge, who attended him up to the time of his death.—On Wednesday morning Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Bradley Hotel, and evidence in accordance with the above facts having been given a verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.
