CRICILIT.—St. Paul's and St Elphin's C.C., Warrington: A match was played between the above clubs on Saturday, and ended in a victory for the former by 32 runs. Scores: St. Paul's, 69 ; St. Elphin's, 37; Williams and Cooper bat- ted well for St. Paul's, and Draper for St. Elphin's—St. James', Latchford, v. Earlestmon, St. John's: This match was played on Saturday afternoon, at Earlestown, and re- sulted in a victory for Latchford by 76 runs. The batting of the visitors was very satisfactory. This was their first match of the season. Although Earlestown tried several changes of bowling, Latchford were notdismissed until they had scored 1015. St. John.'s 30, St. James' 106.—St. John's v. Warrington Clarence : A match between the 'above clubs was played last Satard ty, on the ground of the latter. St. John's, who batted first, scored 05, the chief I contributors being E. Earle, 16, and T. Bibby 9. The 1 Clarence team in Unir innings could make no stand what- ever against the enlondid bawling of J. Wilcock and E. Lightfoot, and were all out for 26 runs, thus leaving St. John's the victors by 39 rune.--Springfield it. Crescent : This match was pkayed on the ground of the former on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the Springfield by 57 runs. Scores.: Springfield 100, Crescent 43. RUNCORN BOARD OF COUMISFFONERS.—A special meeting was held on Thursday morning under the presidency ef Mr. J. Meadowonft. There were present Messrs. Norman, Shaw, I Fisher, Briscoe, Williams, White, Brookes (secretary). and ' Barker (serveyor).—Genera* District Rate: Mr. W. Fishef moved the adoption of a recommendation of the Finance Committee that a general district rate of 2s in the should be laid. The estimates of the various committees for the ensuing year had been drawn up. The canal boats and hos- pital committee estimated an expenditure of £49, general purposes £1,007. highway and sanitary £1,945, parliamen- tary and legal £5OO, finance including library £1,493. The rents and market tolls were expected to realise £393, in ad- dition to which they had £413 lie 91 in the bank, and these sums deducted from the estimated expenditure of £5,160 8s left £4,328 16a 3d to be raised on the rate. A rate of 2s. in the Lon £43,600 would produce £4,360, so that they would hove about £3O over and above the present require- ments; and the committee therefore tQlt justified is re- commending a reduced rate this year. The rate last year was 2s 3d in the t--Mr. Norman seconded the motion, and expressed his satisfaction at the reduction that had been made. lie wished the rate to be is 10d, but it wee found impossible to lay en small a rate.—The motion was carried unanimously and the proceedings terminated.

THE WIDNES t-,SSISsSIIENT APPEAL : SUCCESS SOF THE APrELLLNTS.—At the Kirkdale Court of Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, in the case of the appeal ef Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, aad Co., alkali manufacturers, of Widnes, against an assessment of the Assessment Committee of the Preecot Union, and which had been referred to tha arbitration of Mr. J. B. Edge, and iwhich has 'been privately beard in Man- cheater during the past three months, Mr. Snarrcw, appear- ing for the apeellants, stated that the award bad been made, I and be aeked that it shoald now be confirmed 'by the court. —Mr. Swift, far the respondents, agreed to the acceptance of the award, and it was accordingly confirmed.—The Arbitra- tor, in his award, stated that the appeal was against a rate or assessment-in which the gross estimated 'rental of 'the alkali works of Messrs. Gasket, Deacon, and Co., wat alleged to be the sum of £8,333, and the rateable value to' be the sum of £EB73. He awarded that the gross estimated rental of the works and hereditaments owned by Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. was at the date of the assessment, at the beginning of last year, £5,7k8 (and not £8,333 as alleged), and that the rateable value thereof was at the same date a,039 (and not £5,873, as alleged by the Assess- ment Committee), and that the rate at 2s 6d in the pound appearing on the said rate ought to be £504 17e 6d instead of £734 2s ad, and he ordered and directed the rate and assessment tube altered and reduced accordingly. He fur- ther ordered that the costs and charges of the appeal and the referee should be horns and ,aid by the Assessment Committee.—lt is understood that a number of other cases of appeal will be affected by this important judgment,which also affects the value of the alkali manufacture generally.— The court then proceeded with the trial of prisoners. - ST. EDWA.HD'S AMATEURS, RUIZ:CORN:The amateur dramatists in connection with St. Edward's Catholic Schools gave their annual performance in the 'Public Hall, on Mon- day evening, in aid of the Catholic institutions in the town. A large audience assembled, and seemed highly pleased with the entertainment, which combined music with the drama. The programme commenced with a masterly rendering of the song, "Erin, my country," by Mr. Joseph Motrison, who later in the evening delighted the audience with sing- ing "Norah, the pride of Kildare," and he was heartily encored. Miss Jamieson sang" Laddie" with much pathos and sweetness, and in response to an encore she repeated the , latter portion of the song. Miss Florence Haves, of Liver- pool, a lady who possesses a voice of consitierable parity of tone and power, contributed GADS'S Charming song, " Sing, sweet bird," with tacte and feeling, and she won a hearty encore. She then favoured the audience with "Kathleen Mavourneen." Mr. McElhenny, of Liverpool, gave ceveral comic songs. The interest of the evening's entertainment centred, however, du the drama, "Pike O'Callighan," which has been previously performed by the Amateurs with suc- cess, and was reproduced by general deeire. The piece affords much scope for good acting, as it abounds with humorous and exciting situations, but on this occasion, al- thongh there had been vary little alteration in the east, we cannot accord the members the approbation we had ithe Pleasure of doing two yeats ago. The most excellent parts fell flatly, the services of the prompter being too often c died into requisition. To Mrs. Hutch and Mies Parker and Mr. Thomas Williamson mast be accorded the credit of any re- deeming features in the performance, and a good word must , also be said for Mr. J. Parker. The cast was as follows: Sic Jamec Blackadder, Mr. James Coleman; Neil O'Connor, Mr. J. Byrne; Pike O'Callaghan, Mr. Thomas Williamson. ; Red Burnie, Mr. John Parker; Captain Wilson, Mr. T. ; JAines, Mr. Robert Williamson; Lady Broaghton, W The enter- tainment jlueldnytc,hiviasHteorsnoreoo;eCraaall:gahnad illiamson. e, Miss M. Parker; Biddy I concladed with tile farce, "That Rascal Pat," is which Mrs, match, Mies Parker, Messrs. Thomas William- son, Bernard Conies, aad James Coleman took part. Mr. • Carr, of Liverpool, furnished the scenery, which was highly appropriate. Mr. Ravenscrott ably acted as accompanist. The Irish National Band was in attendance, and during the . evening gave several selections.

DRUNK flO COURT.—Mary Ann Wilson and Mary Spencer, young women .of bed character, were summoned for being drunk in the It ancern Police Court on the 15th inst. The case was proved by Superintendent Williams and P.C. Bos- sons, and the defendants were fined se, and costs 9s 6,1, or, in default, seven days. SERVICE OF SONG AT WIDNES.—The choir of the Star of Temperance Lodge of Good Temp Lars, assisted by several, friends and instrumentalists. on Monday evening, render3d the service of song "Poor Mike," in Widnes Public Hall, to a good audience. Mr. S. Palin pr sided. The Rev. W. Vause, of Runcorn, read the interesting narrative, and the choir was conducted by Mr. Geo. Bullivant. ROYAL SOCIETY FOR THE PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO ANIMALS.—The Mayor and Mayoress of Liverpool distri- buted this Society's prizes, consisting of elegantly bound volumes of the " animal world," together with a certificate of merit to the succeisful essay competitors at the annual meeting, on Friday, at the Liverpool Town Hall. Amongst the recipients were Clara B. Clarke awl William McLean, both of. Weston Point. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AT WORII.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, the following persons were each fined 5s for neglecting te send their children regularly io school :—Witliam Moores. Peter Crogan, John Cotterhall• Henry Skelding, Isaac Bostic; Richard Clynch Thomas Billington, Mary Ann Horton, Martha Hillidge, William Brazendale Adam Peacock, William Lightfoot, Thomas Conway.—Mr. Bowyer proved the cases on behalf of the School Board. LICENSING MATTERS AT WIDNEI. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the magistrates being Messrs. H. S. Hall and Holbrook thiskell, jun., the following transfers were granted :—fhe Vine Inn, Waterloo-road, from William Ormesber to Edward Bankes ; the Beehive Inn, Albert-road, from Joshua Thomson to John Smith-, the Central Hotel, Victoria-road, from J. W. R. Fowler to Alfred Parkes ; the Railway and Commercial Ina, Victeriairoad, from Alfred Parkes to Wm. Ormesher. A VIOLENC YOUTH AT WESTON POINT.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Molyneux, 12 years of age, was summoned to answer a charge of assaulting Mary Elizabeth Ritchley, 10 years of age. On the Bth inst the girl was taking a basket containing eggs to a place at Weston Point. She bad to pass through a gateway, hut the defendant stood there and refused to allow her. She then sat down on the grass, and after solos time the defendant said he would let her go; but when she grit to the gate he seized her, threw her on the ground, sent some water upon her, and other wise ill-treated her. He smashed all the eggs in the basket. The defendant, wine pleaded guilty and took the matter very coolly, was fined 5s and costs. DAMAGING A WIDNES PUBLIC-HOUSE.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and J. Brock,John James Miller, a coloured man, who stated that be had been a slave in Sonth Carolina, was brought up on remand, charged with wilfully breaking a pane of glass at the Market Hotel, occupied by Alfred Machin.—lt ap- peared that on Saturday evening the prisoner entered the hotel in an intoxicated condition, and refused to leave when requested. Machin was at length compelled to thrust him forth. Whilst this was being done the prisoner smashed the window of the folding door, doing damage to the extent of £2 108.—The prisoner said the breaking of the window was an accident. He eppealed to the Bench to deal leniently with him as he had a wife and two children, and if he were 3ent to gaol he would lose a whole summer's employment. —I-le was ordered to pay a fine of fie end eosts $3 81, and the damage, total £3 2s 6d. AN EXPENSIVE DRONE AT HALTON.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph and Charles Howard, young men, were summoned for having, on the 11th inst. at Hal- ton, by falsely representing themselves to be travellers, ob- tained intoxicating liquors, to wit, beer, during the period when the house should have been closed. The defendants pleadedeguilty. It appeared that the defendants on the afternoon of Good Friday went to the Norton Arms and re- presented that they came from Appleton, beyond Widnes. They were each served with a glass of beer. It was sub- sequently discovered that they lived in Lock-street, Run- corn, and the landlord issued a summons.—Mr. 0. Thomas (ehairomeN paid the miblicane were placed in a very awk- mird position through such conduct as the defendants. Bach defendant was fined 20e, and toots Os 61.—Superin- , tendent Williamson asked that half of the fines should go 'towards the police superannuation fund, and the magistrates granted the req,aest. A WIDNES BOILER MAIER IN TROUELII.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, Enoch Walton, a boiler maker, from Widnes, was cllarged with stealing a flannel coat, worth 235, the property of Edwin unison, pawnbroker, Church-street, Runcorn.—About half-past four on the previ- ous afternoon the prisoner was. observed to take the coat, which was hanging on a hook outsdle of the shop, and Mr. Colley, the pawnbroker's assistant, chased the prisoner and eventually captured him. He had the coat in his possession. P.C. Brown took him into custody.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and remarked that h'e had been drinking heavily for some time past and scarcely knew what he was doing. He hoped the Bench would deal leniently with him —Superin- tendent Williamson said inquiries had been made of the Widnes police, and he found that the prisoner had borne a good character. He was in a very nervous condition through drink.—A fine of Ll and costs was imposed. ASSAULT ON A. WIDNES POLICEMAN.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, before Messrs. Holbrook Gas- , kell, junr., and John Brock, John Clare, a watertvan, living lin Fryer-street, was charged with being drunk and disor- derly and with assaulting P.C. Holbrook. Oa Wednesday the constable saw the prisoner and two other men go into several public-houses in Waterloo-road. They asked to be supplied with drink, but were refused, and they then went to the Bridge Inn, Church-street. From this place they were ejected, and commenced a disturbance in the street. The constable asked them to quit the street, but Clare de- clined, and when he was taken into cuttody be strack the constable in the face with Ins fist, and kicked trim. He was remeved to the police station with the aid of the ticket collector at the Runcorn Bridge.—The Bench fined the pri- soner 5s and costs 63 6d, or seven days for being drunk, and 10s and cost 43, or 14 days' imprisonment for the as- sault. WIDNES i'.:CIIOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting ws held on Thursday, Mr. T. S. Tinamis in the chair. There were present the Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon. Shaw, Glover, Davies, Imison, and I anby (clerk.) . . . . .

INCREASES OF beLARY. - The minutes of the General Purposes Committee which were passed on the motion of Mr. J. Brock, contained the following recommendations:— That the salary of Mr. W. Peacock, the junior clerk, be in- creased from £4O to £5O per annum: that the wages of Caretaker Hughes, of the Simms Cross Schools, be increased srom 218 to 25s per week; and that the wages of Caretater Birkenhead, of the Warrington-road Schools, be increased from I.Bi to 20s per week.—A scale of salaries for payment of school attendance officers was adopted. The salaries are to rise from £65 at the first year's service to a maximum of £lOl.

DEFAULTERS'-The District Education Committee reported that during the month of March (four weeks) there had been 64 applications for the payment of school fees, and that 249 persons had appeared before the committee for con- travention of the Act. Fees were recommended to De paid in 55 cases, and 57 persons were prosecuted before the magistrates, 52 being convicted. Two children were sent to intustrial schools, two cases were withdrawn, and ohs attendance order was obtained.—The minutes were passed, on the mo- tion of Mr. Deacon. 'SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.—Tho School Management Com- mittee recommended that the resignation of Miss M. Urqu- hart, assist, et mistress in the junior girls' department of Simms Crosa School, be accepted. It was also recommended that Miss A. Mullen be engaged as teacher of cookery in the Board Schools ate salary of £BO per annum, the engage.ment to date from June I,t and to be determinable on either side by one month's notice.—The Rev. Father Finegan moved the adoption of the recommendations, and the mo- tion was passed. FINANCE.—Mr. Shaw presented the report of the Finance Committee. Accounts amounting to £1,385 3s 3ci were re- ctums-landed for payment. During March there had been paid into bank £ll2 94 3a on account of school fees; hire of rooms, £3 18s 84: gas consumed by contractors during alterations at Simms Cross Schools, £37 Is di; goods sold to children, £1 14s 3d; from overseers on account of pre- cept, £1,000; total, £1,125 3s 81—The report was adopted. OVER-PRESSURE IN BOkilD SCHOOLS: HOME LESSONS CONDEMNED.—III acc6rdance with the notice he had given at the last meeting, Mr. Glover asked the chairman of the School Management Committee what arrangements existed, or were to be made, to prevent the possible abuse of home lessons in the Board schools. Allow him, he said, to say t hat he did not believe in home lessons at all; and he wished Father Finegan, in reply, would state that the com- mittee proposed. to abo :oh them. In his opinion they were of very littlJ va.rae, and caused a lugs amount of friction One of the best teachers in the neighoourhood, who was not under the Board, had told him that they were a loss of time, as they bad to be set at night to ba examined in the morn- ing, and were frequently found wrong, and punishment had therefore to be administered. In the absence of any friendly hand to guide them through their home lessons, the children had to do them themselves, and he believed the Board would be doing a good thing when they could say they would abolish them altogether. There was the question of the abuse of home lessons as they now existed. Abuse arose mit of the very system becauso children under ten years of a g Were geTh blate reSsone, The infant schools certainly were exempt, but children who were precocious rose from the infant department into the junior and even the senior departments at the age Of t*Ven Or eight years: and these children were having these tasks as tire home lessons used to be c riled. He thoui.ht they would all agree that children of 10 years of age ought not to be burdened with these things. Those members who sat on the district Education Committee were quite aware that they were forcing to attend school regularly children who were weak, and subject to nervous excitement and head- aches, and who, their parents said, were sick in the morning. It was desirable that the Board should have some regulation to prevent children of this description from being over- worked or given these lessons at all. He had had to exer- cise his parental authority in two such cases in his own family with manifest advantage. It might be said that it would not be desirable for all parents to exercise their right in this matter. The Boyd took the right out of the hands of parents saying how the child should be educated. He advocated that children in standard one, and chileren under ten years of age or of delicate constitutions should be exempt from home lessons. Another abuse was that about the tune the schools were to be examined by the inspector, the chiliren were kept in school until five o'clock. He could not find fault with this, because the teacher might find a number of scholars who did not understand the lea- sons, and he thought it would be an advantage to stop with them and explain the matter. But having been kept in until five o'clock he thought they should not have any tasks at home and he should like the School Management Committee to have a regulation to prevent that. Respect- able parents bad come before the Education Committee and told them that their boys, who used to be bright lads, fond of going to school, had been made into truants by the ex- cessive application of home lessons and the chastisement they had received in consequence. It was a fact that the greater number of punishments were administered to chil- dren who had failed to learn their home lessons. The time was cerning when the pressure of lotime lessons would have to he dealt with, and he thoueht the Board ought to do 'something at once.—The Rev. Father Fiotgan said per- sonally he almost agreed with Mr. Glover, but the difficulty the tcommittee had to contend *ith was how to bring about the desired result. They were very anxious indeed to es.- tattish, if they ceuld. a system that would not be injurious to the _ children, And he assured the Board that .

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The first week of the resumption ef Parliament after the Easter recess has been unusually momentous. We have had the Budget introduced, important statements made on Egyptian affairs, and a defeat of the Government. . This last was not of the kind that affects the duration of Minis- ters. If 20 Liberals went into the Opposition lobby 10 Conservatives supported the Government. The division ' was strictly on the lines of pocket, not on the lines of party. It turned out that 185 members had been convinced—in some cases with reference to their own personal position, in others by pressure of their constituences-that it was desirable to have butcher' meat dear; 161, representing large consti- tuences, were emphatically in tavour of having meat cheap, and of course the larger number settled the question. It would be interesting and instructive if someone were to tabulate the names of the "ayes" and the " noes" in this division, showing the number of the constituencies severally represented. In spite of a majority of 24 it would prob- ably appear that as far as actual representation of the people went cheap meat was declared for by five to one. Yet, un- less the Government can find some way out of the difficulty, we shall have dear meat; very dear meat, possibly meat at famine prices, for the amendment introduced into the Cattle Plague Bill in the House of Lords, and approved by a ma- jority in the Commons on Tuesday, makes it possible that at any day the Privy Council might find themselves com- pelled to cut off the United States and Canada as sources of the supply of the English market. Mr. Gladstone came back to the House on Mn day look- ing surprisingly well. But the event of Tuesday upset all the good that had been accomplished by his ten days coun- try rest, and no one was surprised to hear, yesterday morn- ing, of a return of his weakness. ,If he could only take things quietly there is apparently no limit to the duration of his energy. But that is impossible. His power of re- cuperation is phenomenal. Apparently hopelessly worn out on a Friday night he comes back on Monday, having spent the interval in the country, as fresh and bright as if he had not done a day's work for six months. Then something goes wrong. He plunges into the middle of the trouble. ineists upon taking it all on his own shoulders, and else evil is done again. He had absolutely nothing to do in the House on Monday night after questions were over, but he could not stay away, re-appeared after dinner, and became profoundly interested in the discussion on the civil service estimates. He waited for the division that took place at half-past twelve, and then began to write that letter to the Queen which always seems the last straw that breaks the back of the overburdened minister, a straw which the late Mr. Disraeli, wiser in theee emelt things, passed over to his feithtel. efeepanion, Lord Barrington. Thanks to the engrossing discussion on procurator iscals and legal postmasters in Scotland which the rules of debate in the House of Commons mike masters of the situation, the civil service estimates came on for discussion at so late an hour that they were not fully reported in the newspapers. This is a pity, as few things in a comparatively small way are so interesting as these debates. They bring to light the existence of some astounding things in proof of the in- eradicable tendency of royalty to make incursions great if possible, small it it must ee, upon the public parse. Most people would suppose that having palaces provided they would be kept in repair out of the sufficient civil list, which is not too heavily drawn upon from semi-public directions. But the discussion on Monday night disclosed that this year £36,603 are paid fur the maintenance of Royal palaces, a reduction of £4,000 on the expenditure of last year. A curious fact was brought out with respect to Marl- borough Rouse. When the Civil List was settled it was agreed that a reasonable sum should, in addition, be allot- ted for the maintenance and repair of Royal palaces. That, of course, establishes the principle and dotes the contro- versy, the yearly debate in the House of Commons being directed against the palpable extravagances of such charges as, for example, £1,251 for a year's repairs and maintenance of the Royal Mews. When the Prince of Wales set up a separate establishment there was a choice open to him among the palaces unoccupied by the Sovereign. There was not to go further afield Buckingham Palace, centrally situated, and which everyone would like to see tenanted. Bat the Prince chose his own residence. For the first year or two, he, aftet the fashion of ordinary householders, paid ter repairs himself. Then an occasional vote was got through the estimates, and finally, whilst the courtly Lord Henry Lennox was First Commissioner, an arrangement was made by which a sum of £2,000 a year should annually appear in the votes on account of Marlborough House. Last year this had ran up to £2,958, nearly 50 per cent on the allowance. There was some ominous growling, and this year it has been be:eight down to £2,160, a triumph for the little band of economists who keep a watchful eye upon this elastic expenditure. Funny little episodes, rarely reported, take place in the House of Commons towards one o'clock in the morning. There was one yesterday morning in connection with the count out. ilk. Love Jones Parry—whose parliamentary fame has hitherto rested upon his introduction of the sys- tem of delivering a speech in two parts, sitting down abruptly in the middle of his remarks with intention, not yet fulfilled, of concluding them an another occasion—under- took the duty of preparing for a count. Whilst Mr. Meldon was warming to his work, redelivering a familiar speech on thettatus of school teachers in Ireland, Mr. Parry, moving aboetrthe House with comical assumption ot secrecy, was *Melly getting members out of the way. He had in the oourse of ten minutes reduced the numbers low enough for a count to be essayed, and the Speaker's attention was ac- cordingly called to the fact that there were not forty mem- bers present. Mr. Parry, baying piloted a member out, re- turned to the doorway, and noticing one other member whom he felt sure he could induce to leave, and not observ- ing that the Speaker was Already on his feet counting, stole Into the House and crept along under the shadow of the gallery towards his friend.. "Fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eigh- teen," said the Speaker with the three-cornered hat outstret- ched, indicating members at he counted. Mr. Parry had just ' 14301100 within range of the hat, and to his manifest consterna- ton and the uproarises reerrimeat of the House he was him- ' self counted in. But no harm was done. There were only thirty-three all told, and the House adjourned. This is the canniest thing that has happened at this witching hour since Warton, remaining on guard with intention of blocking number of bills, fell asleep behind the Speaker's chair, and woke when the gas was turned out to learn that the bills ehad been advanced a stage. Itill the evening papers came out. Mr. Warton says that,, if not directly due to the machinations of the Liberal Govern- ment, it is a remarkable fact that no earthquake befel during the nearly seven years the Conservative Government were in office; a statement which is certainly incontestable. I happened to be in San Francisco when an earthquake oc- curred, which was said to be the worst known in the city for , twenty years, and an earthquake in California is of quite ordinary occurrence. The reeking is indescribable and un- mistakeable. I was not expecting an earthquake at the time, had no earlier experience of the sensation, but had not the slightest doubt as to the meaning of the phenomena. An English officer who conspicuously distinguished him- self in the late campaign in the Soudan is not so enthusiastic about the pluck of the Arabs as we are in England. He has fought both with Zulus and Arabs, and holds the former in- comparably superior ell the score of bravery. The Arabs wear shot, proof shirts (made of English calico and blessed by Osman Digma) and other charms, and, strong in faith, they rushed upon the English square. Bat when once they Ind the charm is not invincible, they are not by any induce- ment to be led a second time under British lire- whereas the Zulus would charge again and again. Front this characteristic the gallant colonel, though amongst the most strongly insistent upon the relief of Khartoum, protests his belief that Gordon is in no danger. "The Arabs," he say,. "will not attempt to take the place by assault, and if they do Gordon is quite able to give them a useful lesson."

I received this morning from Nice a box cf dowers, which I observe cost for postage 30 centimes, being a fraction under 33 in English money. I weighed the box, and found that, being empty, I could not have sent it across London for less that 2id. This is a curious anomaly considering that it came ad across Europe from Dover to St. Martins- le-grand, and thence to my louse all for another half- penny.

snt GILBERT GREENALL AND THE TRADE INTEREST OF WARRINGTON. Sir,—Having found that my letter upon the above sub- ject had caused some little commotion in the hearts of Sir Gilbert and his friends, I considered it would be wise to allow the "storm in the teapot" to subside before I ven- tured to trust my barque again upon its troubled waters. Judging from the offence my letter has given in certain quarters, one would be inclined to think that the ex-member had gone through a piefcess of transmigration that placed him above the region of human criticism. But, sir, though he may be in thought "upon the side of the angels," like the late Lord Beaconsfield. yet to my vision he isstill human in shape. lam certain those who had the good fortune to hear Sir Gilbert deliver his famous speech at the Latchford Ward meeting must have felt a great amount of pity for their leader to see what a struggle he had to appear as the gay humourist while he was visibly affected at the rude conduct of a Radical. He stated that he was much indebted to Mr. G. Woods for hi able support. I was myself amused at the very able defence set up by this esteemed friend of -mine. I was reminded of a trial scene described by Charles Dickens in his famous Pickwick papers. Why, sir, the ap- pearance of Mr. G. Woods at the two recent Conservative meetings is easily explained, and for those who understand what has brought him to the front it does not require a moment's consideration. I deny the right of Mr. G. Woods or any gentleman in his position to become a judge of my motives in entering into a correspondence with another per- son when his assumptions have Ant one meaning upon the face of them. Allow me to tell Mr. Woods that, while grate- ful to him for the manner in which he eulogised my humble efforts, I am a stranger to the system of wire-pulling. Neither am I compelled by force of the circumstances of my position to do anything except that which I feel myself at liberty to do. Therefore I beg to be excused from holding any correspondence upon this subject with any person only Sir G. Green ell. and him alone. I hone any one of his friends who feels eager to take up arms in his defence will take this gentle hint. To any impartial persons my letter could not have given any offence, but when subject to the political horoscope of some of my Tory friends, I do not doubt the hitter seemed a deg !tar or some other monster. But to the main issue of my letter—l insist upon an answer from our esteemed ex- member. I ask again to what extent has he assisted to build up the trade interest of Warrington. This is a question which requires to be answered with lucidity and not by am- biguous expressions. This he shonld do at nice to put him- self right in the estimation of his fellow-townsmen, and I suppoee he, like most public men, has set his heart upon the pursuit of that -ambition. lam prepared to admit that he is a most charitable man, but like the Tower of Pisa his charity has a great leaning in one particular direction. Per- haps I touched a tender chord when I mentioned the new church at Walton, but I spoke the truth about it. I find that some strange fatalism seems to hang about it. It's present condition must be a great source of disappointment, and upon that point I would beg to offer him my sympathy, trusting at the same time that he will do me the honour of answering my letter.—Yours truly, THOMAS FLOOD. 9, Catherine-street, Bewsey-road, Warrington, April 22nd. A WESLEYAN MINISTER ON THE "ELOQUENT AMERICAN." Sir,—l formed one of a large congregation who listened with great pleasure to an interesting discourse by the Rev. J. Colwell, of Liverpool, on Sunday evening last, at Run- corn. Touching on social matters, the preacher said some very sensible things. And as the members of "the cloth" are not noted for any great wisdom in their pulpit deliver- ances on such subjects, it may be well to refer to his re- marks. It is only in the pulpit, however, that the members of the preaching profession display their ignorance of mun- dane affairs, and descend to the region of turgid twaddle; for those who have had to do business with the class have found them pretty wide awake. "The children of this world "are not now a-days "wiser than the children of light," if the parsons are to be taken as a sample of the lot. But on this occasion Mr. Colwell said some very per- tinent things on the subject of the social condition of the masses, ahont which so much has been said and written of late. He told us that the life and teaching of Jesus threw light upon the question of "bow the poor live." A gentleman was seated on the top of an omnibus in a large town and saw a great number of working men leaving a factory, some of whom he noticed had exceptionally good Goats on their backs, and carried umbrellas. Turning to his neighbour on the 'bus, who happened to be a policeman, he inquired the reason of the difference between the work- people. " 0," said "Robert," " them's Methody chaps. When they get converted they recken theirsels as good as anybody else, and think they 'av a re'et to wear a good coo at every day, an' they get a nmbereller to keep it dry." The effect of a man getting religion has an influence on trade. "Suppose," said Mr. Celwell, that instead of men spending their money on drink and gambling and other wickedness, they fitted themselves op with good clothes and did the same for their wives and children, and made their homes comfortable with requisite furniture, what an impetus would be given to our home trade. The tens of thousands of people who are in enforced idleness would find immediate and remunerative employment, and peace and plenty would be the order of the day." Christianity on its practical side needs cultivating. The political economist has too long overlooked this f ictor in the nation's well-being. I should like to know why drapers, grocers. ironmongers, butchers, and bakers are content to see their money going into the tills of the publicans, who are almost the only ready money shopkeepers in the town. But Mr. Colwell had no occasion to misrepresent the author of " Progress and Poverty," whom he styled the "Eloquent American." He lead scored pretty well in showing clearly how religion, if applied, would be the remedy for the social ills from which the State is so sadly suffering; and there was all the less need for this cheap sneer at Mr. Henry George. In spite of Mr. Colwell, and of the order to which he belongs, there are thousands who are seriously studying Mr. George's pro- posals; and they are not, as he supposed, the Tay and drunken, but the toilers who wish to receive a fair return for the expenditure of muscle and brain in the nation's workshop, and not to have the heart-breaking prospect before them of grinding toil till past work and then the refuge of the Workhouse, where they may end their days among the vilest of characters and under the rod of iron wielded by officials only a trifle less vile. Are the hard-working patient fellows who keep the wheels of the country's trade in motion likely to countenance any scheme of robbery? It WAS an insult to his congregation for Mr. Colwell to have 30 garbled Mr. George's theory of Land-Nationalisation, and to make believe that he had studied the works of the "Eloquent American" when it is questionable whether he has even read them. His story about the girl and her "pa" was miserably weak. If the strong-minded female who proposed to sell all her "pa's" furniture, rte., and distribute the money to the poor could have proved that said "pa" had stolen the articles which were to be sold, then there might have been some force in the illustration. But her " pa," we suppose, had honestly earned the money with which he purchased the articles which were so ruthlessly sold by auction for the public benefit. Such a thing cannot be said of the great landowners, nor of their ancestor,. Private property in land is at the root of England's poverty, which is increasing daily, while the rich are getting richer, and in course of time it will occasion little surprise that men will have sunk so low that they will sell themselves and their offspring into slavery, and your landowner will also be slave owner. "Britons never shall be slaves !' Non. sense. The grit is going out of the race, and another "Primrose Day" will see the so-called " sovereign people" under the iron heel of the bitterest tyranny the Tory party has ever exercised. "The price of liberty is Eternal 'Vigilance," and the people have ceased to keep their eyes open.—Yours, CASSANDRA. Runcorn, April 21st, 1884.

TIIN CZONCH RISPIITS AT ST. HELENS: MEETING OF Faw-ownaes.—The dispute with respect to the payment for pews at the-Parish Church of St. Mary, St. Helene, is at- tracting some attention, and an adjourned meeting of the pew-owners WAS held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday after- noon. According to the circular convening the meeting the business WAS to consider the pew-owners position in regard to the action of the lato churchwardens (Menrs. Wind us and eachley) in doing away with pew rents and assesstnents. About a dozen pew-owners were in attendance, including Colonel Gamuts (rave was elected to preside), Mr. A. Sinclair, Mr. Benwis, Mr. G. J. Critchley (late people's warden), Mr. J. Kitchen (preect vicar's warden), Mr. F. J. Brown, and Mr. W. Lllmb. At the commencement the Chairman said he noticed the reporters were present, but as that was a private meeting of pew-owners to consider their own position and their own intereaie he thought it only right that the non peo-ownefh and reporters should retire. After this intimation the reporters and several per- sons present who were not pew-owners left the room and the matter was discussed in private. We Learn, however, that a letter was read from the present wardens setting forth their intended course of action, which will provide free seats for the accommodation of the parienionece. The meeting unanimously approved cf the prugiainine !mounted by the wardens.

ST. HELENS. SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY. A shocking occurrence, resulting in the death of Sarah , Silver, 31 years of age, wife of Arthur Silver, bottle maker, residing at 53, Glover-street, St. Helens, occurred on Satur- day night. The exact facts of the affair are somewhat , shrouded in mystery, and considerable excitement was soca- , sioned in the district —lt appears that the husband of the , deceased returned home about ten o'clock, and at once fell , asleep on th sofa. Nothing was definitely known as to what , afterwards transpired, but about twelve o'clock the husband was awakened with the screams of his wife, who was in the kitchen with her clothes on fire, while their infant child was on the sofa and its nightdress wasalso in flames. Two neigh. bours burst open the door, and with the assistance of the husband the tire was extinguished. The child was badly burned about the legs, but the poor woman was shockingly burned over her body and legs. She was carried into a neighbour's, and Dr. McNicoll's assistant attended shortly afterwards, but it was seen that the woman was past re- covery. She was never able to give an account of how she had her clothes ignited, but she lingered until ten o'clock on the Sunday morning, when she expired. An inquest on the , body of the deceased was held at the Running Horses Hotel, Liverpool-road, on Tuesday at noon. The following • evidence was given :—Arthur Silver, glass bottle maker, 53, Glover-street, deposed that the deceased was his wife. When he returned home about 10 o'clock on Saturday night last, he lay down on the sofa and fell asleep. He was awoke about a quarter past twelve by hearing screams and he saw his wife in the back kitchen. Her clothes were all in flames—he could scarcely see his wife for the flames. At that time some one came and burst open the door, and 1 , one or two neighbours came L. Witness ran for the police- I man. and Dr. M.Nicoll afterwards saw her. She died about 10-30 on the following morning. He could not say how she got on Ere, and had not the least idea how it happened. There was a big fire in the grate in the kitchen. When he awoke he found their child on the sofa, and its nightdress was on fire. He did not know how the child got on lire, but it was burnt about the leg. Witness burned himself in try. mg to extinguish the dimes—The Coroner: When you came home on the Saturday night were you sober ?—Wit. Hess: I had had some ale, and was not properly sober. In reply to a juror witness added that he tried to put his wife's clothes out, but was compelled to run out in consequence of the fire and smoke.—Martha Aspinall, residing in Glover. street, said she was passing Silver's house on Saturday eee, sa ,acs newt% dwha nlh then ld ansmht heebseucrat deceased's et rrcioeeoudapgs eethnhd thbhe husbanddywoi aonwrd. aoywA.. extin- guished msS hah nee ' night whendarsmeLh, narmeaemdedPtheie liu)ropirn,akta,,advaendtebvewi daesnoefe, drunkenaftafter w habits.— which st. e had no idea at all how the Ere ir ricinated. div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL 26, 1884.

• EARLESTOWN. CTOOD TEMPLARS MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.—A meet- ing of the members of the Hope of Barlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. when theie was a good attendance, and Bro. John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. After several items of business had been discussed a social party was held. After an enjoyable tea had been partaken of, a miscellaneous en- tertainment was given, the various selections being much

appreciated. FIRE AT A DEAFER'S ESTABLISHMENT.—ShortIy after two o'clock on Saturday afternoon last, an outbreak of fire occurred at the establishment of Mr. E. T. Evans, draper and clothier, Market-street, Earlestown. A portion of the wood-work in close proximity to a stove in-the tailors' room above the back portion of the shop got over-heated and burst into a blaze. Some alarm and excitement was tem- porarily, occasioned, and the room was Soon filled with smoke. Fortunately the fire was early discovered and ex- tinguished before much damage was done. THE HOIISHHOLD STORES TEA PARTY AND CONCERT.— As reported last week the annual tea party aid concert pro- moted by Mr. Molyneaux, of the Household Stores, Market- street, for the benefit of his customers, were held on Easter Tnesdrty in the new building erected off Wargrave-road, by Messrs. Slee and Co. On Saturday evening a sort of sup- plementary gathering was held in the same place. A large number of persons were present, and indulged in dancing to the strains of Mr. Appleton's string band up to about eleven o'clock. Everything passed off as pleasantly and success- fully as was anticipated. SINGING CLASS TEA. Pawn, &c.—The annnal tea party and dance in connection with the Newton St. Peter's singing class was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday evening, the annual concert having been held on the previous evening, as reported in our last issue. An ex- cellent tea was provided, and about 150 persons were pre- sent. The cdmparny heartily enjoyed themselves in dancing until about half-past three on the following morning, the music being supplied by Mr. Burgess's string band. The dances were interspersed with selections of music by mem- bers of the class, which were much appreciated. The masters of ceremonies were Messrs. John Hall and Thos. Fairclough. THE CHURCH SCANDAL AT EARLESTOWN. FURTHER SCENES.

It is with regret we cannot record a settlement of the un- seemly squabble which exists at the church of St. John the Baptist. As would be gathered from the report of the en- thusiastic vestry meeting held last week, the parishioners manifested a determination not to retire from the ppsition they have taken up, and after the unanimous re-appoint- ment of the old officers--including Mr. If. J. Darman as organist and choirmaster—a renewal of the unseemly scenes which have recently been witnessed in the church was a foregone conclusion, unless the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Mat- thews) submitted to the unmistaketbly expressed wish of the parishioners. But this course, judging from the past, was net expected. During the week many rumours were circulated, the truth as to which it was difficult to ascer- tain. It was freely asserted that the vicar had decided to close the church, and another statement was to the effect that the vicar had received a letter from the Bishop's Secretary stating that his Lordship bad made up his mind to take im- mediate steps to bring the Earlestown Church dispute to a close. Some weight was given to this latter report by the visit of Mr. Gamon (the Bishop's legal adviser) and the Rev. G. Carson, of Liverpool, to Earlestown on Friday. An inquiry of a private character was held in the vestry of the ehurcn and several persons were examined. None of the parishioners' representatives, however, were called to give evidence before the gentlemen holding the inquiry. Consider- able doubt and uncertainty existed amongst the parishioners as to what the result would be, but it was pretty generally understood that summonses had been applied for against certain persons for brawling in the church and interrupting the service. It will be seen that this latter statement is correct, and that an attempt to compromise has failed. Up to Sunday morning opinions were about equally , divided as to whether or not the church would be open for service, but about ten o'clock in the forenoon all doubt was set at rest by the tolling of the church bell as usual, prepa- toiy to service. A large number of persons attended at the , usual hour, many evidently having gathered in the expec- tation of witnessing another scene between the vicar and the supporters of Mr. Darman and the choir. Those who did so, however, were disappointed. It was ascertained that the vicar left Earlestown presumably for Liverpool on the Saturday evening, but before departing he left written in- structions for the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate) for the con- duct of the service on the following day. They were to the effect that there was to be no singing; that the organ was not to be played, and that if the parishioners and wardens in- sisted upon singing and organ playing the service was im- mediately to be concluded after the publication of the banns of marriage. The curate acquainted the wardens and sidesmen with the instructions he had received, but he was informed that the parishioners and church officers meant to haves nging in church, and that if he (the Rev. H. E. Smith) concluded the service it would be carried on by the parishioners themselves. The curate was thus placed in a most awkWard and painful predicament; as he has been in fact ever since the dispute commenced. Anxious to avoid a recurrence of the scandalous proceedings of the previous Sunday he ultimately consented to give out cer- tain hymns which had been selected, and consequently the services—both in the forenoon and evening—were of the usual character. Mr. Durman presided at the organ, and the members of the choir were in their usual seats. The hymns and psalms were heartily sung by the whole con- , gregation, and apparently the service was greatly enjoyed and gave satisfaction to everyone present. The curate was I the preacher on both occasions. Shortly before the sermon was preached considerable commotion was occasioned by a person who entered the pulpit and wished to "make peace" , in the church; ut fuller particulars of the extraordinary I doings of this " remarkable individual" are narrated below. The church was crowded to its utmost extent in the even- i ing, but no untoward incident occurred. In addition to singing the hymns and psalms, the choir impressively rendered the anthem "0, give thanks unto the Lord." The Rev. H. E. Smith afterward preached an excellent and earnest sermon from the words God is light" (St. John. let chap., sth verse). At the close, he spoke in a feeling and affecting manner as follows :—My dear friends, I thank God we have had a peaceful Sunday to-day. I can assure you I have dome my best to explain the words of our text, but I I feel it has not been as well as I ought to have done it. I never thought that this church would be open this Sunday, but God has ruled it otherwise, and we have had a peaceful Sunday, and you have paid greaf attention to my words. Yet I think it is not fair that one does not get notice in time to preach to congregations such as this. But never mind; this ehapn b wassbunronbodyknetwe b until opened til othened last tmbioememnteralmost that I hope that by God's blessing it will be always open, and that we shall always have our praise aid thanksgiyisg to God. Now it is not for me to say anything msay bntdaesertrheed fromrs have ar lea d lettersore from this from this pulpit ult shouldne t b have a letter here from my good mother, who says, "Sun- day will be here when you receive this. Ido hope that the Lord's Day will be a quiet one to you and all at Earlestown, and that you will all be able to join in prayer and praise to God in His Church, forgiving each other as we hope to be forgiven." My dear friends, I only thank you again—l do thank you for listening so kindly. After all, it is not what we say or the quantity or quality of the words we use; no, my friends, let us repair to God and trust in Him, for it is , through Him and Him only that we have hdd a service here to-day. Believe Him, my dear friends; trust not any man, but put your trust in God •, He knows the hearts ef all. wemake mistakes, we have all made mistakes; but lithe heart be true, then God will bring things right. I thank you for your kind attention, and I hope that you and I shall thank God this night that for once no one has disturbed His , house to-day, but everyone peacefully given the greatest • attention.—Several persons in the congregation were Visibly affected during these remarks. The service was conclude • in the usual manner.

"CHRIST'S AMBASSADOR" IN EARLESTOWN. The congregation assembled in St. John's Church on Sunday morning last were witnesses of an incident of a pecular character—and one which, for the moment, created mere talk and conversation in the town than even the dis- pute between the Vicar and his flock. Shortly after the service had been commenced by the curate, a shabbily. dressed individual, unshaved and with slightly grey hair, sentered the church, and audibly asked those seated near the door, "Can VDU find room for Jesus ?" The individual, who had in his possession a large well-worn black canvas bag, was provided with a seat, and as he intimated that he wished to be near the pulpit, a seat was found him about half way up the centre aisle. While the hymn, before the Comnlunion Service, was being sung the visitor inquired if the sermon was next, and ha was, by an unintentional error. given an affirmative reply. Before the hymn had been finished the " mysterious stranger" suddenly left his place and walked towards the chancel. Those who had witnessed his movements saw him turn to enter the pulpit, and as he mounted the steps leading thereto much surprise was manifested. Apparently unconcerned by this fact, the intruder bowed his head in his hands as if engaged in $ silent prayer for a few moments, and then standing up in the pulpit he produced a large manuscript book, and 'after opening it was about to commence reading, when Mr. Corlett (the people's warden) entered the pulpit and seiz,d the man by the arm. He asked him what he was going to do there, and the reply was that he had come to preach. Mr. Corlett informed him that be could not be Permitted to do so, and he must come down). but tho mm replied that he had heerd of the church disputes and -Le had come to make peace, adding the injunction, "Bleed %re the peace-makers, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." He showed a reluctance to retire and Mr. Corlett was com- pelled to seize him and partly drag h9n down the pulpit steps. Here Mr. Slion-(vicar's warden) came to the assis- tance of Mr. Corlett and between them the man was taken into the vestry, and the service was afterwards gone on with as usual. In the vestry he was questioned, and he give tic name of William Peace, of Middleton. On leaving the church by the vestry door be retired to the plot of land in Wil- anoson-'street, where he addressed a few words to several persons, intimating to them that he wouli give an adnire3s on that spot in the afternoon. About three o'clock Mr. "Peace " was observed making his way up Market-street, and he gave a cordial invitation to all be met to follow him to "the Green," where he was going to preach. fie had again hit black bag in his posses-

sion, wore a tall hat which had seen a much better day' and also a pair of old fashioned broad-rimmed spectacles - He took his stand in the middle of what he called the Green," and proceeded to announce that he would commence the service with a short prayer. This over, he read a por- tion of the Scriptures from an old copy of the Bible which he took from his bag; and he subsequently also took therefrom the large manuscript from which he intended reading in the pulpit of the church in the fore- noon. Remarking that he would give them the "sermon," he Wa3 prevented from preaching in the church, he went I on to say that though they had turned him out of the church that day they would one day gladly receive him. He astonished his hearers by the assertion that only on the previous Sunday he had "dined" with St. Matthew and Martha, who anointed Jesus's head with the ointment; but even this was surpassed by the crazy statements which he subsequently made. The preacher, growing warm in his enthusiasm, solemnly and earnestly declared that he had come from his Father in heaven, who had endued him with power from on high, and added "Any man coming to stand beside me without a leg et an arm, if I say receive thy arm or receive thy leg he shall instantly receive it." Many sc-ptics were found among the congregation, ad one indi- vidual who had had the misfortune to lose two fingers step- ped forward and asked the "miracle worker" to replace them. But, evidently too much interested in his subject, the " preacher " did not seem anxious to perform the oper- ation, but went on to say, "He that bath ears to hear .let him hear." After a brief reference to his "asthmatical confinement in bed" for three , weeks he said he had not come like church I ministers to pump money out of the people. An encouraging "Hear, hear" induced him to continue. "If there is a church minister or a man influential with his tongue they I get him to come and preach and so make a good collection. , They make him into a pumping engine—to pump the money out of your pockets, but I don't want money pumped out of you—l want to pump your pockets full. lam now 53 years of age, and there is not a man on the face of the earth can come and aay that lever took my Father's name invain." He added: "1 was laid hold of on Monday, and treated as if they wanted to put me out of the vestry"—(query, which vestry ?) " but I said that all the men there is in cannot put me out, and I was doing my duty to them when they behaved to me , in a very wicked manner, I said I will put out my hand and I will ask for fire from heaven in a minute. He stated that they would all have seen references in the Bible, especially I in the Old Testament, to the" Lord's Ambassador en earth," and he added that "if you look at me you see. His Ambassador." He afterwards described his present condition as almost penniless with a wife dependent upon him," and in reply to a suggestion that a collection should be made on his behalf, he said if they offered him a thousand pounds he would not accept it. This absurd "sermon," which had occupied over an hour in delivery, was then concluled, and a prayer finished the "service." As he left the ground he asked them to "open their ranks" for him, and said that next time he came the doors of the church would be opened before him, and they would gladly welcome him. He then made his way along Market-street and through the Mesnes to Newton Bridge Station, where he booked to Middleton.

Later enquiries which have been made show that the 1. man's name is not Peace, but Robert Butterworth, a silk haudloom weaver, living at Tongs, near Middleton. Butter- worth has had religious mania for some years past, and has on one or two previous occasions conducted himself strangely in places of worship. lie states that his idea in going to Earlestown was to re-establish peace in the parish. It is the first time he has been known to give his name as "William Peace," but he always represents him self as Jesus Christ. Last Easter but one, so impressed is he with the idea that he is the Christ, that he gave out that there was going to be a resurrection in Tunge, and for this he made elaborate preparations. He has given the church authorities at Middleton very considerable trouble. On one occasion he left his seat in the parish church, and, proceeding up the aisle, attempted to prevent the curate (the Rev. A. R. Edgar) from conducting the service, saving that it was proceeding improperly. It was only when threatened with imprisonment that he was prevailed upon to desist. He I then wrote to the rector (the Rev. W. Brewster) stating his I intention to preach in thii church, and this gentleman, not I thinking it would go any further, told him that he could not allow anyone to preach in the church unless they were duly licensed by the bishop. Butterworth went straightway to the bishop's house, and is said to have had an interview with his lordship. He is exceedingly "well up" in Scripture and the Church service, being able to quote at any length from either; and he has a large number of sermons, homi- ' lies, and poems in his possession which he has written. He has visited on different occasions every place of worship and Sunday school in the neighbourhood, and on one occasion caused some excitement at St. John's Church, Hopwood, where, on the close of a special sermon by the bishop, he put himself in front of the bishop, clergy, and choristers, arid accompanied them into the vestry.

PRESENTATION OF PRIZES TO THE SCHOOL CHILDREN. The annual distribution of prizes to the scholars attend- ing St. John's Sunday School took place in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Saturday evening. As the vicar of the parish (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) had refused the use of the school-room additional interest was centred in the gathering, and there was a very large attendance, the room being crowded. After the audience and school children had heartily sung the hymn, "Come let us join our cheerful songs" (accompanied on the pianoforte by Mr. H. J. Dur- , man), Mr G. Makin, jun., remarked that that was a rather I peculiar place in which to have a distribution of prizes in connection with a Sunday school, but seeing that Mr. Matthews had refused the use of the school-room they had no other alternative. Mr. Matthews had also objected to distribute the prizes. He therefore had great 'pleasure in proposing that Mr. H. J. Durman preside, as it was through , I that gentleman's instrumentality that the money had been I raised for the prlzA. (Applause.)—Mr. E. Kenyon seconded the motion, which was passed with acclamation.--On Mr. Darman (as chairman) rising to address the meeting, he was very warmly received. He said he would like to make an ' explanation as to their position that evening, and to de so he would have to carry them back to the beginning of the year, when their funds amounted to £2 is id. A meeting of teachers was held, and it was decided in order to raise more money that a children's concert should be arranged, and as they all knew it proved a great success, over' eight pounds beint raised. Things went on for some time, but as no prizes turned up and as the children ought to have received them at Christmas, in- quiries were set on foot as to the reason. Mr. Matthews ' stated that he had not received any money for them, and that until he received the money no children's prizes would be bought. To this the treasurer replied that if Mr. Mat- thews would be kind enough to select the books and send the bill to him he would pay for them- but this however, the vicar refused to do. Consequently four of this, went ' to Liverpool and selected the books, and this year there were more prizes than ever. They found that for their £9 ' of books they got £3 as discount—(applause)—so that really they had got £l2 worth of books. They afterwards ' asked Mr. Matthews if be would distribute them, but he re- plied he would not, and added that any child taking a prize , ; from anyone's hands but his would be dismissed from the school. ('' Shame" and hisses.)—Miss Florenc3Laithwaite then sang "Tha cnckoo" in a pleasing manner, and a num- ber of school children gave "The stars are with the voya- gars "in an equally appreciable style. " Good night to ' Dolly," by Miss Katie Wildman, and "Sabbath Bells," by Miss Ada Davies, were well applauded.—Mr. Darman after- wards distributed the prizes to the successful scholars, each of whom was greeted with suitable remarks as they re- ceived their gifts. At the close of this interesting cere- mony Mr. Birkhead amusingly remarked that Earlestorgn 5 had lately come to the front, and what with football and church squabbles they were getting their names ' up. (A laugh,) Formerly people had to ,inquire where Earleatown was, but now everybody seemed " to know, and he bad been asked over and over again what kind of a man this organist of theirs ' was. Well, he would just tell them. He pointed out that though Mr. Durman was paid a salary of £4O a year, yet he was a hard worker for the church and schools, and through his instrumentality the debt on the organ had been reduced ' £6O; a harmonium, value £2O. had been purchased for the Sunday School, while about £B5 were raised every year in aid of the church expenses, choir fund, dm. (Applause.) That was the sort of an organist they had got—(renewed applause)—and he had, therefore, great pleasure in asking the meeting to accord its hearty thanks to Mr. Dorman for the manner and willingness with which he always came forward, ready to assist any gqod work that was going on. (Enthusiastic applause, mingled with "cheers for Mr. • Birkhead.")—ln acknowledging the compliment, Mr. Dar- , man said he sincerely thanked them for the kindness he had ' received at their hands, for if he had not been backed up ' by their kind words and sympathy he would never have been able to go through what he had done. He added that ! not only did be receive sympathy from Earlestown people alone, but from all parts of the country and even from : people that he did not know. He proceeded to read two letters of sympathy be had received, the reading of which was applauded. He afterwards called upon Miss Katie Corlett. Master Willie Jackson, Miss Bertha Jackson, and Miss Kate Glover, each of whom took part in musical selec- tions—tbeir efforts being duly appreciated. The proceedings ; concluded with thetinging of the doxology.

CHANCELLOR ESPIN ON THE DUTIES OF The Rev. Chancellor Espin, delivering his Arcbi-diaconal charge, at Warrington, on Tuesday, in dealing with the church dispute at St. John's Church, Earlestown, referred at some length to the respective legal rights of the incum- bent and churchwardens There was the question as to whether the keys of the church were under the custKly of the minister. The incumbent lead an nndoubtei right, by reason of his office of vicar, to take pselsession of the fabric s be of the church, and with it the keys, subject to the legal right of hi parishioners to present at all .celebrations of tue public worship of God: Ail these legal rights and pri- vileges of the vicar were also vested in a perpetual curate. The churchwardens possessed no strict right to keepand use the keys of the church, except by permission of the incum- bent. On this point there was no dispute, because it had ,been decided again and again in the Ecclesiastical Courts in was another important point which they should bear in mind, and that was that no churchwardea could act without the sanction of his colleague, even when requested to do so bY the Vestry, and even when his sctins would un- doubtedly be beneficial to the parish. This was also quite settled by law. In all things the churchwardens were the officers of the ordicary of the parish. Their office Las on, of observation and complaint. The vicar's rig! ts gave bin control over all the furniture and articles accessory to

Divine worship. These things the churchwardens had cue tody of, and they were bound to keep them in proper re- pair; but the minister had the use of these things, and not the wardens. It followed, also, that access to various parts UT adjuncts of the church, or to things ordinarily kept and locked up there, also pertained exclusively to the incumbent. The bells could not be used without his consent, and the same was time of the organ. /although, doubtless, the cus- tody of an organ devolved upon the churchwardens, that fact did net give them the control and use of it. The minister had the exclusive right of ordering and conducting the services, and'herein of directing also what musical Ac- companiment there should be. This was a matter that had been expressly decided and ruled by the courts. Respecting the appointment and dismissal of the organist, there was not so clear and so strong a body of autheritative .decisions, partly be- canes the general introduction of organs into parish churches was not of very old date, and the organist was not—as were the clerk and parish sexton—an officer of the Church recognised by the Ecclesiastical law from old times. There were also a few cases in which endowments have been left for the organist, and in some of these he be- lieved the appointment had been placed in the vestry. But even if the appointment and dismissal of organist belonged to the vestry or churchwardens the minister could undoubt- edly suspend the organist from playing during divine ser- vice. As A general principal, and in the absence of any special custom to the contrary, the appointment and dis- missal of organist, he had no doubt, pertained to the minis- ter alone, and that even when the whole salary had to be provided by the vestry or churchwardens. In support of his opinion, the Rev. Chancellor quoted Sergeant Wheeler's judgment at the Liverpool County Court in 1870, in the action brought by Mr. Byre, organist, St. Mathias's Church, Liverpool, against the incumbent, by whom he had been dismissed, for arrears of salary. Mr. Eyre, who was non-suited, had been appointed by the pre- vious incumbent and having drawn his salary from church- wardens. Any organist who persisted in playing in church against the prohibition of the incumbent committed an illegal act which might be attended with serious conse- quences, and the churchwardens would be quite wrong in encouraging or upholding such act. He thought that in a diocese like this the incumbents generally deserved great consideration at the hands of the churchwardens, of ten corn- ing, as they did, comparative strangers to the parishes. A little help was always valued by a wise incumbent. Let the churchwardens present try, therefore, to discharge their various duties in a right spirit, as acting for the Bishop and answerable to him, and as having for their official concern the moral and religions welfare of their fellow-parishioners. It was certainly not a very difficolt matter to live in peace, and act in harmony with the clergyman of the parish; and if they really could not do that it was far better to decline the office of churchwarden.

div.head: SERVING SUMMONSES.
div.p: SERVING SUMMONSES.

Definite steps arO--at--da-s-t -be-in—g-aerTrri—order to test the legality of the proceedings which have recently been wit- nessed in St. John's Church, Earlestown. Throughout the week many rumours were circulated as to legal proceedings .which were alleged to have been taken or were about to be taken, but the public were not aware of anything definite having taken place until Wednesday last, when P.S. Com- mins served summonses upon Mr. Birkhead (sidesrnan), Mr. Corlett (people's churchwarden), and Mr. H. J. Durman (organist), for having on various dates been guilty of "riotous, violent, and disorderly behaviour " in church. The information in each case has been laid by Mr. Gamon (the legal adviser to the Bishop of Liverpool), and the charges will be heard at Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday. Mr. Birkhead and Mr. Nevitt are each charged with having been guilty of "riotous, violent, and disorderly beha- viour " on three different occasions, namely, the 13th March, 6th April, and the 16th April; Mr. Durman is sum- moned for two dates, 13th March and 16th April, and Mr. Corlett is summoned for the 16th April. When the sum- menses were served upon the defendants they were dis- played in their shop windows, where crowds of persons gathered to read them. The fact that the summonses had been served spread rapidly throughout the town, and created considerable excitement.

On Thursday, Mr. White, solicitor, of Warrington, acting on behalf of the defendants summoned for disorderly con- duct in Earlestown Church, received a telegram from Mr. Canoe, solicitor to the Bishop of Liverpool, offering to withdraw the summonses if they had not been served, on condition that the defendants would acknowledge thetn- selves in the wrong, and discharge Mr. Darman organist. A reply was sent that they would do ne such things, and, con- sequently summonses will be beard.

ALLEGED ILLEGAL DISTRESS. At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Mr. W. , W. Ffoulkes, judge, and a jury, were occupied for several hours in hearing a claim for damages sustained by reason of an alleged illegal dirress at Earlestown. in which the plain- tiff was Ann North, of 72, Church-street, St. Helens, and the defendants John Lane and Edward Edwardson, both of Earlestown.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendants were represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift.—Mr. Riley, in explaining the case for the plaintiff, said that one of the defendants was an auctioneer residing at Earlestown, and the other was the landlord of the shop upon which he was induced to make a distress. The plaintiff claiin-d damages for the wrongful entry into the shop 4, Bridge- street, Earlestown, for wrongful seizure of the stock-in-trade, and for depriving her of the use and occupation of the said shop, whereby she was injured in her business and repute-. time. The plaintiff claimed £5O an Honour said that Mr. Riley ought not to mention the amount of the damages.—Mr. Riley said that perhaps he ought to be al- lowed to mention the extent to which the jury were allowed to go under the jurisdiction of the county court. His Honour: You must not really. Mr. Swift thought that Mr. Riley should not have proceeded with the matter after his Honour's first obser- vation.—Mr. Riley: I shauld like some authority.—His Honour said that his authority was sufficient, and it was not for Mr. Riley to ask it.—Mr. Riley : My friend inter- Honour Quite right, after the observation on no s your ti u—r rt.. —Mr Riley, proceeding with the case, said that on the 24th of February, 1884, the plaintiff, Mrs. North, was and for some time had been in possession of a house and shop at 4, Bridge-street, Earlestown, which be- longed to the defendant Lane, and undoubtedly if he had pias any difficulty in recovering his rent he had a right to re- sort to distraint for the purpose of obtaining the rent owing to him. But in resorting to this summary proceed- ing for the recovery of a debt the landlord was subject to certain conditions, which, he contended, had not in this instance been fulfilled. They were required to make an inventory of the full value of the goods that they took, and amongst the conditions that a landlord must observe was one to the effect that the distress must be made be- tween sunrise and sunset, but in this case it was made be- tween 8 and 9 o'clock in the evening, which of itself would make the distress illegal. If the jury were of that opinion the plaintiff was entitled to have back from the defendants the full value of the goods that they took. But that was not the only irregular and aggravating circumstance in the conduct of the land- lord and the auctioneer. Not only did they go at that hour of the night, but they took with them a policeman, and did not, as by law directed, make and give to the plain- tiff a full inventory of goods seized. His Honour: You do not seem to complain of an irregular dis- tress, but of an illegal act altogether? Mr. Riley: Yes. His Honour : Not taking an inventory is merely an irregularity. Mr. Riley submitted that it was a further circumstance of aggravation. • Assuming that in every other respect this distress had been valid, ' where the tenant was willing it was the duty of the land- lord to keep the goodsseiz ai upon the premises for a cer- tain specified time. If the tenant objected to the goods re- reaming, the landlord could remove them before the expire- once removed to a neighbouring public-house. One would tion of the period. But in this instance the goods were at have thought that the auctioneer would have had a suitable place to remove them to, and to keep them until the expira- tion of the five days in which they could be redeemed. Plaintiff alleged that the goods were afterwards sold below their value. The landlord's claim was for £6 ss, and the goods removed had been recently valued at over £6O. He thought that when they considered these facts they would come to the conclusion that not by accident, but by design, the landlord and his auctioneer, having seine spite ag A s instttth he is plaintiff determined to break up her shop she was carrying on the busi- nesseif a boat and hoe dealer, and she bad before been at a shop at St. Helens, which, through misfortune, she had had to give up. establishment.a She was doing what she could to recover her position, when the defendants swooped down upon her under circumstances calculated to damage her reputation, taking the whole of her gods and selling them by the light of a paraffin lamp on a Friday evening.—He then called witnesses in support of his statement.—For the defence Mr. Swift called a number of witnesses, who justified the con- duct of the defendant; and spoke of the sale as haviug been conducted under favourable circumstances. Witnesses were also called to speak to the value of the goods.— Ihe case was then adjourned till Saturday, when Mr. Swift will make his speech for the defence.

FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.--ALLEGED MASSACRE OF FUGITIVES.—THE PLANS OF • GENERAL GORDON. CAIRO, SUNDAY.—A Greek merchant here has received a message to-day (Sunday) from Khartoum saying that the town is safe at present. General Gordon intends to send Colonel Stewart and Mr. Power back by way of Abysinia, and that be will in future use his own discretion.—Daily News.
