No news of the Admiral's movements lees been received since he started inland. PREPARATIONS FOR AN EXPEDITION TO BERBER. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY—At a council held this morning at the British Diplomatic Agency—Mr. Egerton, Nubar Pesha, and Sir Evelyn Wood being present—it was decided to recommend the British Government to despatch a mixed expeditionary sorce of British and Egyptian troops for the relief of Berber. It is calculated that the expedition would reach Berber in two months. The Standard correspondent says :—Nubar Pasha dis- tinctly refuses to hold office any longer utaless help is sent immediately to Berber. His position is generally approved, and Sir Evelyn Wood is accordingly pushing forward pre- parations for the almost instant despatch of troops, which, unless vetoed by England, will probably start within a week. I feel bound to record the very general opinion here that unless this force is supported by English and Aughalndian troops, the expedition runs something more than a risk of meetinz with the fate that befell Hicks Pasha's army. This conviction has, of course, no weight with the gallant Euglish officers of the Egyptian army ; but their mission is felt to be a very desperate one, and it is useless to blink the fact that a sacrifice will have to be made.

CAIRO, THURSDAY—An extraordinary Cabinet Council, under the presidency of the Khedive, was held this morning to consider the military situation. Riaz Pacha and Cnerif Pacha also attended in obedience to a special summons from his Highness. The Council adopted a resolution declaring the immediate despatch of troops to Upper Egypt to be im- peratively necessary. Nubar Pacha was charged to submit this resolution to the British Government. REVIVAL OF THE SLAVE TRADE. The Daily News has received from a correspondent at Dongola a long letter, dated March 23, describing the posi- tion of affairs in that region. With regard to the slave trade he writes :—" In the old days of the slave trade Dangola was a flourishing centre Tor that nefarious traffic, and it is by no means certain that a considerable trade in Diggers has nut been carried on up to the preaent day. Certain it is the trade is opening up again under the influence of Gordon Pasha's proclamation declaring the buying and selling of slaves lawful. As this proclamation is in force as far as Aesouan it practically re-establishes \ the slave trade in Egypt, because it will be next to impnssible to prevent a contraband trade growing up between Egypt and the Sou- dan, as a few days' march through the desert will always enable the slave dealers to pass Assouan and enter Egypt unobserved. This is the more likely because they will be protected by the sympathy of the whole population. FRANCE, CHINA, AND TONQUIN. Pasts, Sexustnev.--The Temps of this evening publishes the following telegram from Haiphong, of to-day's date " It is stated that the bands of Chinese and Annanire rebels, who are in retreat, have entered the province of Tanhoa, with the intention of proceeding to Annam. General de Briars de L'lsle has started in pursuit, the force under his command proceeding towards the sea by the Day River and along the base of the mountains. The French victories are Producing a great impression on the population of Toequin. The campaign is at an end. General Millot has returned to Hanoi. A violent storm raged over the Delta last night, and rain has commenced to tall at Saigon." SHANGHAI, WIEDNNSDAY.—The Viceroy of Yunnan has diedsuddenly at Hangsoa. It is reported that he committel suicide. PARIS, WEDNRSDAL—The Temps publishes the following telegram from Haiphong, of to-day's date :—" The occupa- tion of Thai Nguyen has been decided upon. The troops of General Negrier's brigade will occupy this important posi- tion. The French gu lboats can easily ascend the Songcan river. Aff airs in Tonquin are in an excellent condition." The National states that M. Patenotre has been specially instructed to take measures with the view to ensuring the fulfil orient of the treaty of the 25th 'August, providing for the opening of all the ports of Annam to free trade. Rants, MONDAY—La Patrie to-day states that a portion of the French troops now in Tonquin will return home at the end of May next, being replaced by native battalions, which General Millot proposes to organise. ANOTHER CONGO TREATY. PARIS, MONDAY.—The France states that a communica- tion from a member of the De Brazza Mission' dated from a station on Upper Ogone River, was received &ire by the latest mail from Portugal. It is stated that M. de Brazza had concluded a treaty with a powerful West African sovereign, of whom Makoko was the vassal, in virtue of which the whole of the right bank of the Congo from Braz- zaville to the Equator was placed under a French protec- torate.

div.head: TRANSVAAL DELEGATES IN PARIS.
div.p: TRANSVAAL DELEGATES IN PARIS.

PARIS, THURSDAY,—The Transvaal delegates were re- ceiv,d to-day by President Grevy. M. Ferry was present at the interview' which lasted 'about half an hour. This even- ing they willbe entertained at a banquet at the Grand Hotel, given by the Geographical society, at which M. Ferdinand de Lesgeps will preside. The delegates will leave to-morrow morning for Lisbon, viS Bordeaux._

div.head: QUEEN AT DARMSTADT.
div.p: THE QUEEN AT DARMSTADT.

DARMSTADT, MONDAY.—The reports of Her Majesty's in- disposition are totally without foundation. The Queen has been driving out every day, but is still unable to walk much out of doors, or stand for any length of time, in consi,quence of her accident a year ago. The Queen and Princess Beatrice, accompanied by the Grand Duke of Hesse, drove out this morning in an open carriage to the Emil Garden, where they were met by the Princess Irene and Afloat Hesse. Her Majesty took a second drive this afternoon. The weather is now better. Detat5TADT, TIIESDAY.—Last evening the Queen visited the mausoleum of the late Princess Alice, and laid 3 wreath on the tomb. DIscOVEHY OF INFERNAL MACHINES.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY."
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY."

.• 'Published by Mr. E. L. Kibblewhite, 31. Tavistook-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] THE GROWTH OF THE LANDED I;iTEREST. In a hundred chapters I have briefly sketched the agrarian history of the majority of our most notable aristocratic houses. In my selectien I have not been guided mainly by the greatness of their possessions, but rather by their historic interest or present prominence. 'Thus I have included some like the Erskines and Fanes, whose estates are small, and have altogether omitted peers like Lore redegar, with over 100,000 acres, and Lord Penrhvn, wizh a rent-roll of £66,000. I have dealt in all with 122 nobles, owning in round numbers nearly 5 millions of acres, with a rent-roll of nearly 51 millions, an average ownership of 45,000 acres, and an average rent-roll of over £46,000. It certainly has not been my object to seek out examples of what, for want of a better word. I will call the illegitimate acquisition of landed property. When once I have selected a house for inquiry, I have never desisted from completing its story because I found that it had a clear record. Yet the result is that those who can claim that they have ob- tained their lands by money solely acquired in commercial or professional pursuits, are singular), few—perhaps about a dozen in all. Compared with other people we are a landless nation, and We are a landless nation in consequence of continual en- croachments upon the rights our ancient forefathars Possessed. On this point let me quote Mr. Freeman, who says in his Norman Conquest:—" In the realities of history, the king and the lord—that is, the lord on a great scale, and the lord on a small one—are each something which has crept in unawares, something which has grown up at the expense of rights more ancient than its own. Etch alike, king and lord, grew to his full dimensions by a series of gradual and stealthy encroachments on the rights of the people. As the king swallowed up the powers and possessions of the nation, Se the lord swallowed op tile rights and possessions of the 'mark.'" That which was true in ancient times is also true in modern days. Throughout the reigns of the Hanoverian Xings landowners' Parliaments were constantly passing en- closure Acts, desirable, for the most pert, with a view to increased production, but resulting in the appropriation of between seven and eight millions of acres of common land, of which the common people retained but a very small pro- Portion—not rno,e than three-quarters of a million acres in la Occasionally I have been able t, point out where vast estates have been increased by these Acts; but generally it has been impossible to obtain exact information. Whenever the agricultural labourers are sufficiently powerful to press their claim to the cultivation of " public lands," especially to charity lands, they will find in the injustice with which their fathers were treated a powerful argument for the equity Of their demands. It is worthy of notice that anciently the lavish grants of the Crown were checked by the power of Resumption. Most of the vast estates seized and retained by William the Con- queror were dissipated by William Rufus, who was compelled subsequently to resume the grants which he had made. Henry IV. was called upon by his Parliament to resume the grants, parcel of the ancient inheritance of the Crown, which had been alienated by Edward 111. and Richard 11. Similar demands were made and acted upon in the reign of Henry VI., Edward IV. and Henry VII. In fact, from Henry 111. to Henry VIII. ;here was only one reign in which one or more Bills of Resumption were not passed. Had it been impossible for English monarchs to alienate the estates appropriated to the support of the dignity of the Crown, we should have had no occasion in modern times for Royal grants or dowries. Repeated attempts were, indeed, made to restrain the Crown from alienating its lands, but they Were generally opposed by crafty and greedy Ministers. The lateat instance of a successful Resumption Bill was in the I reign of William 111. About the middle of last century the grasping avarice of one of the Lowthers, in attempting tO obtain for himself a large tract of Crown lands, which had bee a previously granted to the Bentineks, occasioned the Lar"ipg of what is known as the Nullus Tempos Act, which -",eured the grantees of Crown lands against any resumption Of their properties. It is obviously impossible to reckon up acre by acre the 'quantity of land which has at various times been obtained Otherwise than by purchase. The agrarian history of many of the great houses is complicated by the acquisition of pro- perty by marriage. I have, however, traced the previous history of such lands in a sufficient muini er of cases to show that we may safely presume that, as a rule, they have been acquired in much the same way as the rest. After a careful consideration of all the homes I have noticed, bearing in mind modern Enclosure Acts, and the increased value of lands due to the improvements of tenants, I cannot but arrive at the conclusion that not one-tenth of the estates in question have been acquired for value received. All the rest, in one way or another, has been obtained for nothing. - In Ireland the great majority of the landlords owe their Possessions to successive confiscation. In the North of Scotland, where the so-called rights of property have been Pat into force with almost unexampled cruelty and injus- tice, the landlords owe their position to the iniquity of law. Let me quote Mr. Freeman once more :—" When, as in the Celtic parts of the British Islands, the old constitution of the gens or clan went on longer than it did amongst our- selves, we can see the actual process by which, under the influence of an alien jurisprudence, the chief of the clan Changed into the lord of the soil. The land of the clan was held to be the land of the chief, and the body of the clans- men, it truth his fellow-owners, came to be looked on as - tenants holding of him." With regard to Irish landowners, it ought to be borne in Mind that in a very large number of cases it is the labour Of successive generations of tenants which has given to the land almost all the value it possesses, and that not a few landlords have improved their properties by the aid of the State. When the Corn baws were repealed a sop was given to the landowners. In the darkest days of commercial (lis- tless no statesman ever proposed to find out of the public revenue capital for manufacturers or shopkeepers; yet this was what was done for the landlords after the repeal of the 9Orti,Laws. Acts were passed which declared, "Whereas it is desirable that works of drainage should be encouraged in order to promote the increased productiveness of the land and the healthiness of the districts when it is required, and tO supply the demand for agricultural labour, especially at that season of the year when other sources are expanded, L'2,000,000 were allotted to English landowners, and £1,000,000 to Irish landowners, in order to make advances to them, to be gradually repaid at a low interest. Nor was the accommodation of the State Loan Office resorted to by comparatively small proprietors. Among the Irish recipients was the wealthy Ma:quie of Waterford. For the most part, too, the landlords were content that the farmers should do the work of improvement, and we have the authority of Mr. Caird for stating that sometimes they borrowed of the Government for their permanent advantage, and charged the farmer, who had only a temporary advan- tage, one and one and a half per cent, more than they them- selves paid. The popular theory that in England and Scotland all permanent improvements have been effected by the land- lords is only very partially true. Take, for instance, the great riclamations of land in the Eastern Counties. Anciently, when the embankments gave way, the sheriff had full authority to impress the labour of the county. At different times Acts of Parliament were passed authorising the construction of drainage works, and tenants as well as Owners were made contributories. I know I shall be met with the theory that it is the landlord who pays rates in the end, because the tenant would take them into considera- tion in making his bargain. But until very recent times the tenant brought up to agriculture had no choice in the matter but to submit to the terms of the owner of that , natural monopoly—land. We, who live in days when the large farmer has many opportunities of employing his Capital profitably at home, and can with comparative ease take it to the very ends of the earth, must not make him the standard of measuremen; for the ancient farmer who lived when he was practically shut up to one employment and one locality. If we turn from the lowlands to the hills, the same truth holds good that the cultivator has done the greater part of the Ark of reclamation. Bad I but the spice I could give multitudinous examples. Only give a young and energetic izan a nineteen years' lease of an uncultivated waste con- tiguous to his farm, and he will work miracles. In a mul- titude of cases it has needed not even that small security, t, the landlord's or aient's word was enough. But when the lease expired, or the ld landlord or the old tenant died, the Permanent gain at once became the property of the owner of the bare soil. I have walked on land, not more than a long laY's walk from London, which is now paying its owner "'tee times what it did a generation ago, and the owner has net laid out a single sixpence upon it. Landowners may try to throw dust in the eyes of the public b complaining that they cannot just now get three per cent. interest on the Present purchase-money of agricultural land ; but when I read that a little farm in Carmarthenshire, which in the Middle of the last,century only brought in £lO a year to its Owner now pave his des .en lant ten times that amount every Fear, I laugh them to scorn.

THE JUBILEE OF FACTORY LEGISLATION. The annual report of Alexander Itedgrave, Esq., C. 8., her Majesty's Chief Inspector of Factories, for the year ended October 31st last, has just been. issued. He says :—lt is now 50 years since the passing of the first effective Factory Act; and thus 1883 may be distinguished as the "jubilee" year of factory legislation. It is true an Act was passed on the 22nd June, 1802, "for the preservation of the health and morals of apprentices and others employed in cotton and other mills, and in cotton and other factories ;" but this was never put into operation. The regulations were literally confined to the two above-stated objects. Children, without restriction as to age, were not to be employed at actual work for more than 12 hours—between 6 am. and 9 p.m. The premises were to be limewashed at least twice a year, and provision was made for medical aid in case of infectious disorders breaking out. So much for health. Morals required a more elaborate code. Every apprentice was to be instructed on each work-day in reading, writing, and arithmetic, or either of them, by some discreet and proper person. Every apprentice was to be in- structed for one hour on every Sunday in the principles of the Christian religion. In the case of apprentices being members of the Church of England they were to be ex. amlued once a year by the rector, and be duly prepared for confirmation, and to be confirmed by the bishop. In the CABO of members of the Church of Scotland they were to be examined once a year by the minister of the parish, and to receive the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper. Appren- tices were to be taken to church at least once a month, and when not so taken divine service must be performed in some convenient room in or adjoin- ing the factory at least once on every Sunday. The morale of any apprentice or other person not of the Church of England or of Scotland were left out in the cold. The Act did not apply to Ireland; but the reason was that there were not in that country "cotton or other fan. ' Lodes" in which apprentices were employed. This code for ensuring -health and morals was left, practically, to ad- minister itself. The justices in quarter sessions were em- powered to appoint at least two visitors, one of whom must be a justice of the peace, and the other a clergyman of the Church of England or of the Church of Scotland, who were invested with full power of entry and examination. It is unnecessary to inquire what was the effect of this law— which would appear rather to be an emanation from the statesmen of the Stuarts than of the present century—or what was the nature of its administration. The Act of 1802 was not repealed but ignored by the effective legisla- tion of 1833, which was adapted to the spirit of the times, and laid the foundation upon which subsequent amendments were built up until the one code was formulated and passed in 1878. The Act of 1833 was confined, much as was the Act of 1802, to factories in which the processes of spinning, weaving, ikc., were carried on in cotton, woollen, worsted, flax, silk, Sic. The age below which children might not be employed was fixed. The hours of com- niencing and ending work, and of meal times, the restric- tion of the number of hours during which children might be employed for half and full time, were de- termined. Means for asceftaining the age of children and their physical ability to work were devised. Children were required to attend day school, and vouchers of their attendance were to be produced. The limewashing and cleansing of factories were compulsory. Those principles, modified and enlarged, are the basis of the existing regulations. I have no means of aecertainir g what number of cotton and other factories existed in 1802. It could not have been large, for the manufacture by steam or water power was in its infancy. Water was the principal motive power, and the establishment of factories where water power existed in country districts necessitated the hiring of apprentices from the town workhouses, as the neighbourhoods did not afford a sufficient supply of labour. But with respect to 1833, I have the reports of the inspectors of factories appointed by his Majesty under the provisions of the act of that year, and from them it appears that there were then 'about 3,094 cotton and other factories in the three kingdoms, as under: —ln England, 2,642; Scotland, 388; Ireland, 64; total, 3,094. Such were the number of industrial establishments, and such the regulations to be observed in them in 1833. As time wore on other industries were added to the list of those requiring inspection, until at the present time every establishment in which mechanical power, whether of steam, water, or gas, is used for the purposes of manufac- ture, is a factory; and Almost every place in which the preparation of any article, or adaptation of any article for sale is carried om is a workshop. Further than this, the improvement of the means of the education of factory children, which was in 1833, and for many years after- wards, a most interesting portion of the duties of the Inspectorsof Factories, is now under the charge of a distinct department of education. The bringing under our inspection all the varied industries of the country rendered it absolutely necessary that regulations, which in cotton factories could be fixed and determined, ehould be elastic and appropriate for such establishments as blast furnaces, brickfields, or dressmaking; hence there are a variety of customs and exigencies which had to be considered and met. But the Act of 1878 cleared up man Y doubts, and released, from what appeared to be unnecessary inspection, many places which, under a strict interpretation of previous Fac- tory Acts, were workshops and subject to workshop regula- tions. For Instance, the following places are altogether exempt from inspection :—All places in which men only are employed, and in which there is not any machinery moved by mechanical power. Industrial schools in which any handicraft is carried on for the purpose of instruction. nooses in which straw plait, pillow lace, and glove making are carried on by the members of a family residing in the house. Houses in which any handicraft is carried on by the members of a family residing in the house, as an occa- sional occupation and not as the principal means of living. The following places are subject only partially to the re- quirements of the Act:—ln houses where the members of a family residing therein work, the labour of adult females is unrestricted; that of young persons may be taken between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m., and until 4 p.m. on Saturdays. In work-, shops where notice has been given that neither children nor young persons are employed, the labour of female adults may be taken between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. In the two last- named places the exhibition of an abstract and the allow- ance of holidays are not compulsory, nor do the enactments as to ventilation or limewashing apply. The administra- tion of the law has been greatly facilitated by these various enactments, and the work was lightened in many localities; but while, previous to 1878, it was a matter of general complaint that if a manufacturer wished to see precisely the regulations which applied to his occupation he had to pick out those clauses which would affect bins from 15 Acts of Parliament, it remains our duty to be conversant with a vast variety of enactments and exceptions which did not exist in any previous Act of Parliament, and, in districts where there is a great variety of occupations in which differ- ent special enactments and exceptions apply, the greatest care is necessary in explanation and instruction. But it is not in explanation and instruction in factory rules alone that our aid is Bought. I have applications for advice in almost all the relations between master and servant. Although I cannot satisfy all my correspondents, it is a pleasing proof that we are looked upon as impartial judges, and our advice sought as that of unprejudiced persons. Two subjects have always occupied much of the attention of the Inspectors of Factories, the protection of machinery, and thereby the prevention of accidents, and the improve- ment in the sanitary condition of factories and workshops. It has been noticed how year by year the number of acci- dents reported to this department have increased, and as there is a power vested in the inspectors of issuing a notice in the case of machinery, which may appear and be likely to cause personal injury, it is of much importance that the circumstance attending the accidents which are reported to me should be thoroughly investigated. This is a duty both of magnitude and responsibility; of magnitude because there are annually about 9,000 such reports to be carefully examined, and subsequent investigation to be made; and of responsibility, because very great care must be taken to dis• criminate between that which is feasible and necessary, and that which, while it is apparently advisable, would unduly hamper the processes of manutacture without affording corresponding immunity from injury. For instance, there is a large quantity of machinery which is dangerous unless it be kept covered. The incidence of manufacture requires the covering to be constantly removed, and it is frequently alleged that the loss of time in unscrewing and in unfasten- ing the coverings becomes an item of importance not com- mensurate with the chances of accidents, which it is further alleged could only arise from inattention or carelessness. Nevertheless we urge in the strongest manner that cover- ings be placed over all exposed machinery of such kinds as experience has shown to be the cause of accidents There are two circumstances which have caused an increased num- ber of accidents to be recorded of late years. The definition of "Factory" was made by the Act of 1878 to include all places in which steam, water, or other mechanical power was used, and thus a large number of accidents which were not required to be reported when the places were workshops are now reported, and the extensive use of gas engines to drive machinery in places were hand power was alone used, has again caused additions to the number of accidents to be reported. It is thus very desirable that there should be at intervals a general resum6 of the accidents reported to us in pursuance of the Act. H.M. Superintending Inspector Henderson thus reports as to accidents canted by shuttles flying from looms in ' Scotland and the north of England Comparatively few accidents caused by the shuttle flying from the loom occur in Scotland, because, as a rule, the power-looms in that por- tion of my district are not run at so high a rate of speed as in Lancashire and Yorkshire. There is not much plain weaving done in Scotland, and in fancy weaving the looms are now at a lower rate of speed. In the North Lancashire portion of my district, and more especially in Preston, acci- dents of this kind are of common occurrence, anti as they not unfrequently result with loss of an eye to the person injured, it would be very desirable to preveat them if pos- sible. From the inquiries I have made it would appear to be somewhat difficult to do this in all cases, Various attempts have been made to devise some means of prevent- ing the shuttle from leaving the loom, but, unfortunately, every appliance of this kind interferes more or less with the conveniencc of the weaver, and is therefore very un- popular among the workpeopie. From all I can make out, these accidents almost invariably arise from some slight ' defect in the adjustment of some portion of the loom or in the shuttle itself. Power-loom makers, cotton manufac- turers, and overlookers whom I have consulted nu thie point agree in this opinion. When a shuttle is thrown across the shed of a power-loom, a very slight defect in the bevil of the shuttle itself, or in the picker which impels it, or in the slay which carries it, will tend to throw it nut. The best security against such accidents, therefore, is to keep the loom in thorough good order, and this in a weaving factory is mainly the duty of the overlooker, Messrs. Gregeon and Monk, power-loom makers in Preston, have furnished me

Mr. Greg4on some years ago was so impressed with the import- ance of preventing these accidents, if possible, that he took out a p :tent for a guard to be attached to the loom which I would prevent the shuttle from doing any damage in the event of its being thrown out of the sled. But the guard was complained of as clumsy and interfering with the free action of the weaver, and was on this account strongly objected to. Mr. Grejpon therefore turned his attention to seine improvements in the loom which would aid the over- looker in his endeavour to keep it in thorough goon order, and his efforts in this direction appear to have been attended with some measure of success. I examined, when last at his works in Preston, a newly-patented appliance which will enable an overlooker more carefully to adjust the crank' wheel of a power-loom when it becomes slightly worn, and this, no doubt, would obviate ode of the causes from which shuttle accidents arise." Referring to the state of trade and the wages paid, Mr. Henderson says:—" The wages here quoted as being paid in cotton factories in Scotland are much lower than those paid in Lancashire. From Preston I have received a return which I think very fairly represents the average wages paid in that district. It is as under:- 1860. 1810. 1875. 1883 Card-room hands (fe- males) los. lie. ills. 14s. Nttil, spinners (men) Strippers and grinders (men) 145. 155. 189. 175. Winders (females): —9 s. 108. 10s. 6d. 'Ne‘ivers — 125. to 16s. 13s. ed. to 189. 16s. to 225. Average per loom he difference in the rate of wages paid to men in Scot- land and England is not great if indeed there is any dif- ference. A self-actor minder—that is, a spinner—in Scot- land will earn on an average 28s. a week, and the amount in Lancashire would probably not be very different. But it is not the case with respect to women and girls; I do not think I am overstating the case when I say that the wages of women and girls will average 50 per cent, more in the textile districts of Lancashire and Yorkshire than they do in Scotland. The unprofitable character of nearly all branches of manufacturing industry during the last twelve nionthe is now manifesting itself by a general demand on the part of employers for a reduction of wages, and the year closes with several serious contests impending between em- ployers and their workpeople. In Scotland generally chi oughout the various branches of the iron trade a reduc- Lion of 10 per cent has been accepted, but in Lancashire a proposal to reduce wages 5 per cent, in the cotton trade has resulted in a strike which is seriously deranging the trade . of the district." An appendix to the report gives a return of the fatal acci- dents and accidents arising from machinery. It shows : Causing death, 401 ; amputation of right hand or arm, 71; amputation of left hand or arm, 54 ; amputation of part of right hand, 565; amputation of part of left hand, 433; am- t pqtation of attly part of leg or foot, 67; fracture of limbs or 'ook:es of trunk, 498; fracture of hand or foot, 325; injuries 1 to head and face, 9uB; lacerations, contusions, and other 1 injuries not enumerated above, 5,624; total, 8,996 1

Wri AND 1-101()Uti • "That tired, sinking feeling" which medical men speak of is umaly experienced by people who fall overboard from a boat and can't swim. A man who was too fond of the bottle, upon reading in a novel that the the heroine's beautiful face " coloured with pleasure," remarked, "Now I know what's the matter with may nose." Hearing people speak of age and appearance, a young coxcomb said one day, "Jerrold, don't you think I look much younger than lam ? " The reply was," It is not your looks, my boy; it is your conversation." SLIGHTLY MIXED. —Teacher : "And what was the reply when Crarnbonne was called upon to surrender ?" Boy, whose remembrance of what he has read is not very clear: "The old blackguard dies, but never surrenders." An ingenious individual advertised that for half-a-crown he would disclose a plan whereby halfpenny postage stamps could be made to do the work of penny ones His plan was perfectly simply. His answer was, " Use two of them." "If you would be truly happy, my dear," said one young lady to another, "you will have neither eyes nor ears when your husband comes home late from the club." "Yes, I know," answered the other, who abominates tobacco, wea- rily. "But what am Ito do with my nose?" The master of his college summoned the late Charles Stuart Calverley one day, and said, "I don't know, Mr. Cal- verley, how it happens, but whenever I took out of window I see you jumping over that wall." " Well, master," re- plied he, "it certainly has often struck me as odd that when ever I jump over that wall I see you looking out of win- dow !" A little cockney girl recently went to visit her grand- father in the country. She is fond of milk, but firmly re- fused to drink any while there, without any reason. When she returned, she was asked, "You had nice milk there to drink, hadn't you ?" "I didn't drink any of that milk !" she replied indignantly. "Do you know where grandpa got it? 1 saw him squeeze it out of an old cow !" At the Pont des Arts, in Paris, is a blind man who carries a board around his neck with this singular sign—" Blind by Birth and by Accident." "See here, my good man," said a passer-by, "your sign is positively distracting. Can you tell us how you happen to be blind by birth and by accident at the same time ?" "Easy enough," said the old man. "You see, I'm blind by birth myself, and I've bought out a blind man who did business at the other end of the bridge. He was blind by accident." A well-known clergyman in the North of England ones entertained a brother clergyman from some distance. The evenine• being unpropitious he asked him to remain for the night. 'At dusk the clergyman asked his guest to step into the manse while he gave orders to have his conveyance ready in the morning. As the visitor entered the manse, the clergy- man's wife mistook him in the dusk for her husband, and, I seizing the pulpit Bible which was on the iobby table, brought the full weight of it across his shoulders exclaiming emphatically, " Take that for asking the ugly wretch to stay all night !" WHY HE LOVED Mustc.—"Your wife is quite a vocalist." "Yes; and I encourage her in it, as far as in my power." "Quite right too; for music is a divine art. I think it is the most elevating and purifying of all arts; and Shakespere was right when he said that the man who has not music in his soul is fit for treason, stratagems, and spoils. Don't you love music ? " "Very much indeed!" "And your wife's singing, I should think, would please you greatly ? " "It does, it does, I assure you; for, when she sings, she can't talk, and—o—" The lady came in at that moment, and the convetsation was not continued. A bunparsa.—The Northern Pacific Railway is but just finished when it begins to put on uniform the same as other railways. An order was recently made requiring all the servants of the company to dress in uniform, and a tailor was employed to get out the suits. To facilitate matters, the tailor started on a measuring tour, telegraphing ahead to all officials—" Take off everything hut your pantaloons and shirt, and be on platform, when train arrives, to be measured fer uniform." When the train arrived, the man would be found, measured, and the tailor ready to enter the train when it was time for it to go. Everything was working like a charm, when he stopped at one of the stations, but found no man waiting in his shirt-sleeves. He found, however, a very pretty little lady, the station-mistress, and her big brother waiting to receive him. He concluded not to take the mea- sure. He then telegraphed to head-quarters—" How many agents have you that don't wear shirts and pantaloons, and where are they located? Answer." . .

"A friend of mine, says a writer in a contemporary, ; "lately asked another friend down to tke country for a day with the hounds, promising him a mount on one of those aicest little horses in the world ' which are sometimes apt 1 to prove a little disappointing. He was represented as being ' a wonderfully clever fencer; you 'couldn't throw him down if you wanted to,' the visitor was informed, though he had not expressed a desire to do anything of the sort, and indeed' had a decided preference for animals that stood up. Was the horse quiet ?—the visitor preferred them that way—was the next question, and the creature's demeanour was de- scribed as habitually lamb-like. The next morning the steeds were brought round to the door, and the visitor per- ceived that the animal he was destined to mount, if it resembled a lamb at all, resembled the most frisky and frolicsome of the race. 'Quiet as a lamb,' when you core to think of it, is an expression susceptible of two meanings. In the face of the curvets, buckings, and other performances, it was a little hard for the owner of the animal to renew his praises. But he was a man of resource. The horse stopped for a moment, planted his fore-legs firmly down, and launched out mightily with his hind ones. The visitor looked at his host, but the host only smiled affably. 'Won- derfully easy kicker, isn't he?' he observed with admire-

HELENS—The St. Helens School Attendance Committee held their monthly meeting at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon, when there were present Couocillors Cook, Hanson, Johnson, and Fisher. The reports of the school attendance officers showed that during the month the names of 2,840 atsent and irregular scholars had been reported from the schools in the different districts; that 35 parmts wire fined the usual sum of be, k and that six boys were committed to the Truant and Indus- trial School at Liverpool. There was no business of Interest. A FORGIVING PROSECUTOR. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Thomas Pilkington, Esq.,,james Hankinson was charged with stealing ,a quantity of pota- toes,' value Os, the property of Captain M•Tear.—On the case being called, Mr. Swift said he had been instructed to priisccute the prisoner on the charge mentioned, namely, that of stealing six shillings worth of potatoes which he had been 'entrusted to sell. But he understood that the prisoner's wife was near her confinement. and the defen- dant seemed to have gone on the 'Spree" for a few days. The prosPentor, therefore, with the permission of the Bench, would allow the case to drop, as the man had been locked up one night and ha 4 lost his situation,—Mr. Pilkington said he would accede to the application, but he hoped it would be a warning to the prisoner. He had had a narrow escape,—The prisoner was then discharged. SAVAGE Anal= ON POLICE OFFICERS.—A brutal case of assault on police constables was heard at the St. Helens Town Hall on Tuesday Morning before Mr. W. Pilkington ana Alderman Cook, when John Roughley, a rough-looking fellow was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C.'s David Marsh and Enock Moss on the previous day.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to being drunk, and said he did net know anything about the as- saults—P.C. Marsh deposed that the defendant was creating a disturbance in Thomarketreet, and when he was requested to leave he would not do so nor would he give his name. Witness then tried to Like him' to the police office, but the prisoner struck him several times, knocked him down and kicked him. He thereupoe called for assistance, and P.C. Mess who came up was also kicked.—P.C. Moss said that he saw the disturbance and went to the assistance of last witness. The prisoner was very violent and while wit- ness was lying en the ground he kicked him en the body several times and also on the face which bore marks of vio- lence.—The Bench imposed a penalty of 103 and costa or 14 days imprisonment in each of the three cases. ALLEGED ROBIERT FROM A DRUNKEN Max.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Harrison and Mr. C. J. Bishop, Thomas Molyneaux, a collier residing in Elephant-lane, Thatto Heath, was charged.with stealing the sum of £1 163 40 from the person of Richard Dawson, on Tuesday.—Mr. W. Swift appeared for the pri- soner.—Superintendent Johnston stated that the prosecutor was not fit to attend that day, and he had accordingly to ask for a remand. The prosecutor, a man named Davis, and the prisoner, had been drinking in a public house at Thatto Heath on Tuesday night, and shortly after closing time the three men, all the worse for drink, • were passing " Knobstick " whoa the prosecutor fell down—not simply through the drink, but in consequence of a stroke he was then suffering from He asked the prisoner to take him home, and promised him 5s for so doing, but the pri- soner knelt upon him and completely ransacked his pockets, taking a purse containing the money from a vest pocket. They afterwards visited a friend's house, and the prisoner gave the purse back but it then contained no money.—Wm. Mills, a lad, gave confirmato,y evidence, arid the prisoner was remanded until next Tuesday.—On the application of Mr. Swift prisoner was admitted to bail, himself in £2O and another surety of like amount. WILFIJL DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY AT GREENBANK. —At the St. Helene Town Hall, on Friday last, before H. S. Hall and J. C. Gamble, Esqs., five lads named John Grady, Patrick APNulty, Patrick, Swift, John Muldoon, and John Barrow were summoned for doing wilful damage to property at Greenbank, belonging to Mrs. Sarah Hill, on the 30th ult. APNulty and Barrow pleaded not guilty; the others pleaded guilty.—Mr. Thomas, solicitor, stated that be ap- peared for Mts. Hill, owner of certain premises on the canal bank at Greenbank, the windows of which had from time to time been broken on Sunday afternoons. On the afternoon of the 30th March the windows of one of the workshops was broken, the yard having been entered from the canal. There had been a very considerable amount of damage done to the property, and considerable difficulty was met wit.. in cap- turing the offenders. Tne defendants were seen breaking the windows, one of the lads haying a piece of gas-piping smashing the windows right and left, the other lade throwing stones. Altogether damage was done amounting to about £3. Owing to the repeated destruction going on it had been deemed necessary to take those steps in order to have a I stop put to it. The destruction of property at Greenbank had been immense, whole houses in some cases having been taken away. The abutters had been removed, the windows broken, the stairs removed, and 'ultimately the bricks had been takes away.—Several witnesses were then called, proving that the defendants were seen about the property, and all the lads except Barrow and Grady were seen break- ing windows.—The Bench dismissed the summonses against the lads named, and fined APArulty, Swift, and Muldoon 55 and 12s 6d costs each, the Chairman remarking that they would put a stop to the destruction going on at Greenbank.

ASSAULT UPON A WOMAN.—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. John Fairclough and Alderman Burgess, Joseph Birchall, Charles-street, an engine cleaner, was charged on remand with assaulting a married womm named Mary Quinn, residing in Sugar-house-yard. The evidence was to the effect that Quinn and her husband ha l lodged together at the house of the prisoner. They wished, however, to have a place of their own, and Temoved part of their farditure, whereupon the prisoner locked the house with the remainder of their furniture in it. Prose. matrix paid Mrs. Birc:iall what WAS due, but the prisoner wanted to be paid over again. On her refusing be struck her with something on the eye, and she went te the In- firmly, where she was told that her eve had been struck wits a knife.—Junn Quinn, the husband, for whose attend- ance the case had been adjourned, swore that he saw a knife in the prisoner's hand.—The prisoner tad that prosscutrix was rushing at him with a brick in her band when her hus- band seized her uplifted arm, causing the brick to fall from her hand against her eye, thus causing the wound —The Bench dismissed the case on the prisoner undertaking to return the furniture that had been detained. HORRIBLE SUICIDE NEAR CREWE.—On Tbursday after- noon a man named John Gibson, a blacksmith, aged 89, residing at Barthomley, was killed on the North Stafford- shire Railway between Radway Green and Crewe. It appears that as the 12-45 train from Stoke was approaching the Bar- thomley level crossing, the driver saw the deceased walking on the footpath along the line. When the train got within 100 yards of him he deliberately stepped into the four-foot. The driver did his utmost to stop the train, but it was im- possible to bring the train to a standstill before the man was run over. When the train stopped, one of the guards went back, and the train proceeded to Crewe. The body was in a horribly mutilated condition when found by the guard ; the head had been smashed so as to be utterly unrecognig• able. It appears that the deceased left his house at 11.40, as if he was going for a walk. His wife asked him to atop as dinner would bo ready in a few minutes. He refused to stop, and she never saw kim alive afterwards. It is stated that for some time be has been in a low state of mind ow- ing to adverse circumstance&

Warrington, April 24th, 1884.

My dear Rigby,— have long been of opinion that the representative of Warrington should be a younger and stronger man than I am. My hop' of restoring my health by residence abroad has been disappointed, and it now becomes my duty to inform the electors, which I do threugh you, that it is not my intention to offer myself as a candidate at the next election. I value highly the position in which I was placed four years ago, and I regret exceedingly that advanc- ing age and declining strength compel me to relinquish it. I acknowledge with gratitude the forbearnce which has been shown to use by the constituency, especially by my own pirty, but also my opponents, from many of whom have received expressions of kindly consideration. In a less public capacity I still hope to have opportunities of render- ing services to my fellow townsmen. Jam,

Mr. O'Connor Power, M.P., has formall7 left the benches occupied by the Irish party, and has taken his seat on the Liberal side M the House as an independent supporter of the Government. LORD GRANVILLE'S CIRCULAR Norul—Lord Granville's note to the Powers on the Egyptian question has at length been issued. It amounts to an invitation to consider the Law of Liquidation and the finance of Egypt. The choice of a !fleeting-place is left to the Powers, but London will ia all orobabaity be selected if the Powers agree to accept, in principle, the Conference thus limited in its functivas and that they will all de so there is little doubt. •

div.head: My Dear Rigby, Yours very faithfully, . J. G. McMINNIES.
div.p: My Dear Rigby, Yours very faithfully, . J. G. McMINNIES.
- Samuel Rigby, Esq., President of the Warrington Liberal Association.
We may add that Mr. MeMinnies was in Warrington on Wednesday. lie was looking far from well, but left on Thursday morning for London with a view to resuming his Parliamentary duties.
THE WIREDRAWERS' STRIKE.

With regard to this strike we regret that we are not able to chronicle an amicable agreement between masters and men. During the past week Mr. Win. Carson, of the White Cross company, has published the following letter from Mr. John Crosfield. yiz.:—" To William Carson, Esq., White Cross Wire Works.—Dear Sir,—At your request, I have to-day examined your sales book, and I find that the prices you obtained in January, 1879, were as follows : Al X v. d. Na. 4,5, and 6, beet annealed wire net 9 7 6 No, 8 net 10 7 6 No. 10 net 11 17 6 Nos. 9by it oval steel wire net 14 15 0 And the prices you obtained in March, 1884, were as fol- lows :

• e s. d. Nov. 4,5, and 6, best annealed wire net 8 0 0 No. 8 net 810 0 No. 10 net 910 0 Nos. 9by 11 oval steel wire net 9 10 0 Some of the men on strike have, Mr. Carson says, stated that the prices which the masters were now obtaining for wire were not less than those obtained in 1879, when the last redaction in wages took place. Mr. Jobe Crosfield had, at his request, examined the sale books of the Whitecross Company, and as the result of that examination the above letter. It was perhaps not too late, Mr. Carson adds, to ask for a little sympathy for the employers of the men on strike under the circumstance disclosed in Mr. Croefield's letter.

At the meeting of the Wire Manufacturers' Association, on Thursday, a proposal was received from the wiredrawers relative to the list of prices to be paid far wiredrawing. After careful consideration, it was unanimously agreed that, although the employers recognised the disposition of the men to treat on the basis of the new list,.it was found im- possible to accept their proposal as it stood; but that the employers are willing to receive a deputation to discass and remedy any hardships in the list, providing that the repre- sentatives of the men come to the meeting with full power to act. The employers are prepared to have a meeting for this purpose as soon as the men have appointed their re- presentatives. The offer on Thursday of the men on strike was a further reduction on the thicker classes of work, at the same time asking for 12i and 10 per cent on the masters' list on smaller sizes.

A meeting of the wiredrawers was held list evening, when, it is stated, considerable unpleasantness occurred in consequence of Mr. Whitham, who has been prominently connected with the strike since its commencement, being charged with arguing in favoar of the employers and against the men. The result is that he expresses hie determination to throw up all responsibility in connection with the matter, refusing at the same time to represent the men for the future.

div.head: SHOCKING DEATH FROM TIE BITE
div.p: SHOCKING DEATH FROM TIE BITE
OF A DOG.

A shocking death occurred at Warrington on Wednes- day morning, when a man named Thomas Brown, a hair- dresser, residing at 24, Powys-street, Bank Quay, 24 years of age, died in great agony, exhibiting unmistakeable eigna of hydrophohia. At an in/linty into the cirenm. stances of the death, held at the Bowling Green Inn, on Thursday morning, before Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, the evidence given below was adduced. Kate Brown, widow of the deceased, said that about two months ago her husband, who knew a good deal about dogs, got an Airedale terrier from a Mr. Skelton, to cure it of mange. The deceased was about to give the dog some medicine, witness holding the bottle containing it le her hand, when it bit the fore finger of his left hand. On the SAM day, on the advice of Mr. Skelton, the deceased had the bite burnt, or cauterised, by a chemist, and the dog WAS returned to its owner two days afterwards. About three weeks ago the deceased complained of a pain in his chest, but continued to attend to his business, thinking it was only a cold. On Saturday last witness consulted Dr. Joseph and got some medicine, but she did not tell him ' about the bite, still being under the impression that her I husband was merely suffering from a cold. On Monday witness told Dr. Joseph that the deceased could not take the medicine, which was liquid, and in the delves presence ; she offered him some in a wine glass. Seeing that be could not swallow it, Dr. Joseph examined the deceased, and then asked if he had at any time been bitten by a dog. Her husband told him about the bits, and then he called witness aside and said that it was a bad case. He said, that he thought it was hydro- phobia and ttAat he had better have a consultation with an- other medical man. Dr. Joseph and Dr. White afterwards examined the deceased, who was growing worse, and pro- nounced it a ba.l case of hydrophobia. Deceased, who had every attention from the doctors, died at 6-30 on Wednesday morning in great agony, having to be held down in bed. In the night the deceased several times held up the finger that bad been bitten, and said "That dog, send it downstairs." James Roughley, labourer, 11, Chapel-street, step-father of the deceased, said that on Monday he was with the de- ceased and alsoduring the night of Tuesday. The deceased was in great agony before he died. He gridned, and spat, and barked, and asked the witness to send tho dog away. A took five or six people to hold him, and he called for cold water and asked them to kill him. He died at 6-30 on Wednesday morning. . . .

Wilfred Skelton, shapkeeper; Sankey, deposed that at the suggestion of the deceased he sent a deg to him to be cured of the mange. The dog was always very quiet, and be had no idea there was anything the matter with it but She mange. The deceased told witness that the dog had bittten him four or five days after the occurrence, and he (deceased) went to the chemist to have it dressed. As far as witness could see it was not a bad bite. Deceased .said that he had been bitten several times before, and witness believed that it was the only time be had the wound cau- terised. Deceased returned the dog to witness. It disap- peared the same day as returned, and although he had ad- vertised for it he had never beard or semi anything of it since. (The Coroner : Perhaps a good thing for you.) Witness had known the dog to have been fighting, but not to have been bitten by a rabid dog. It bad been bitten by a sheep dog, which also belonged to witness. That dog had never exhibited any signs of rabies. The Coroner : Ido not know much about dogs, bat I would suggest that yon keep that dog tip.—Witness: I am doing.—Has a veterinary surgeon seen it? No. The Coroner said that it would be an absurd idea to poison the dog until it was known whether anything was the mat- ter with it or not, but at the same time Mr. Skelton should bs most cautious, in fact the word must was not strong enough, he must be awfully cautious, that the dog did not get at anybody, in case of accidents. The police, no doubt, would make inquiries about the missing dog in case it was I still at large, but ha did not think that was possible. As far as he knew about rabies it would be impossible for the animal to be alive now. Mr. Skelton said that he had done all that could be dote to trace it. It was a young dog, and was a quiet one. Tbe deceased was a dog fancier, and had had it several times at his own suggestion. °The Coroner observed that it was a pity they could not arrive at what bad become of the dog, for the sake of other people. Anyone might COllle across it if it was not dead, but he thought that when •it suffered from rabies two months ago, it must have dick After showing symptoms of hydro- phobia, animals were se quickly destroyed that veterinary surgeons were not given an opportunity cff knowing how long the disease would tahe to kill them. Everything seemed to have been done for the deceased that was possible. The Jury returned a 'verdict of " Death from. natural causes, probably from hydrophobia," the Corona: remark- ing that it was one of the most horrid illnesses and cruel deaths that he knew of.

div.p: A nEFRACTORY PAIIPER —l(o9terChy, at the WarriNton Borough Police Court, before Captain Reynolds and Mr. Ziba Armitage, a labourer, named Martin Noon, of no settled residence, was charged with refusing to perform his task of work whilst a casual inmate of the vao.7,.nt ward of the Warrington Union, and with using malicious threats to James Curry, the warder.—Curry stated that on the previ- ous morning he went to the stone yard and asked the prisoner why he was not performing his task. In reply, prisoner threatened to knock his brains out with the harnmer, and said "I'll do for you when I catch You outside." Mr. 'lackey. Workhouse master, said that the prisoner had been at the Workhouse several times, au& bed al way s been a nuisance; be was about the worse that they ever had.—lie ' was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

A CRUEL lit"SPAND.—A man named Isaac Birkley, a sawyer, of Morris's-yard, Silver-wreet, was charged before Captain Reynolds and Mr. /Armitage, at the, Warrington Borough PUlice Court, yesterday morning, with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, on Thursda7, and with assaulting his wife at the same time and place.—lnspector Norman said that be saw the prisoner drunk in Winwick-street, His wife was following him, evi- dently wanting him to go home. As she was saying some- thing to him primmer made a " punch " at her, seized hold of her hair, dragged her down to a stooping positioni and then "gave it her " right and left with his fists. Witness held prisoner until a constable came, when he was taken to the police station. Witness had visited the prisoner's house on several occasions, and One time he found the wife and four children in a state of starvation, and in a most neg- lected condition.—Prisoner was lined 10s. and costs or one month.

SINGULAR ASSAULT CASE —At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thursday, before Captain Litton and Alder- man Webster, Matthew Statham, wheelwright, 8, Prances- street, Latchford, was charged on a warrant with assaulting Nicholas W. Woodward, a nail manufacturer of Chowhent, on the previous day.—Complainant said that he called upon Mr. Wheeler, blacksmith, Golborne-Erreet, Warrington, to solicit an order for nails, when he saw the prisoner there. Prisoner, with whom he had previously been acquainted, asked him what he wauted there, and afterwards seized hold of him, pushed him against the wall, amd gave him a vio- lent blow. Witness got out of the place, and saw prisoner at the door with a piece of iron in his hand. Prisoner owed witness some money for an order he executed for him (pri- soner) when he was in business as a wheelwright at Lycam, and he probably thought witness was going to ask him for the money.—Prisouer said that the complainant had fol- lowed him about for the money that was due to hirn,,aud had injured his character by telling his employers that he (pri- soner) was one of the greatest villians in the country. fle was fined 5s and costs, El 4s in all. DOMESTIC TROURLBS.—WiIIiam Thomas Meredith, a respectable-looking man, was summoned by Mary,lderedith, his wife, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- .day, for assaulting her on Easter Monday.—Complainant said that her husband had very much neglected her, and frequently remained, out all night. In consequence, when he left the house on Monday, she told him that if he was not back by- a certain time she should go and sea, where he was. He did not return at the proper time and she went to the sports, where she found him on the river side in company with a strange man. He asked her what she wanted, and she said, "I've come for enjoyment, but it's poor enjoyment for me." He told her that she was not wanted there, and that home was the hest place for her. He aleo said, "I'll pitch you into the river, and drown you." She, replied, "I am not afraid; if you do I shall not sink." Her husband and his companion then winked at each other, and said that they were going for a sail. She said that she should go with them, when her husband again threatened to pitch her into the river, and, on her making some further observation, he struck her with his clenched fist on the ftce.—The defendant and his wife had since the assault endeavoured to corns to some arrangement and live separate, hut had failed to agree, and as the defendant now said he was willing to pay his wife such a sum as the Guardians should think fit, the Bench allowed him to take that course, and bound him over in two sureties of £lO each to 'Jeep the peace for si.n months.

ALLEGED, THEFTS BY A CARTE 3.-011 Tuesday, at the). Warrington Borough Police Court...before Mr. Broadbent (In the chair) and Captain Litton, John. Wright, a carter, was cbarged with stealing a cart sheet, valued at Si 65.. the property of Peter Hosker.—Mr. Hunt (chief constdole) alated that the prosecutor was a carrier, at Si, Legh-street, Warrington, and the prisoner was a carter, residing at 94, Longford-street. It appeared that daring the last twelve months the prisoner had done nal,l jobs for Mr. Hosker,.and for the past week or ten days he had been permanently in the employ of the prosecutor.. On Tuesday, the Sth Mr. Hosker and his men wore engaged in removing some furniture to Stretton, when, the cart sheet was used. At six o'clock in the evening the sheet was all right and safe in the cart in the prosecatar's yard, and at seven o'clock it was missing. Information was subsequently received by the police to the affect that the prisoner lad sold a sheet to a coal dealer in Longford-street. That sheet was traced, and had the name "Once e upon it, and it was afterwards ascer- tained that a Mr. Brice had sold a sheet to the prosecater. The prisoner had sold it for 17s. 61 As there were other things missing, which. the prisoner was suspected of steal- ing, Mr. Hunt asked for a remand, which was grantert—The prisoner was again charged, yesterday raorning, More Cap. tam n Reynolds and Mr. Ziba Artnitage. He was also further charged with stealing a ridgthand, a horse cloth,and a home collar. He pleaded guilty, and urged poverty in extenua- tion, saying that he and his children were starving at the time he committed the thefts.—He was committed for three months,

The 4A, DRANE-smitritET. fact is the Curate, the Rev. H. E. Swill-, LIVERPOOL, Near St. John's Market who was left in charge on Sunday last, is a man of peace, and the result was that, not- withstanding the instructions he had received as to what he was to do under certain circumstances, he chose rather to disobey orders than provoke another row. He vas instructed to close the service if the wardens insisted upon singing and organ-playing, but, finding that the wardens were not likelY to budge in the least, he set an example of humility and conciliation by yielding 'lira-, self—deciding to go forward with the usual services, regardless of the fact that the objectionable wardens, organist, and choir were in full possession and having things their own way. There are those who will say, the Vicar perhaps among the number, that the Curate showed himself too weak for the occasion, but if this was a failing it was surely a fai,ing which "leaned t° virtue's side." He has pointed the way out, both to Vicar and Wardens—the via); of mutual concession—and it is to be hope° that, instead of whetting their swords for further fight, they will humbly tread in it The Vicar will do well to remember that, although he is master of the, situation so far as control of the services goes, his vie' tories over his wardens will be more disas- trous than defeats when they lead, as the)' are likely to do, to rowdy scenes, and, finally, to empty pews. It will be but small comfort to him in such a crisis to recollect tha he is "there for life," and that there is nothing to prevent his preaching to the Church fabric when he has lost sight of the, people. The Waidens, on the other hand ought to realize that their position is a yeti , critical one; however popular their policy 0 ; resistance many be, they may find themselves A entangled in the meshes of the law, or, if theY escape themselves, they may unwittingly be the means of bringing harsh punishment upon unsuspecting culprits. There is such an offence as "brawling in Church," and it can hardly be doubted that, if there is 3 renewal of the scenes that have brought St' John's into such ill repute, one disagreeable outcome will be a number of police court, trials. With regard to the Organist,. it woul° seem on the face of it that, having been ap- pointed by the parishoners at the vestrY meeting, there should be no "let or hind: ranee' in the performance of his duties, 10,', when it comes to a question as to what shy." or shall not be done in Church in the regula- tion of divine worship, we are disposed t°, think the authority of the Vicar will he foal°, to be supreme. Indeed, it is the placing of so much power in the hands of one man that makes the mischief, and calls for such a remedy as is not to be obtained so long as Church and State arc held in unholy alliance. The Public Worship Regulation Act of 1874 provides for reference in certain cases of dig' ' pute to the arbitration of the Bishop of the diocese; and, although the law has not generally been successful in its operation, there is no reason why any merits ft may possess should not be brought to bear in the settlement of the Church dispute in Earles- town. Of course, if neither side is dispose/ ' to approach the other they must "grin an, bide as best they can in their tribulation. is a delicate task to intervene between parson and peopJe—almost as delicate as interference between husband and wife. In the latter case, when matters reach the worst pass, the Divorce Court affords the only possible rel:ef. What is now wanred for the relief of rnanY who are suffering in another way is the divorce of Church and State.

Mr. Justice Williams is obliged, through ill-health, to leave London for a few days. Yesterday morning Sir Evelyn Baring and General Graham arrived at Brindisi on their way to London. „ Notice is given in last night's Gazette that her Majesty's birthday will be kept on Saturday, the 24th of May. According to present arrangements her Majesty accom- panied by Princess Beatrice will return to Windsor Castle from Germany on the 6th of May. Mr. Justice Denman, sitting yesterday in the Chancery Division, having received a threatening letter, a detective has been placed in that court to watch any suspicious move- ments of strangers. A New York Herald storm warning says that unsettled weather will prevail over the British Islands and France until My 2nd. Several centres of disturbance are crossing. There will be easterly to northerly winds, with squalls and rain. ELECTION lerrEtraonercs.—The Hon. H. F. Cowper has definitely announced his intention of retiring from the representation of Hertford at the end of the present Parlia- ment. The Liberals intend to bring two candidates forward at the next election, one of whom, Mr. Frederick Seebohm, of Hitchin, has already been selected. Are ABSCONDING ACCOUNTANT.—Mr. B. Humphrey, fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, has is- sued a circular stating that his partner Mr. Edward Mast has absconded, and that, in consequence, the firm of B. Humphreys and Co., accountants, of 5. Throgmorton Avenue, London, are compelled to suspend payment. THE MURDER OP A BOY.—At Newcastle ASSiZeS' ' yester- day Sarah Jane Holmes was sentenced to death for the murder of John Holmes Burns, aged eight years, the son of a solicitor's clerk, with whom she cohabited. The prisoner and her paramour quarrelled and separated the latter taking the boy away. The prisoner subsequently surreptitiously obtained possession of the lad, whom she poisoned with vermin killer. THE PROPOSED EXPEDITION TO BERBER. Canto, FRlDAY—Nothing is known here to confirm the report that the British Government had approved the pro- posal for the despatch of an expedition to Berber. Mr. Egerton has not yet received any intimation to that effect. The report that the French 'commander intended to blockade Canton is semi-officially denied. A MESSAGE FROM BERBER. CAIRO, FRIDAY NIGHT—The Governor of Berber tele- graphs, imploring help and stating that he can probably hold out if he is enabled to tell his garrison that assistance is coming. I learn, however, on the highest authority, that no immediate action 18 contemplated here. MOVEMENTS OF OSMAN DIGNA. SUAZIAI, FRIDAY NIGHT.—OSMan Digna with numerous followers is at Handuk, only seven miles from here. The decks of Her Majesty's Ships Briton and Ranger have been cleared for action in view of probable attack on the town. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House metal four o'clock. GENERAL GORDON.—EarI GRANVILLE, replying to Lord Donoghmore, said Ministers recognised the fact that Berber was in danger, but they felt reassured with regard to Khar- toum, on learning that day from Sir Henry Gordon that his brother was in no military danger.—The Marquis of SAMS- BERT complained that Earl Granville pushed the traditions of the House too far when refusing to answer questions with- out notice being given.—Earl GRANVILLE replied that he should adhere to his usual practice in this respect. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. STOCKTON RAILWAY BILL.—On the motion for the third reading of.the Stockton Carrs Railway Bill, Mr. J. LOWTHER objected, and said Colonel Yol land had in his report said the railway was riot required, and that, as there were two level crossings in the scheme which would occasion danger to a great number of workmen daily, it was one he could not approve. He then stated the proceedings that had taken place in the Stockton Board of Health with regard to the Bill, the result of which was that they now opposed the Bill, as did the residents in the neighbourhood. He moved the rejection of the Bill —Mr DODDS emphatically declared that he had no personal interest in the Bill and defended his conduct regarding it. He contended that the railway was an abso- lute want to the neighbourhood, and that it was opposed only by three or four firms who had persbnal interest in the matter.—Mr. PEMBERTON and Mr. DAWNEY opposed, ' and Bir A. tkrwaY supported the Bill,—For the third read- ing there were 126, against 117, the Bill priming by a ma- jority of 9. GOLD COINAGE —Lord R. CHURCHILL gave notice that he should move the rejection of the Bill for debasing the gold coinage. FLOODS, &c.—Mr. Donsoer, replying to Sir R. Peel, said he could not promise the introduction of the Bill for the Better Prevention of Floods and the Conservancy of Rivers this session. THE PROPOSED RELIEF EXPEDITION.—Mr. A. BART- LETT asked whether it was true that the Egyptian Govern- ment had abandoned the expedition for the relief of Gor- don owing to representations from the British Government. --Mr. GLADSTONE said he had no information on the sub- ject. THE CATTLE BILL.—Mr. DODSON said with regard to the Cattle Diseases Bill, he intended to propose another amend- ment to 01,111.01. Tito amendment would in errodo accept the decision of the ROSSO with the qualification that the Privy Council should have power to admit cattle from one p irt of a country although there might be disease in another part of it. He proposed proceeding with toe Bill. next Tuesday at two o'clock.—Mr. MACIVER gave notice to move the rejection of the amendment.
